findings.title: The approximation theorem used to establish the posterior rate is false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-13-233__I01 — The approximation theorem used to establish the posterior rate is false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem7 and RKHS norm in Lemma6, PDF p.8; cyclic basis(4), p.5; proof of Theorem7, p.20; its use in the concentration bound for Theorem9, p.22. The related claimed uniform analytic-strip bound is equation(10), p.21.

**Claim.** For any fixed \(S_0\in S_C(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\), the paper asserts that there are constants \(K_1,K_2\), independent of n,m, and approximants in its cyclic-basis RKHS with

\[
 \|h\|_H^2\le K_1\sum_{j,k}\phi_{jk},\qquad
 \|S_0-h\|_\infty\le K_2(n\wedge m)^{-\alpha_{(1)}}\log n\log m.
\]

The proof treats the fact that the cyclic basis spans Fourier polynomials as sufficient to obtain uniformly bounded cyclic-basis coefficients. This coefficient/norm assertion supplies the approximation input to the claimed near-minimax posterior convergence rate.

**Error and evidence.** Set all conditional precisions \(\phi_{jk}=1\), which are valid positive values. Define the fixed periodic function and surface

\[
 f(u)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}2^{-3\ell}\cos(4^\ell u),\qquad
 S_0(u,v)=((3+\cos v)\cos u,(3+\cos v)\sin u,\sin v+f(u)).
\]

The derivative series \(f'(u)=-\sum_{\ell\ge1}2^{-\ell}\sin(4^\ell u)\) converges uniformly. Splitting it at \(4^\ell\le1/|a|\) gives \(|f'(u+a)-f'(u)|\le6\sqrt{|a|}\) for \(|a|\le1\). Thus \(S_0\in S_C(3/2,3/2,3/2)\). It is an actual embedded C¹ torus: its xy radius is \(3+\cos v\ge2\), which determines u, and then \((\cos v,\sin v)\) is recovered from the radius and \(z-f(u)\). This is a vertical C¹ shear of the standard torus, not a degenerate nonsurface.

Expanding the paper's normalized basis gives the exact Fourier multiplier

\[
 B_j^n(u)=\frac1{2n+1}\sum_{r=-n}^n a_{n,r}
 e^{ir(u+2\pi j/(2n+1))},\qquad
 a_{n,r}=\frac{\binom{2n}{n-r}}{\binom{2n}{n}}.
\]

Let p=2n+1,q=2m+1. For an approximant with coefficients \(c_{jt}\), the z-coordinate coefficient at frequency(k,0), using normalized Haar measure, is

\[
 \widehat h_z(k,0)=\frac{a_{n,k}}{pq}
       \sum_{j,t}c_{jt,z}e^{2\pi i jk/p}.
\]

The asserted RKHS bound is \(\sum\|c_{jt}\|^2\le K_1pq\), so Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(|\widehat h_z(k,0)|\le\sqrt{K_1}a_{n,k}\). For1≤k≤n,

\[
 a_{n,k}=\prod_{r=1}^k\frac{n-r+1}{n+r}
 \le\exp\!\left[-\frac{k^2}{n+k}\right].
\]

Now choose n=m=8^ℓ and k=4^ℓ. Then \(a_{n,k}\le e^{-2^{\ell-1}}\), whereas \(\widehat S_{0,z}(k,0)=2^{-3\ell-1}\). Since the uniform error bounds each Fourier-coefficient error, every approximant obeying the claimed norm bound satisfies

\[
 \|S_0-h\|_\infty
 \ge2^{-3\ell-1}-\sqrt{K_1}e^{-2^{\ell-1}}.
\]

The promised error is only \(K_2 2^{-9\ell/2}(\ell\log8)^2\). The ratio of the lower bound to that promised error tends to infinity like \(2^{3\ell/2}/[2K_2(\ell\log8)^2]\), for every fixed positive K₁,K₂. Theorem7 is therefore false. Spanning the correct finite-dimensional polynomial space does not control the coefficients in this increasingly ill-conditioned basis.

The same rate proof also applies a real partition-of-unity bound at complex arguments. Its equation(10) says every unit-RKHS element has modulus at most1 throughout the fixed complex strip when all φ=1. Take n=m=16 and the unit-norm element \(h=(B_0^{16}(u)B_0^{16}(v),0,0)\). At(u,v)=(i,i), inside the stated strip, \(\cosh1>3/2\) and \(c_{16}\ge1/33\) imply

\[
 |h(i,i)|>\left[\frac{(5/4)^{16}}{33}\right]^2>1.
\]

Thus the fixed-strip inclusion used for the entropy/sieve argument is also invalid. Both controls show why uniform bounds on this basis cannot be inferred from finite Fourier spanning and real nonnegativity.

**Reason for rejection.** Near-optimal posterior contraction is an explicit central contribution in the abstract, introduction and Theorem9. Its proof invokes the false Theorem7 to obtain the needed prior mass at the advertised scale, and also relies on the invalid degree-uniform analytic-strip inclusion. Correcting constants or logarithmic factors cannot repair the approximation theorem: the discrepancy grows exponentially in ℓ relative to the claimed rate. One must change the approximation/norm scale, the coefficient prior/basis or the posterior analysis substantively. This report demonstrates a false central approximation theorem and an unsupported main rate guarantee; it does **not** claim that Theorem9's conclusion itself has been disproved by a posterior lower bound. Qualitative support and useful fitted surfaces may remain.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the prior-concentration proof, I noticed that uniformly bounded coefficients were inferred solely from Fourier spanning. I computed the basis Fourier multipliers and tested a fixed lacunary smoothness example.

**Verification method.** Read all26pages and the entire appendix; rechecked the rendered original basis, norm, theorem and proof on pp.5,8,20–22. Derived the exact binomial multiplier, the norm-to-Fourier bound and the C¹⋅⁵ embedded-torus witness. The main helper checks exact binomial/product identities and the complex-strip bound; a separate reviewer independently checked2,144 exact binomial cases,126 basis expansions and100 exponent inequalities and confirmed the central proof dependency. Both helpers exited0. Continued checking geometry, computation and all experiments after finding the issue.

**Confidence.** Very high. The contradiction is analytic for every possible fixed K₁,K₂, uses the paper's actual normalized basis and RKHS norm, and has independent original-PDF verification. Numerical controls supplement the proof.

findings.title: The proposed unconstrained prior assigns positive probability to nonmanifold images
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-13-233__I02 — The proposed unconstrained prior assigns positive probability to nonmanifold images
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Definitions1–2, PDF pp.3–4; Lemma5 and its proof, p.5; Gaussian control-point prior(5), p.6; closed-surface claim on p.8 and geometric posterior-feature claims on p.14.

**Claim.** A closed surface is defined as a compact two-dimensional manifold without boundary, and a parametric surface is required to be injective. Lemma5 claims that the cyclic-basis construction gives a closed surface for any control points, so the proposed Gaussian prior needs no geometric constraints to generate the claimed closed-surface model.

**Error and evidence.** Periodicity of the parameters does not make the image a manifold. Already with n=m=1 the basis represents

\[
 S(u,v)=(\sin u,\sin v,\sin(u+v)).
\]

Writing \(\varphi_j=2\pi j/3\), the actual control points are

\[
 d_{jk}=(-2\sin\varphi_j,-2\sin\varphi_k,
                       -4\sin(\varphi_j+\varphi_k)).
\]

The distinct torus points(0,0) and(π,π) both map to0. Their derivative matrices are

\[
 J_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 J_\pi=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Each has rank2, but the tangent planes have different normals(-1,-1,1) and(1,1,1). The difference-map derivative \([J_0,-J_\pi]\) has rank3: the determinant of its columns2,3,4 is±2. The two local sheets therefore intersect transversely, so their image is not an embedded two-manifold. A manifold cannot contain both crossing patches as neighborhoods of the same point: invariance of domain would make each patch open, whereas their intersection is only a curve.

This is not just one exceptional coefficient vector. The implicit-function theorem for the rank3 difference map preserves a pair of distinct nearby preimages under every sufficiently small coefficient perturbation; the two rank2, distinct tangent planes persist as well. Hence a nonempty open set of coefficient vectors produces nonmanifold images. The conditional Gaussian coefficient prior has positive density on that set, and the degree prior gives positive mass to n=m=1. The proposed prior consequently gives positive probability to objects outside its claimed closed-manifold class.

**Reason for rejection.** A Bayesian model that generates smooth closed surfaces without geometric constraints is the paper's central construction. The construction instead guarantees a smooth periodic map, whose image can have stable self-intersections. Restricting it to embeddings requires genuine geometric constraints and changes the prior, conjugate computation and support analysis. Merely changing “closed surface” to “periodic map” withdraws the advertised manifold model and its claimed interpretation for interior volumes and numbers of holes. The failure is independent of the approximation-rate issue and does not rely on showing that a particular published fit self-intersects. It does not prove that posterior regression is inconsistent or that every particular fitted volume is incorrect.

**Discovery method.** While checking the closure proof, I noticed that it establishes equality at opposite parameter edges but never establishes a manifold image or injectivity.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original geometric definitions and Lemma5. Constructed exact coefficients in the n=m=1 basis, verified the identity on169parameter pairs, and computed the two derivative matrices and a nonzero integer minor. Used the resulting submersion argument to establish an open set of failures and positive prior probability. Independent review confirmed the identity, rank and open-mass mechanism. No historical empirical attribution is assumed.

**Confidence.** High. The explicit basis representation and transverse intersection are exact; openness prevents dismissal as a measure-zero Gaussian draw. The distinction between a boundaryless parameter domain and a manifold image is material under the paper's own definitions.

findings.title: Local rank does not imply the claimed global parameter recovery
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-14-241__I01 — Local rank does not imply the claimed global parameter recovery
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 9, PDF page 15, and the first paragraph of its proof on PDF page 16; global Stage-II estimator in equation (12) and Figure 3 on PDF page 10; the dependent parameter conclusion of Corollary 10 on PDF pages 18–19. The generic correlation family is defined on PDF page 3 and the no-nugget convention is stated on PDF page 13.

**Claim.** For an interior true spatial parameter, positive variance, a twice continuously differentiable correlation vector, and linearly independent vectors \(r(\theta_\rho^*),r'_1(\theta_\rho^*),\ldots,r'_q(\theta_\rho^*)\), Theorem 9 asserts that a global Stage-II minimizer satisfies \(\|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta^*\|\leq\epsilon\) with probability at least \(1-n^{-M}\), for an appropriate sample size of order \(N_0/\epsilon^2\) and the prescribed regularization. The estimator is defined by a global argmin over \(\Theta_\rho\); it is not restricted to a neighborhood supplied by knowledge of the truth.

**Error and evidence.** Consider two sites \(x_1=0,x_2=1\) in \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\), one spatial parameter \(t\in\Theta_\rho=(0,\infty)\), no nugget, and the correlation family

\[
r(x,x';t)=\exp\{-(2+\sin t)(x-x')^2\}.
\]

For every real \(t\), its rate lies in \([1,3]\). Thus this is a stationary squared-exponential correlation with positive definite covariance at any finite set of distinct sites; it is smooth in \(t\) on all of \(\mathbb R\). Choose true variance 1 and \(t^*=\pi/6\). Writing \(a=e^{-5/2}\), the true covariance and the relevant two columns are

\[
C^*=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\a&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
r(t^*)=(1,a,a,1)^\top,\qquad
r'(t^*)=(0,-\sqrt3a/2,-\sqrt3a/2,0)^\top.
\]

The minor using the diagonal and first off-diagonal rows is \(-\sqrt3a/2\ne0\), verifying the theorem's local rank assumption. The true parameter is interior. The precision eigenvalues are \(1/(1+a)\) and \(1/(1-a)\), approximately 0.92414 and 1.08943, so the legal Stage-I bounds \(a^*=1/2,b^*=2\) contain the truth. Figure 3's normalized distance penalty is the all-ones \(2\times2\) matrix. Independent zero-mean Gaussian realizations with this covariance meet the sampling assumptions.

Nevertheless, \(t\) and \(t+2\pi\) generate exactly the same covariance, including at every unobserved location. In particular, \((\pi/6,1)\) and \((13\pi/6,1)\) satisfy the assumptions and have identical data distributions for every sample size.

The problem affects actual global argmins for every possible positive definite Stage-I output, rather than only a zero-probability sample. Let \(\widehat C=\widehat P^{-1}\), \(A=\operatorname{tr}(\widehat C)/2\), and \(B=\widehat C_{12}\). Its positive definiteness gives \(A>|B|\). Set \(z=e^{-(2+\sin t)}\in[e^{-3},e^{-1}]\). Profiling the variance in equation (19) gives

\[
\widehat v(z)=\frac{A+Bz}{1+z^2}>0,\qquad
\widehat z=\operatorname{clip}(B/A,[e^{-3},e^{-1}]).
\]

The last expression follows by differentiating the profiled loss; its derivative has the sign of \(Az-B\). A valid global Stage-II minimizer is therefore

\[
\widehat t=2\pi+\arcsin(-\log\widehat z-2),\qquad
\widehat v=\widehat v(\widehat z).
\]

It always lies in \([3\pi/2,5\pi/2]\), so \(|\widehat t-\pi/6|\geq4\pi/3>1\), for every sample and every \(N\). Taking \(\epsilon=1,M=2,n=2\), Theorem 9 claims success probability at least 3/4 for some \(N\); this legitimate global-argmin selection has success probability zero for all \(N\).

Independently, a fixed estimator cannot be consistent simultaneously at the two aliased truths. Their unit neighborhoods are disjoint and their observation laws are identical. At every fixed sample size, the two success probabilities sum to at most one, so at least one is at most 1/2. Increasing the amount of data supplies no information that identifies which alias generated it. The preceding far-argmin construction already contradicts the theorem's existential sample-size statement for the single fixed truth \(t^*=\pi/6\), since it fails for every \(N\).

The precise proof failure is on PDF page 16: after constructing the unique minimizer over a small truth-centered set \(\Theta'_\rho\), the proof treats its being in the interior as implying equality to the global solution over \(\Theta_\rho\). Interior local optimality supplies no such implication. At the exact population covariance, this example already has infinitely many separated zero-loss global minima. Lemma 7's local Hessian conclusion remains valid and does not resolve global identification.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper explicitly identifies Theorem 9 as its main result in Section 3.2, and uses it to support the promised global parameter guarantees and the corresponding conclusion of Corollary 10. Under the supplied assumptions, parameter recovery is information-theoretically impossible, even with the exact covariance and unlimited independent realizations. A repair needs an additional global identification/separation condition with a global argmin argument, or a truth-dependent local search restriction unavailable to the stated SPS procedure. The claimed general guarantee cannot be retained by correcting a proof line or changing constants. Standard globally identifiable covariance models in the numerical examples may remain valid; this finding does not claim those tables are wrong, that precision estimation fails, or that the method lacks practical utility.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma 7 into Theorem 9, noticed that the proof constructs only a local minimizer and then identifies it with the unrestricted estimator. Tested whether the stated local derivative condition excludes parameter aliases.

**Verification method.** Read all 41 PDF pages, including Appendix A and the complete supplementary ADMM proofs and numerical results. Rechecked full rendered PDF pages 3, 10, 13, 15, 16 and 18 against the domain, estimator and hypotheses. Derived the rank minor, precision bounds, periodic covariance identity, closed-form global minimizer and indistinguishable-distributions argument. The primary control script passed 1,000 profile-periodicity comparisons. Independent bounded original-PDF QA separately derived the closed-form minimizer, checked 250 positive definite covariance fixtures and 25,250 grid-loss comparisons, and confirmed the scope and rejection consequence. These are mathematical controls, not reproductions of published empirical tables.

**Confidence: High.** The same explicit valid Gaussian model satisfies the theorem's sampling, smoothness, interiority, rank and precision assumptions while making the global parameter conclusion impossible. The failure is exact and independent of numerical optimization accuracy or the quality of the Stage-I estimate.

The precise proof failure is on PDF page 16: after constructing the unique minimizer over a small truth-centered set \(\Theta'_\rho\), the proof treats its being in the interior as implying equality to the global solution over \(\Theta_\rho\). Interior local optimality supplies no such implication. At the exact population covariance, this example already has infinitely many separated zero-loss global minima. Lemma 7's local Hessian conclusion remains valid and does not resolve global identification.

The paper explicitly identifies Theorem 9 as its main result in Section 3.2, and uses it to support the promised global parameter guarantees and the corresponding conclusion of Corollary 10. Under the supplied assumptions, parameter recovery is information-theoretically impossible, even with the exact covariance and unlimited independent realizations. A repair needs an additional global identification/separation condition with a global argmin argument, or a truth-dependent local search restriction unavailable to the stated SPS procedure. The claimed general guarantee cannot be retained by correcting a proof line or changing constants. Standard globally identifiable covariance models in the numerical examples may remain valid; this finding does not claim those tables are wrong, that precision estimation fails, or that the method lacks practical utility.

Rechecked full rendered PDF pages 3, 10, 13, 15, 16 and 18 against the domain, estimator and hypotheses. Derived the rank minor, precision bounds, periodic covariance identity, closed-form global minimizer and indistinguishable-distributions argument. The primary control script passed 1,000 profile-periodicity comparisons. These are mathematical controls, not reproductions of published empirical tables.

Confidence: High. The same explicit valid Gaussian model satisfies the theorem's sampling, smoothness, interiority, rank and precision assumptions while making the global parameter conclusion impossible. findings.title: The proposed CEC algorithm does not satisfy the limit used to establish its main theoretical advantage
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-14-368__I01 — The proposed CEC algorithm does not satisfy the limit used to establish its main theoretical advantage
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page9, Equation14 and its explanatory paragraph; page15, Section3.2.6's assertion that Equation14 holds for either ensemble-learning approach. Equation5 and the immediately preceding paragraph on page6 define the actual interleaved prediction. Algorithm3, page19, lines2–10, preserves the observed labels and updates only unobserved ones. Equation14 is used explicitly in the variance/bias analysis on pages10–14, including the proof of Theorem4.2, which concludes zero inference variance in the infinite-ensemble/inference limit.

**Claim.** For an interleaved ensemble, as the number of base models and inference iterations both tend to infinity, Equation14 identifies its prediction with the expectation over both learning and alternative partial labelings, namely the unconditional true marginal `P*(Y_i=t_i | X,G)`. The stated justification is that interleaving predictions simulates alternative observed-label sets. The paper then asserts the premise applies to the proposed CEC algorithm and uses it to establish that CEC eliminates inference variance, with no increase in bias, beyond the reduction offered by ordinary relational ensembles.

**Error and evidence.** Interleaving does not resample or remove observed labels. It retains their information even when all uncertainty from training and numerical inference has vanished. The following strictly positive three-node binary joint makes the discrepancy exact.

Take a graph with nodes `u,a,b`, an edge between `u` and `a`, and constant observed attributes. Let `A` and `B` be independent fair bits and let `P*(U=A | A,B)=9/10`. Thus each state `(u,a,b)` has probability `9/40` when `u=a`, and `1/40` otherwise. All eight states have positive probability and the true marginal is `P*(U=1)=1/2`. Train and test graphs can be independent draws from exactly this population, as assumed on page5. An admissible relational learner may return this correct joint for every training set; then the expected learned joint is exactly the true joint required by Equation2. The paper permits arbitrary relational learners (page18), and does not require a positive lower bound on their learning variance.

In the test graph, leave `u` unlabeled and observe `T={a,b}` with `A=1` (either value of `B`). This is a partially labeled graph in the stated setting. Select any realized test graph with `U=1`, which has positive probability, so the notation `Y_i=t_i` here means `U=1`. Every summand in every Equation5 update is

`P_k(U=1 | A=1,B=b) = 9/10`.

Consequently `y_c=9/10` for every number of models and every number of inference iterations, while Equation14 predicts `1/2`. The gap remains `2/5` in the claimed double limit. There is no unobserved other label in this update, so the calculation requires no assumption about applying a discrete conditional distribution to fractional inferred labels, initialization, mixing, or update order. The known labels remain clamped in both Equation5 and Algorithm3. For `A=0`, the corresponding exact prediction is `1/10`, again different from the marginal `1/2`.

The discrepancy also persists with nonconstant learned models. For example, let half the models have `P_k(U=A)=17/20` and half have `19/20`, retaining the same fair `A,B` margins. Their average joint is exactly the true joint, and their average clamped-label prediction is still `9/10`. In the paper's idealized independent-training-graph setting, a learner can choose these two joints using the independent fair `B` bit in its training graph; the strong law gives the same limit with independent model draws. Thus the failure is not dependent on every base model being identical. Bootstrap resampling of training graphs likewise does not change the held-fixed observed test labels.

The reproducible control `helpers/ensemble14368-controls.py` enumerates the eight states with exact rational arithmetic, verifies positivity/normalization and that the two nonconstant model joints average to `P*`, and checks64 finite clamped-label updates across both observed label values, model counts2/4/10/100 and iteration counts1/2/10/1000. Every update has the asserted `2/5` discrepancy. The all-model/all-iteration conclusion above follows directly from the conditional-probability expression, rather than from extrapolating those finite tests.

**Reason for rejection.** The first two principal contributions on PDF page3 are the theoretical framework and its analysis of error reduction; the abstract and conclusion also present the theory as an explanation for the method's advantage. The proof of the distinctive zero-inference-variance conclusion explicitly substitutes Equation14. This witness demonstrates that the proposed algorithm does not satisfy that substituted limit even for a strictly positive correctly specified model with independent train/test graphs and no inference-mixing obstacle. The analysis therefore does not establish its advertised guarantee for CEC. Keeping Equation14 as an extra abstract assumption preserves conditional algebra, but removes the demonstrated connection to the proposed algorithm; it does not repair that central theoretical contribution. Altering CEC to average over different observed labels would change the inference task and discard available information. The empirical curves are not claimed false by this witness, and empirical success on those datasets does not prove the false general algorithm-limit assertion. As written, a principal claimed contribution requires replacement by a valid analysis with materially different conclusions or conditions, warranting rejection.

**Discovery method.** Traced the zero-inference-variance proof back to Equation14 and noticed that its stated averaging over alternative observed-label sets conflicts with the clamped labels in Equation5 and Algorithm3.

**Verification method.** Read all37 PDF pages, including AppendicesA–C and all proofs. Rechecked original full rendered pages6,9,14,15,19 for definitions, the assumed limit, the proof substitution, the promised Section3.2.6 justification and the full algorithm. Constructed and executed the exact finite joint/conditional-probability controls described above. No loop or training-resampling step changes the observed test labels. This finding concerns a false asserted applicability premise, not a claim that a theorem remains false after imposing that premise as an independent axiom.

**Confidence.** High for the mathematical error: exact positive joint, every update and its limit are explicit, and the discrepancy is bounded away from zero. The rejection judgment rests on the paper's explicit positioning of the theoretical analysis as two principal contributions, rather than on an unverified empirical failure.

Independent bounded QA additionally reread the relevant original definitions/assumptions/algorithm/proof pages and verified400 exact positive-joint conditional fixtures. Its scope and checks are retained in `root-bounded-qa.json`; it was not a second complete37page review.

findings.title: A continuous chain rule replaces the finite-jump Bellman generator, invalidating the supplied equilibrium solution
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-17-360__I01 — A continuous chain rule replaces the finite-jump Bellman generator, invalidating the supplied equilibrium solution
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 10, Section 3, Equation (13), propagated into Equations (14)–(16) and Theorem 2; PDF page 11, the constructed solution in Equations (19), (21)–(24). The binary numerical setting is specified on PDF page 13; its value-function interpretation and plot are on PDF pages 13–15, Figure 4. Equations (3) and (6), PDF pages 7–8, define the finite Bayesian jumps.

**Claim.** The paper claims to solve the continuous-time game and construct its unique Markov perfect equilibrium. For sender value function (V(q)), Equation (13) asserts that the expected instantaneous change equals (V'(q)) times the expected belief drift. Equations (14)–(24) use this identity to characterize and construct the equilibrium triple ((p,V,\Lambda_a)). In particular, (V) is asserted to be the sender's discounted expected payoff under that equilibrium.

**Error and evidence.** Observations arrive at finite point-process rates and produce finite Bayesian changes in belief. Let (T_x(q,a)=q+g(x;q,a)) be the posterior after mark (x), when the sender's current intensity is (a). Conditional on a sender existing, the correct generator is

\[
 \mathcal G_aV(q)=\sum_x [\Lambda_0P_0(x)+aP_a(x)]
             [V(T_x(q,a))-V(q)].
\]

Equation (13) replaces each finite increment by (V'(q)[T_x(q,a)-q]). The discarded remainder contributes at order (dt) because each nonzero jump occurs with probability of order (dt); it does not vanish after division by (dt).

This is not merely a possibly loose approximation. The supplied solution fails an exact fixed-policy Bellman identity in the paper's own numerical example. Use the first parameter case on PDF page 13:

\[
 L=c=3,\quad r=1/10,\quad\Lambda_0=1,
 \quad P_0(M)=1/10,\quad P_a(M)=3/10.
\]

Both marks have strictly positive probability under both distributions, all rates are finite, and the distributions differ as required. For (q>1/3), Equation (19) gives (a(q)=1/(4q-1)). Summing the two terms (s(x)) printed below Equation (22) gives

\[
 S(q):=\sum_xs(x)=-\frac{37(1-q)^2}{2601q}.
\]

Consequently, Equations (22)–(23) prescribe

\[
 \alpha=2601/370,\qquad
 V(q)=C(1-q)^{-\alpha}\exp[-\alpha/(1-q)],\qquad C>0.
\]

The constant is fixed by the paper's normalization (p(1/3)=1). Its value does not affect the contradiction.

At (q=1/2), the claimed intensity is (a=1). The two possible observations have the following rates and posteriors, directly from Equation (3):

| Mark | True arrival rate (\Lambda_0P_0(x)+aP_a(x)) | Posterior (T_x) |
|---|---:|---:|
| (M) | (2/5) | (2/3) |
| (N) | (8/5) | (8/17) |

Both posteriors stay above (1/3), so all three values use the same explicit solution branch. Their expected drift is (1/51). Meanwhile

\[
 \frac{V''(q)}{V(q)}=
 \frac{\alpha[(\alpha+1)q^2-1]}{(1-q)^4}>0
 \quad\text{for every }q\in[8/17,2/3].
\]

The strict positivity follows already at the lower endpoint by an exact rational inequality. Strict convexity at both nonzero jumps therefore proves

\[
 \mathcal G_1V(1/2)>V'(1/2)/51.
\]

The printed Equation (16), satisfied by the constructed (p,V,a), is

\[
 rV(1/2)=p(1/2)\cdot1+V'(1/2)/51.
\]

But any discounted payoff function for this very same fixed feedback pair must satisfy

\[
 rV(1/2)=p(1/2)\cdot1+\mathcal G_1V(1/2).
\]

These equalities are incompatible. No maximization or unobserved unilateral deviation is needed to expose the contradiction.

Equivalently, the state remains unchanged until the next observation, whose waiting time is exponential with rate (2). Exact first-jump conditioning requires

\[
 V(1/2)=\frac{p(1/2)+(2/5)V(2/3)+(8/5)V(8/17)}{r+2}.
\]

Using the claimed functions, the right side is approximately (1.2951206584,V(1/2)), not (V(1/2)). The paper's normalization gives the legal receiver action (p(1/2)\approx0.3889718282\). Numerically, the true generator divided by (V(1/2)) is about (0.3440777070), whereas Equation (13) gives (-51/185\approx-0.2756756757). These numbers illustrate the exact strict-convexity contradiction; they are not its sole evidence.

**Reason for rejection.** The central advertised contribution is a solved strategic model with equilibrium strategies and payoffs, used to derive the comparative statics and numerical insights. Its constructed equilibrium triple contains a function that is not even the payoff function of its own fixed policies. Thus the supplied equilibrium solution and value-based comparisons are invalid as written. Correcting the generator changes the local differential equation into a nonlocal Bellman problem and requires a new equilibrium/value analysis. This is not a constant correction or a routine regularity condition preserving the published solution. The finding does not claim that no other equilibrium exists, that the latent strategic model cannot be studied, or that every qualitative benefit of suspicion and source history is false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the sender's dynamic programming derivation, noticed that the ordinary chain rule in Equation (13) was applied to the finite point-process belief updates in Equation (6).

**Verification method.** Read the complete 26-page paper, including every appendix argument. Rechecked the original rendered belief, payoff, Bellman, solution, and numerical-example pages. Re-derived the exact jump generator and the exponential first-jump identity. Substituted the paper's own positive-support binary parameters into the published formulas; verified the rational simplification, posteriors, drift, solution branch, and strict-convexity interval. One hundred exact rational fixtures check the formula and convexity identities; 100-digit numerical evaluation verifies the scale and action feasibility. Independent audit evidence is saved with the review.

 Run the helper with Python and `mpmath`; it uses exact `Fraction` arithmetic for the contradiction's algebraic checks. Original author simulation code, seeds, and raw figure arrays were not recovered, and no original 100-path simulation rerun is claimed.

**Confidence.** **High.** The countercheck uses the stated numerical model with full overlapping support and interior actions. Both possible next states lie on the explicit branch under review. An exact strict-convexity argument proves failure before any numerical approximation, and the necessary fixed-policy identity avoids ambiguity about off-equilibrium filtering or the existence of another equilibrium.

findings.title: Integrating out actions can increase the variance of the complete trajectory gradient
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-012__I01 — Integrating out actions can increase the variance of the complete trajectory gradient
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 9, Section 3.2, Lemma 4 and its proof; PDF page 42, Appendix A.1, Lemma 22 as applied in that proof. PDF page 10 also asserts a finite-trajectory variant. The variance reduction is a principal contribution in the abstract on PDF page 1, the contribution list on page 2, and the conclusion on page 39.

**Claim.** Under the paper's fixed-policy trajectory law, if the score-times-critic random variable has nonzero conditional variance at every state, Lemma 4 claims

\[
\operatorname{Var}_{\tau}\!\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)(\widehat Q(s_t,a_t)+b(s_t))\right]
>
\operatorname{Var}_{\tau}\!\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t I_\pi^{\widehat Q}(s_t)\right],
\]

where \(I_\pi^{\widehat Q}(s)=E_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)}[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\widehat Q(s,a)]\). This compares complete discounted trajectory estimates, rather than merely a single state's action integral. The paper allows finite action sets, a specified initial-state distribution, and any state-only baseline.

**Error and evidence.** Here is an exact counterexample with the true action-value function, no critic approximation, bounded rewards and an ergodic two-state chain. Let

\[
\mathcal S=\mathcal A=\{-1,+1\},\quad s_{t+1}=a_t,\quad
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=\frac{e^{\theta a}}{2\cosh\theta},\quad
\gamma=\tfrac12,\quad s_0=+1,\quad
r(s,a)=sa-\tfrac14.
\]

Evaluate at \(\theta=0\) and use \(b=0\). Both actions then have probability \(1/2\) at every state, and the transition matrix has every entry \(1/2\). It is irreducible and aperiodic, with unique invariant distribution \((1/2,1/2)\) on the entire state space, satisfying the global assumption on PDF page 3. The policy is continuously differentiable in its scalar parameter. Its score at zero is \(a\).

The exact value functions are

\[
V^\pi(s)=-\tfrac12,\qquad Q^\pi(s,a)=sa-\tfrac12,
\]

as directly verified by \(Q=r+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})\) and \(V^\pi(s)=\tfrac12\sum_aQ^\pi(s,a)\). Set \(\widehat Q=Q^\pi\). Then

\[

=s_t-\tfrac12a_t=s_t-\gamma s_{t+1}.
\]

For **each** state, \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t\mid s_t=s)=1/4>0\), exactly meeting Lemma 4's nondegeneracy condition. Nevertheless, the sampled complete-trajectory estimator telescopes:

\[

=s_0=1
\quad\text{on every trajectory},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G_{\rm SPG})=0.
\]

The tail vanishes uniformly since \(|s_t|=1\). In contrast, \(I_\pi^{Q^\pi}(s)=s\), and \(s_1,s_2,\ldots\) are independent fair signs. Thus

\[
G_{\rm EPG}=1+\sum_{t\ge1}2^{-t}s_t,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G_{\rm EPG})=\sum_{t\ge1}4^{-t}=\tfrac13.
\]

Both estimates are unbiased for the true policy gradient. Indeed, writing \(m=\tanh\theta\), the actual objective is \(J(\theta)=m+m^2-1/2\), so \(J'(0)=1\). Lemma 4 therefore demands the false inequality \(0>1/3\); the mean squared error comparison is reversed as well.

The discrepancy is not caused by a nonstationary initial distribution or an infinite-horizon pathology. With a stationary fair initial state, the respective variances are \(1\) and \(4/3\). For the sums through time \(T\), from fixed \(s_0=1\),

\[
\operatorname{Var}(G_{{\rm SPG},T})=\gamma^{2T+2},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(G_{{\rm EPG},T})=
\frac{\gamma^2(1-\gamma^{2T})}{1-\gamma^2}.
\]

At \(T=1\), these are \(1/16\) and \(1/4\). An exact rational enumeration checks these formulas over 88 discount/horizon/initial-distribution combinations, retaining the shared action in the estimator and transition.

The unsupported proof step is the factorization of a current action-derived contribution and the future return after marginalizing out that action. The correct second-moment recursion contains \(E[X_t W(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s]\), where \(W\) is the mean future estimator. The proof instead uses \(E[X_t\mid s_t=s]E[W(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s]\). In this example \(W(s)=s\), so the former is \(-1/2\) and the latter is zero. The action both determines \(X_t\) and selects the next state. Integrating it out separately destroys the negative temporal covariance that made the sampled estimate constant.

For completeness, the same construction can use a real action space: put the logistic mixture masses on uniform distributions on \([-2,-1]\) and \([1,2]\), replace every binary action in the reward and transition by its sign, and evaluate at zero. Correcting the proof cannot retain that general trajectory guarantee: one must withdraw it, substantially restrict action–transition dependence or change the estimator/comparison. Single-state conditional action integration still eliminates that state's quadrature noise, but this weaker statement does not establish the published comparison between complete policy-gradient estimates or the claimed general MSE benefit. Losing this principal general guarantee warrants rejection of the paper as written, while leaving its analytic integration formulas, exploration heuristic and empirical results to stand on their own evidence.

findings.title: The published nonbacktracking objective is neither monotone nor submodular
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-112__I01 — The published nonbacktracking objective is neither monotone nor submodular
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page6, Section3.1, Theorem3; Definition7/Equations3–7 on pages5–6 and Equation8 on page6 define the affected objective. AppendixB, pages29–31, gives the invalid proof. The claimed use in greedy influence maximization is stated on pages2,4,6 and repeated in the conclusion on page25.

**Claim.** For every independent cascade model on a directed graph with independent live edges and transmission probabilities in `[0,1]`, Theorem3 says that its computed upper bound

\[
F(S)=\sigma^+(S)=\sum_{v\in V}\left[1-\prod_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(1-\mathrm{UB}_{\ell,S}(v))\right]
\]

is a monotone submodular set function of the seed set. In particular, it should satisfy both

\[
F(A\cup\{x\})\ge F(A),\qquad
F(A\cup\{x\})-F(A)\ge F(B\cup\{x\})-F(B)
\]

whenever `A ⊆ B` and `x ∉ B`. This property is the paper's express justification for using its deterministic bound as an objective in greedy seed selection.

**Error and evidence.** Consider four fixed vertices `s,u,x,t` with exactly these directed edges:

\[
B_{su}=B_{sx}=B_{ux}=\frac9{10},\qquad B_{xt}=\frac12.
\]

There are no other edges. All existing-edge probabilities lie strictly between zero and one. This is a directed acyclic graph with independent edge trials, so there are no reverse-edge divisions, backtracking ambiguities or repeated-node walks. The same four vertices and the same horizon `n−1=3` are used for every seed set below.

Apply the paper's initialization, recurrence and final product exactly as written. They give:

| Seed set `S` | UB(s) | UB(u) | UB(x) | UB(t) | F(S) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `A={s}` | 1 | 9/10 | 981/1000 | 2691/4000 | 2843/800 |
| `A∪{x}` | 1 | 9/10 | 1 | 1/2 | 17/5 |
| `B={s,u}` | 1 | 1 | 99/100 | 99/200 | 697/200 |
| `B∪{x}` | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1/2 | 7/2 |

Here `UB(v)` denotes `1−∏ℓ(1−UBℓ,S(v))`, including the time-zero seed term. The entries can be reproduced by hand:

- For `A={s}`, `UB₁(u)=9/10`, `UB₁(x)=9/10`, and `UB₂(x)=81/100`. Thus `UB(x)=1−(1−9/10)(1−81/100)=981/1000`.
- The two arrivals at `t` are `UB₂(t)=9/20` and `UB₃(t)=81/200`. Its final bound is therefore `1−(1−9/20)(1−81/200)=2691/4000`.
- With `x` added as a seed, Equation5 makes its later incoming and outgoing seed messages zero. Only the time-one arrival `UB₁(t)=1/2` remains. This is also exactly how Algorithm1/page7 avoids sending messages into a seed.
- For `B={s,u}`, the two time-zero seeds give `UB₁(x)=1−(1−9/10)²=99/100` and `UB₂(t)=99/200`. Adding `x` raises its node contribution from `99/100` to1 and the contribution at `t` from `99/200` to `1/2`.

Consequently,

\[
F(A\cup\{x\})-F(A)=\frac{17}{5}-\frac{2843}{800}
=-\frac{123}{800}<0,
\]

which disproves monotonicity. Moreover,

\[
F(B\cup\{x\})-F(B)=\frac72-\frac{697}{200}
=\frac3{200}>-\frac{123}{800},
\]

which disproves submodularity because `A⊂B` and `x∉B`. These are strict violations away from probability boundaries. The accompanying exact certificate verifies100 strictly interior parameter variations with both failures.

The mechanism is the interaction between the product over different arrival lengths and the seed-dependent stopping rule. For `A`, the bound treats the two arrivals at `t` as separate product factors even though they share the edge `(x,t)`. Making `x` a seed suppresses both later arrivals and replaces them by one earlier factor. The resulting reduction of overcounting can exceed the gain from adding a seed.

AppendixB's proof omits precisely this dependence. It applies a composition rule for monotone submodular incoming functions to the recursive formulas, while overlooking the Equation5 conditions that set later messages at seeds to zero. It also describes the initial `UB₀(u→v)` values as independent of the seed set, although Equation3–4 switch them according to seed membership. Proving the abstract composition rule does not prove these hypotheses for the published recursion.

This counterexample does **not** assert that the deterministic estimate ceases to upper-bound true influence. Exact enumeration of all16 live-edge configurations verifies the upper-bound inequality in all four cases. For example, true influence increases from `6743/2000=3.3715` at `A` to `17/5=3.4` at `A∪{x}`, while the surrogate decreases from `3.55375` to `3.4`.

**Reason for rejection.** Monotonicity and submodularity of the actual deterministic objective are a named theorem and an explicitly advertised contribution supporting its use for greedy influence maximization. Both fail on a small lawful graph, and the computed objective can move opposite to true influence when a seed is added. This removes the paper's claimed structural justification for that application; repairing the proof cannot retain Theorem3 for the objective it defines.

A variant that allows later messages to pass through seeds might yield a different monotone submodular upper bound. That changes the tightening rule and, in general, the computed objective; the published tightness evidence would not automatically certify the replacement. Such a variant needs its own correctness/tightness account and does not make the published theorem true. Withdrawing this principal theoretical advantage or replacing the analyzed bound is a substantive change that warrants rejection of the paper as written. The fixed-seed estimation bounds may remain useful. This report does not claim the paper proves a specific `1−1/e` approximation to true influence, that every possible repaired variant fails, or that a reported experimental ranking has been disproved.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the set-function proof, I noticed that adding a seed deletes later incoming and outgoing messages, whereas the proof treats the message composition as monotone in seed membership. I constructed two paths of unequal length sharing a final edge so that adding their merge vertex removes overcounting.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original rendered definition, Equation5, Theorem3, Algorithm1 and AppendixB. Implemented Equations3–8 with exact rational arithmetic, retained every layer for all four seed sets, independently enumerated all live-edge states for the true influences, and checked100 strictly interior parameter variants. An additional80 small-graph exact-enumeration controls verify the ordinary lower/upper inequalities without conflating them with the false structural claim. The reproducible helper is an unpublished audit file; its successful-run certificate is an unpublished audit file. Independent bounded QA also rechecked original definitions/proof pages, reproduced all four fractions with a separate exact recurrence and live-edge enumeration, and verified100 further interior fixtures. Its record is an unpublished audit file. These are independent published-algorithm checks, not an attributed rerun of original author code.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample satisfies all graph, independence, probability and seed-set assumptions, uses a fixed horizon, and violates both inequalities by exact nonzero rational margins. Its scope is confined to the stated objective's monotonicity/submodularity and the application justified by those properties.

findings.title: The main consistency theorem fails on a bounded checkerbox tensor
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-155__I01 — The main consistency theorem fails on a bounded checkerbox tensor
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 4.2, Theorem 9 and Equation (7), PDF page 13; uniform weights and Assumption 4.2, page 12; Assumption 4.3, page 13; objective (5), page 9. The proof's full-subarray bound (27), Appendix C, page 42, exhibits the missing replication factor. The consistency and blessing-of-dimensionality consequences are stated on pages 13–14 and discussed again in Section 8.4 and the conclusion.

**Claim.** For the estimator minimizing

\[
 \tfrac12\|X-U\|_F^2+
 \gamma\sum_{d=1}^D\sum_{i<j}\frac1{n_d}
 \|U_{i\text{ in mode }d}-U_{j\text{ in mode }d}\|_F,
\]

Theorem 9 asserts, with high probability,

\[
 \frac{\|\widehat U-U^*\|_F^2}{n}
 \leq\frac1D\sum_d\left(\frac1{n_d}+
       \frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n n_d}}\right)
 +\frac{C\log n}{D\sqrt n}\sum_d n_d\sqrt{\prod_{j\ne d}k_j},
 \qquad C=12c_0C_0^2.
\]

Its assumptions are a bounded checkerbox center tensor, mean-zero M-concentrated noise, uniform weights \(1/n_d\), and
\(2\log(n)\sqrt n/D\leq\gamma\leq2c_0\log(n)\sqrt n/D\), for fixed \(c_0>1\). In particular, it asserts consistency for growing balanced three-way tensors with a fixed number of clusters.

**Error and evidence.** The stated tuning forces complete fusion on the following legal signal. This yields an error bounded away from zero, including with independent, nondegenerate, isotropic bounded noise, while the theorem's bound tends to zero.

1. **Model and tuning satisfy every relevant assumption.** Let \(D=3\), \(n_1=n_2=n_3=m=2^{40}\), \(n=m^3\), and \(k_1=k_2=k_3=2\). Put \(s_i=1\) on half the indices and \(s_i=-1\) on the other half, and define

   \[
   U^*_{ijk}=s_i+s_j+s_k.
   \]

   The two nonempty, balanced membership groups in each mode give exactly the paper's checkerbox construction. The center entries are in \(\{-3,-1,1,3\}\); hence even the stronger absolute bound holds with \(C_0=3\). The two mode slices are distinct. The signal has grand mean zero and \(\|U^*\|_F^2=3n\).

   \[
   \sum_{j\ne i}\frac{s_i-s_j}{m}=s_i,
   \]

   because \(\sum_j s_j=0\). Therefore \(A^T\lambda=U^*\). At \(U=0\) all differences vanish, these feasible dual blocks are penalty subgradients, and the objective's stationarity condition is exactly \(-U^*+A^T\lambda=0\). Strict convexity of the squared loss makes zero the unique minimizer. This certificate uses the full expanded subarrays and the original unnormalized loss; it assumes no alternative norm convention.

This noise has mean zero, covariance identity, and independent 1-bounded coordinates, an explicitly allowed M-concentrated example on page 12. For every realization \(\|\epsilon\|_F=\sqrt n\).

   \langle\widehat U(X)-\widehat U(Y),X-Y\rangle\), which proves this property; it is also Proposition 7 of the paper. Applying it to the clean certificate gives

   \[
   \frac{\|\widehat U(U^*+\epsilon)-U^*\|_F^2}{n}

   \]

   \[
   \frac1m+\frac{3\log m}{m^2}
       +\frac{1296\log m}{\sqrt m}.
   \]

   \[
   \frac1{2^{40}}+\frac{84}{2^{80}}+

   <0.035.

\(4C_0^2\binom{n_d}{2}\sqrt{\prod_{j\ne d}k_j}\).

Already at the ordinary finite size \(m=74\), these values are 202612 and 194472, respectively. The bound counts distinct centers without the multiplicity from expanding them into tensor entries. Restoring that dimension-dependent factor destroys the vanishing-bias argument under the stated tuning. This proof diagnosis and the false theorem are one issue.

Its consistency and blessing-of-dimensionality interpretation fail on a fixed, bounded, separated two-cluster-per-mode family satisfying the assumptions, with independent bounded unit-variance noise. A constant adjustment or clarification cannot fix a positive error floor against a vanishing upper bound. A dimension-dependent change of the estimator's weights or tuning, and a new statistical argument, would be needed to recover an appropriate guarantee. Withdrawing or replacing this central contribution warrants rejection of the paper as written. The convexity, some computational properties, and potentially useful empirical clustering can survive; this report makes no claim that the practical nonuniform-weight/eBIC experiments are refuted by the uniform-weight counterexample.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the main theorem, I noticed that the specified \(\gamma\) grows like \(m^{3/2}\log m\) with uniform weights \(1/m\), suggesting excessive fusion on bounded block tensors. **Verification method.** Re-read the original assumptions, objective, theorem and Appendix C; inspected the original rendered pages 9, 12, 13, 42 and 43. Those small solves are controls, not substitutes for the symbolic finite counterexample. A second auditor independently rechecked the original definitions and renders, exact rational calculations, full 216-entry divergence fixture, and nonexpansive Rademacher argument. Review continued through all remaining proofs and experiments after finding this issue.

findings.title: The classification comparator mixes means from one projection basis with observations in another
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-156__I01 — The classification comparator mixes means from one projection basis with observations in another
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 5.2, PDF pages 25–27, and Tables 2–3 on pages 28–29, especially Table 3's Gaussian different-mean cases at training size 100. The associated supplied code is `anc/OptimalBayes.R`, `OB_gaussian`: fold-specific means at lines 47–57, full-data refitting at lines 78–86, and the returned classifier at lines 89–94, particularly line 91. Both supplied classification drivers call this function.

**Claim.** The paper describes OB as the Gaussian-density version of the functional Bayes classifier of Dai, Müller and Yao (2017), with the number of projection components chosen by cross-validation. It claims that the proposed Mahalanobis classifier is generally the winner in its replicated functional-classification study. In Table 3, Gaussian processes with different means and training size 100 give the proposed method versus OB errors of 34.6% versus 45.1% with equal variances, and 22.0% versus 35.7% with different variances. These comparisons support the stated classification advantage of the new distance.

**Error and evidence.** The supplied OB comparator does not use the fitted mean parameters for its final projection basis. It computes them, but then inadvertently uses stale parameters from the last cross-validation fold. This can severely impair the baseline, and repairing just this defect reverses both prominent Gaussian comparisons in matched controls.

### 1. The exact implementation error

Within each validation fold, the function calculates a pooled covariance eigendecomposition `phis`, projects that fold's training curves, and assigns

```r
mu0 = colMeans(xi0); mu1 = colMeans(xi1)
```

After selecting the dimension `J`, it correctly refits the pooled eigenbasis on **all** training curves, reprojects them in that new basis, and computes

```r
m0 = colMeans(xi0); m1 = colMeans(xi1)
```

However, the final returned classifier evaluates its Gaussian log density with `mu0[j]` and `mu1[j]`, rather than `m0[j]` and `m1[j]`. The new curve's coefficients and the fitted standard deviations use the **full-data** basis, while its mean parameters use the **last-fold** basis. R's lexical scoping retains those old `mu` vectors; recomputing `xi0` or `m0` does not update them. There is no intervening assignment that resolves the mismatch.

This is more serious than using slightly fewer observations to estimate the same mean. Refit eigenvectors can rotate or change sign. For example, if a last-fold coordinate has class means 0 and 2, and the corresponding full-data eigenvector reverses sign, the correct new means are 0 and −2. A new coefficient −2 with unit standard deviations gives log density ratio +2 with the correctly transformed means, but −6 with the stale means. The stale calculation is not a valid density evaluation in the new coordinates. This example explains the mechanism; the native controls below establish its actual effect in the supplied implementation.

The cited [Dai et al. paper](https://math.pku.edu.cn/teachers/yaof/papers/2017-bmka.pdf), PDF pages 4–5 / journal pages 548–549, defines the Gaussian density criterion in (4) and estimates the mean projections in the same fitted eigenfunctions as the new-observation projections. It does not prescribe mixing projection systems.

### 2. Source attribution

The authors' arXiv submission [1803.06550](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06550) supplies `Mahalanobis.R`, `OptimalBayes.R`, both classification drivers, other experiment scripts, a README and the extended outlier table. Its README expressly identifies these as the code for the paper's Sections 5.1–5.2. The two classification drivers invoke the defective `OB_gaussian` function. The TeX in the same archive contains the same numerical Table 2 and Table 3 rows as the journal PDF, including the comparisons above.

The recovered source archive has SHA256 `029ecedb5009af5658ce87ba0f95c506fcf5dd3254271afb64cee03b49979856`; the original `OptimalBayes.R` has SHA256 `5b90481ed14638bb54c698ea8b98ca903758c7009a36b648d2c625a882e9a9ea`. The source snapshot predates final journal publication. Original per-run seeds, prediction arrays and a final-run version manifest were not recovered. Thus the evidence establishes a defective expressly supplied experiment protocol, corroborated by matching published aggregate tables; it is not a claim to have inspected the unrecovered historical predictions.

### 3. An isolated native correction changes the result

I ran the original R functions and the supplied generator with 51 grid points, 600 total observations, the original training proportion 0.167 (about 100 training / 500 test), the original ten-fold tuning, the original component search and the original proposed classifier. The Gaussian data use exactly the supplied Fourier expansion, noise and mean/variance choices. Only the final density's two mean references were changed in an audit copy: `mu0[j]` to `m0[j]`, and `mu1[j]` to `m1[j]` **after** the `#Classifier` marker. The original files remain untouched.

For each Gaussian condition I used 20 matched new seeds, `1561201`–`1561220` and `1561301`–`1561320`. Every method used the same saved training and test arrays. Lower error is better:

| Gaussian setting, different means | Original supplied OB | Original proposed method | OB with only final means repaired |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Equal variances | 44.91% | 33.90% | **17.72%** |
| Different variances | 39.11% | 21.99% | **4.71%** |

The mean repair beats the proposed method in **all 20 matched replications in each condition**. The paired reductions relative to the proposed method are 16.18 and 17.28 percentage points, with paired standard errors 1.77 and 1.16 points. The proposed method's rerun means are close to the published 34.6% and 22.0%; the isolated correction reverses the comparison rather than merely adjusting insignificant decimal places.

These isolated runs deliberately retain the original comparator's threshold and cross-validation code, including a separate threshold discrepancy. A separate audit copy additionally corrects the log-odds threshold from 1 to 0 in tuning and prediction, as prescribed by the cited criterion; its corresponding Gaussian errors are 17.38% and 4.12%. A ten-fixture factorial control separates the threshold and mean corrections: correcting the threshold alone does not reproduce the large improvement from correcting the means. The qualifying issue is the inconsistent mean/basis calculation, not an inflated count of every comparator discrepancy.

These are 20-replication targeted native controls, not the original 500-replication runs. They use the supplied generator and R routines under one common R/pracma environment, with new recorded seeds. All 40 isolated mean-repair runs completed with exit 0. The exact source defect, matching protocol and large paired reversals establish the affected comparison's failure; no assertion is made about each unrecovered original random seed.

**Reason for rejection.** Functional classification is one of the paper's two principal application studies and supports its explicit claim that the new distance provides competitive or mainly winning classifiers. An established comparator was materially handicapped by inconsistent fitted parameters. Correcting only those parameters changes two headline Gaussian settings from wins of the proposed method to losses of roughly 16–17 percentage points, while leaving its algorithm and data unchanged. The corresponding published advantage over OB is therefore unsupported by a valid implementation. Although the source edit is short, it does **not** preserve these central empirical results: the comparative evidence and the conclusion drawn from it require replacement and re-evaluation. This warrants rejection of the paper as written. The new metric, valid theoretical properties, other baselines and exploratory outlier findings may remain useful; they do not validate the corrupted classification comparison.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the named baseline and tuning procedure through the recovered experiment scripts, I noticed that final fitting assigned `m0/m1` but the returned density function still referenced `mu0/mu1` from the cross-validation loop. The simultaneously refitted eigenbasis made this a coordinate inconsistency rather than a routine training-size difference.

**Verification method.** Re-read the original PDF's baseline definition, data-generation details, tables and surrounding comparison claims; inspected full original renders of pages 26 and 29 and the independently checked pages 25 and 28. Read all source files and README, checked archive/file hashes and matching TeX table rows, and inspected the original cited Gaussian criterion in rendered page 4 of Dai et al. Independent source/parameter checking confirmed the stale-variable scope. Ran the unchanged native functions, an isolated final-mean audit copy, fully corrected-threshold controls and a factorial ablation. Saved every generated dataset, seed, per-replication error and summary. Review continued across all other theoretical and empirical claims.

**Confidence: High.** The stale-variable and refitted-basis mismatch is explicit in the source. A two-name correction alone produces large, consistent paired reversals under the paper's own Gaussian experiment protocol. The historical artifact limit is stated, and no non-Gaussian generator ambiguity or unverified ranking is needed for the principal evidence. A second auditor independently checked the original PDF, source logic and severity evidence.

 Original and audit-copy sources are under `sources/2020__accepted__v21-18-156/`.

findings.title: The named GP-BUCB comparator omits its defining within-batch variance update
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-211__I01 — The named GP-BUCB comparator omits its defining within-batch variance update
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 7–8, Section 3 and Table 1, identify BLCB as the method of Desautels et al. (2014) and explicitly identify the authors' GPflow comparison repository. PDF pages 11–12, Section 3.2 and Figures 2–3, claim better optimization performance than BLCB; PDF pages 13–14, Section 3.3 and Figure 4, claim better average performance on PPO tuning and characterize BLCB as comparable to random search. The underlying error is in the paper-linked comparison branch's `methods/blcb.py`, lines 35–58, together with `methods/bo.py`, lines 100–136 and 140–190.

**Claim.** The paper claims to compare Optimistic Expected Improvement (OEI) with the batch confidence-bound algorithm of Desautels et al. (2014), using a unified experimental framework. The cited algorithm, GP-BUCB, holds the posterior mean fixed until real feedback arrives but recomputes posterior uncertainty after **each selected pending location**. This distinction allows it to select a diverse batch without knowing the pending function values. Its minimization form uses the fixed mean and the progressively conditioned standard deviation. The paper's principal large-batch performance comparisons use batches of 20; QEI is excluded at that size because of its reported computational cost.

**Error and evidence.** The authenticated comparison implementation never performs this uncertainty update. Its behavior is repeated single-point LCB optimization against the same pre-batch posterior, with a changing positive exploration coefficient.

The provenance and complete call path are explicit:

1. The original PDF identifies `https://github.com/oxfordcontrol/Bayesian-Optimization` as its experimental framework. The [comparison branch README at commit `17a13d6e97920d842e409b6947ae4ed100dd0d75`](https://github.com/oxfordcontrol/Bayesian-Optimization/blob/17a13d6e97920d842e409b6947ae4ed100dd0d75/README.md) identifies this as the code used to evaluate the paper's method against alternatives, and directs users to master for OEI while retaining this branch for the comparison algorithms. The commit is dated 16 April 2018. The current master README also directs baseline users to this branch.
2. [The comparison driver](https://github.com/oxfordcontrol/Bayesian-Optimization/blob/17a13d6e97920d842e409b6947ae4ed100dd0d75/run.py) maps the `BLCB` option to `methods.BLCB` (lines 17–24), instantiates that class and invokes its `bayesian_optimization` method (lines 28–40). It includes the synthetic and PPO benchmark entry points and the Matérn-3/2 default used in the paper.
3. [The BLCB class](https://github.com/oxfordcontrol/Bayesian-Optimization/blob/17a13d6e97920d842e409b6947ae4ed100dd0d75/methods/blcb.py) explicitly identifies itself with the Desautels algorithm. Its acquisition computes the ordinary current GP prediction, then `mean - beta*sqrt(var)` (lines 35–40). For each batch member, `get_suggestion` changes `self.beta`, invokes `BO.get_suggestion(self, batch_size=1)`, and appends the returned location to a local output array (lines 42–58). That array is never supplied to the GP, acquisition function or next optimization.
4. [The parent BO class](https://github.com/oxfordcontrol/Bayesian-Optimization/blob/17a13d6e97920d842e409b6947ae4ed100dd0d75/methods/bo.py) confirms that each inherited call starts a fresh single-point acquisition optimization and does not update the training inputs or condition on a pending location (lines 140–190). The actual GP inputs and outputs are updated only **after** the entire selected batch is evaluated (lines 113–136). There is no outer-loop or inherited pending-variance update that repairs the omission.

In contrast, [Desautels et al.'s original PDF](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/desautels14a/desautels14a.pdf), PDF page 11 / journal page 4063, Algorithm 2 and Equation (7), uses the variance conditioned on all locations selected so far and explicitly computes the next variance immediately after selecting each location. The surrounding text explains its equivalence to hallucinated posterior-mean observations and the resulting reduction of redundant exploration. Thus this is a different algorithm, rather than a choice of optimizer tolerance or exploration coefficient.

A reproducible continuous control isolates the consequence using the paper's Matérn model, input scale and small observation noise. Take the domain \([-1/2,1/2]\), zero GP mean, unit marginal variance, lengthscale \(\ell=0.2\), observation noise variance \(\nu=10^{-6}\), and one observed point \((-1/2,0)\). Write

\[
k(x,z)=(1+\sqrt3|x-z|/\ell)e^{-\sqrt3|x-z|/\ell}.
\]

The pre-batch mean is zero and the latent posterior variance is

\[
v(x)=1-\frac{k(x,-1/2)^2}{1+\nu}.
\]

It is strictly increasing on the domain, so **every** positive coefficient in the released BLCB loop selects \(+1/2\). Adding the constant observation-noise variance, as the source's `predict_mean_and_var` does, leaves this maximizer unchanged. A 20-point batch therefore contains the same location twenty times. Correctly conditioning the variance after the first pending selection incorporates both endpoints; the next maximum is at the midpoint \(0\). On the smooth objective

\[
f(x)=-\cos^2(\pi x),
\]

the initial observation and all twenty repeated source selections have objective zero, whereas the correctly conditioned second selection attains the global minimum \(-1\). The numerical control gives approximately \(-3.75\times10^{-33}\) versus \(-0.9999999999999996\), and verifies the same duplicate-versus-diverse behavior over six lengthscale/noise fixtures. This is a controlled demonstration of the omitted step's practical significance, **not** a rerun of a published benchmark, its ten-point random initialization, its fitted hyperparameters, or its reported rankings.

**Reason for rejection.** Superior performance against established parallel optimization methods is an express contribution in the abstract and Section 3. The batch-20 synthetic and reinforcement-learning comparisons are the main evidence that the proposed relaxation works well at the larger batch sizes motivating the method. At that size the paper excludes QEI and itself reports numerical/repeated-point failures for LP-EI; the attributed GP-BUCB comparison therefore has particular evidentiary weight. Omitting GP-BUCB's principal mechanism for avoiding redundant parallel evaluations invalidates the identification of this comparator and leaves the claimed advantage over the named established method unsupported. The controlled example shows that the change can consume an entire expensive batch on redundant evaluations, while the prescribed method finds a substantially better point immediately. Repair requires changing the competing algorithm and repeating the central comparative experiments; relabeling the implemented stale-posterior heuristic cannot support the published claim about GP-BUCB. This loss of a central comparative contribution warrants rejection of the paper as written. The valid SDP theory, comparisons with other methods, and Figure 1's GP-draw illustration are not refuted by this finding.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the named experimental baselines from Table 1 through the paper-linked source, I noticed that the BLCB batch loop only appended selected points to a return array. I checked whether the inherited optimizer or outer BO loop nevertheless conditioned the GP on those pending locations.

**Verification method.** Rechecked full rendered original PDF pages 8 and 11–14, the comparison README and complete driver/BLCB/parent-BO call path; authenticated all 32 comparison-branch blobs against their Git object hashes. Inspected the rendered original GP-BUCB Algorithm 2. Executed the unchanged authenticated `BLCB.get_suggestion` function body with a deterministic one-dimensional continuous acquisition optimizer and analytical Matérn posterior in `helpers/oei18211-blcb-control.py`; all six fixtures passed, with actual process exit 0. A separate finite-candidate selected-function control also confirmed unchanged conditioning inputs over all 20 selections. Independent bounded QA re-read the original claims and complete relevant source path, inspected the cited original algorithm, and verified six further selected-function controls using an independently calculated Cholesky posterior on three candidates; it agreed with the scoped finding and rejection rationale. These selected-function checks replace the inner optimizer and GP prediction machinery; they are not full GPflow/KNITRO/PPO reruns. The authenticated 2018 comparison commit predates final publication in 2020. No final run manifest, original per-run arrays, final command-line arguments or final plotting inputs were recovered, so no assertion is made that the corrected baseline reverses any particular published ranking or that all published batches contain twenty duplicates. The finding is the demonstrably wrong comparator in the expressly identified paper-evaluation protocol.

**Confidence.** High for the algorithm/protocol error and its ability to materially impair batch selection. The absent update is established by the complete authenticated call path and an unchanged-function control, and the required update is explicit in the cited original algorithm. The final numerical rankings remain unverified; the rejection rationale is loss of the claimed comparison against GP-BUCB, rather than an inferred ranking reversal.

findings.title: The hard-thresholding convergence guarantee is false under its stated restricted-smoothness assumption
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-434__I01 — The hard-thresholding convergence guarantee is false under its stated restricted-smoothness assumption
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF13 Assumptions1–2/Eqs7–8; PDF15–16 Theorem3/Eq14; PDF16–17 Corollary6/Eq15. The proof uses the unsupported gradient-variance estimate at PDF36–37 Eqs38–40. The memory rule and algorithm are PDF11 Definition1 and PDF12 Algorithm2.

**Claim.** Theorem3 and its sequential specialization Corollary6 guarantee geometric expected objective convergence, up to an optimum-gradient error term, for q-memorization hard thresholding. Components satisfy the one-sided restricted upper quadratic inequality in Eq7; their average satisfies restricted strong convexity. Individual component convexity and a two-sided Hessian bound are not assumed for this branch. The guarantee includes the serial case and admissible full refresh q=l.

**Error and evidence.** The expected objective can instead diverge under these assumptions, with correctly initialized gradient memories and strictly positive target sparsity.

Take the following finite dimensions and sparsities:
\[
 N=l=q=100,000,000,\quad k^*=1,\quad k=100,000,001,
 \quad m=4k+2=400,000,006,\quad n=m+2,
 \quad s=2k+k^*=m/2.
\]
Define the matrix implicitly by
\[
 Q=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,I_m-\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/m),
 \qquad x^*=e_2,
\]
and component functions by
\[
 a_1=1-N/2,\quad a_i=1\ (i=2,\ldots,N),
 \qquad f_i(x)=\tfrac12a_i(x-e_2)^TQ(x-e_2).
\]
Then
\[
 F(x)=\frac1N\sum_i f_i(x)
     =\tfrac14(x-e_2)^TQ(x-e_2).
\]
No large matrices or gradient tables need to be allocated to verify the example: its iterates use only coordinates1 and2, and there are only two component types.

All model assumptions hold:

- Every component is a globally differentiable quadratic. The matrix Q is positive semidefinite and Q≤I. Since every a_i≤1, Eq7 holds with RSS constant \(\rho_s^+=1\): the exact upper-bound slack is \((x-y)^T(I-a_iQ)(x-y)/2\ge0\), even for the negative curvature component.
- For an s-sparse vector d, its dense-block part u satisfies \((\mathbf1^Tu)^2\le s\|u\|^2\). Since m=2s, \(d^TQd\ge\|d\|^2/2\). The Hessian of F is Q/2, so Eq8 holds with RSC constant \(\rho_s^-=1/4\).
- F≥0 and F(x*)=0. The optimizer x*=e2 has exactly one nonzero coordinate. F is not globally strongly convex, because Q has the dense-block nullvector; this also meets the problem description on PDF5.
- The optimum gradient is zero, so the entire inherent-error term is zero.

Initialize \(x^0=e_1+e_2\) and \(\alpha_i^0=\nabla f_i(x^0)\). Use q=l, so every memory is refreshed at every iteration to the gradient at the current read point, as in Definition1. Choose
\[
 \tau=0,\qquad \gamma=1/100,\qquad \beta=1/10000,
 \qquad \rho=1999/2000.
\]
The literal printed constant is \(\alpha=1+2\sqrt{k^*}/(k-k^*)=50000001/50000000\). Therefore
\[
 \varrho=\alpha(1+\beta)(1-\gamma\rho_s^-/2)
 =0.998849894977\ldots<0.9995=\rho<1,
\]
and the stated step bound is satisfied:
\[
 \gamma=0.01<\frac1{24(1+\beta)(1+\rho_s^+)}
 =0.0208312502083\ldots.
\]
There is no q restriction from the separate proximal Theorem9 to import into this theorem.

Every iterate has the form \(x^t=e_2+u_te_1\); all other coordinates remain zero. Thus H_k is exactly inactive and cannot introduce a tie or support-selection ambiguity. With full refresh, memories at iteration t contain the gradients at the preceding point. Consequently the exact scalar update is
\[
 u_{t+1}=(1-\gamma a_{i_t})u_t
             +\gamma(a_{i_t}-1/2)u_{t-1},
 \qquad u_{-1}=u_0=1,
\]
where the two curvature values have probabilities1/N and(N−1)/N. Rational enumeration of all resulting paths gives, at iteration5,
\[
 \mathbb E[F(x^5)-F(x^*)]=244,334,099.53179267\ldots,
\]
while the right side of Corollary6, with zero inherent error and \(\|x^0-x^*\|^2=1\), is
\[
 \rho^5\frac{2\rho-\varrho}
 {\alpha(1-\varrho/\rho)((1+\beta)\gamma-24(1+\beta)\gamma^2)}
 =201,800.12260815\ldots.
\]
Even substituting the larger conventional hard-thresholding constant \(1+2\sqrt{k^*/(k-k^*)}=5001/5000\) satisfies the parameter conditions and yields only291,189.92661497. The counterexample does not depend on that typography.

The failure is convergence itself, not just an insufficient initial constant. Write \(K=(N-2)/200\) and \(\eta=1/200\). The first step is deterministically \(u_1=1-\eta\). On the event that every subsequent sampled component is component1,
\[
 u_{j+1}=(1+K)u_j-(K+\eta)u_{j-1}.
\]
At step2, \(u_2=-b\), where \(b=\eta K+2\eta-1>0\). At step3, the negative magnitude is at least(1+K)b. Thereafter, if consecutive negative magnitudes are v_j≥2v_(j−1)>0, then
\[
 v_{j+1}=(1+K)v_j-(K+\eta)v_{j-1}
 \ge(K/2)v_j\ge2v_j.
\]
The prefix event through iteration t has probability \(N^{-(t-1)}\). Hence, for every t≥2,
\[
 \mathbb EF(x^t)\ge\frac{b^2}{4N}
 \left(\frac{K^2}{4N}\right)^{t-2},
 \qquad \frac{K^2}{4N}=624.999975\ldots>1.
\]
This lower bound tends to infinity, contradicting geometric convergence to the zero optimum gap.

The proof's missing control is visible directly: at the initial error e1, the average squared component gradient is \(N/4\), whereas \(4\rho_s^+(F(x^0)-F(x^*))=1\). A one-sided upper curvature bound cannot control this squared-gradient variance. The proximal branch separately imposes individual convexity (PDF6) and gradient Lipschitzness (PDF18); those are not global assumptions for the hard-thresholding branch.

 The `positive_target_sparsity_embedding` entry in unpublished audit files contains exact fractions for all expectations, parameter conditions and bounds. The certificate also checks a separate3-dimensional, k*=0 fixture by full vector hard-thresholding path enumeration; it violates the bound at iteration5 and has a divergent lower bound with growth factor277.7777666. The positive-sparsity embedding above avoids relying on that boundary case. These are independent mathematical implementations, with no historical author-code attribution claim.

**Reason for rejection.** Geometric convergence of AsySGHT-qM is explicitly one of the paper's three principal contributions in the abstract, contribution list PDF7, and conclusion PDF48–49. It fails even without asynchronous interference and with exact, freshly updated memories. Enlarging a constant cannot fix a divergent expectation. Requiring individual convexity removes allowed component functions; replacing Eq7 by an absolute restricted gradient-Lipschitz condition changes the relevant curvature from1 to N/2−1, an unbounded factor, and materially changes the allowed step/rate guarantee. The paper as written therefore does not establish this central convergence contribution. This construction does not claim that the separate proximal/general-SGD results or the plotted logistic experiments fail.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the hard-thresholding variance estimate, noticed that the component assumption bounds curvature only from above, but the proof uses a squared-gradient bound requiring control of negative curvature.

**Verification method.** Read the full53-page paper and its complete proofs, then rechecked rendered assumptions, algorithms and theorem formulas. Verified restricted eigenvalues and every parameter condition; checked exact path expectations and an independent second-moment recursion. Proved the infinite rare-path lower bounds by induction. Independently checked the positive-sparsity embedding proposed during a second review, including both interpretations of the hard-thresholding constant.

Two additional reviewers performed bounded independent checks against the original PDF and completed their helpers with exit code0. The root review independently enumerated256 positive-sparsity vector paths through iteration8, checked a separate moment matrix, and verified the all-time rare-path induction. The Fine review independently checked128 three-dimensional paths, moments,80 rare prefixes, and the positive-sparsity embedding. Both supported the mathematical contradiction and rejection assessment. These were issue checks, not additional full-paper reviews. Their records are `root-bounded-qa.{json,md,log}` and `fine-bounded-qa.{json,md,log}` in the evidence directory above.

**Confidence.** High: explicit finite quadratics, exact initialized memories, exact probabilities, rational path expectations and an infinite-path induction establish the contradiction. The rejection assessment concerns the advertised hard-thresholding convergence contribution and makes no empirical attribution claim.
