Initialize \(x^0=e_1+e_2\) and \(\alpha_i^0=\nabla f_i(x^0)\). Use q=l, so every memory is refreshed at every iteration to the gradient at the current read point, as in Definition1. Choose

\[ \tau=0,\qquad \gamma=1/100,\qquad \beta=1/10000, \qquad \rho=1999/2000. \]
The literal printed constant is \(\alpha=1+2\sqrt{k^*}/(k-k^*)=50000001/50000000\). Therefore
\[ \varrho=\alpha(1+\beta)(1-\gamma\rho_s^-/2) =0.998849894977\ldots<0.9995=\rho<1, \]
and the stated step bound is satisfied:
\[ \gamma=0.01<\frac1{24(1+\beta)(1+\rho_s^+)} =0.0208312502083\ldots. \]
There is no q restriction from the separate proximal Theorem9 to import into this theorem.

Every iterate has the form \(x^t=e_2+u_te_1\); all other coordinates remain zero. Thus H_k is exactly inactive and cannot introduce a tie or support-selection ambiguity. With full refresh, memories at iteration t contain the gradients at the preceding point. Consequently the exact scalar update is

\[ u_{t+1}=(1-\gamma a_{i_t})u_t +\gamma(a_{i_t}-1/2)u_{t-1}, \qquad u_{-1}=u_0=1, \]
where the two curvature values have probabilities1/N and(N−1)/N. Rational enumeration of all resulting paths gives, at iteration5,
\[ \mathbb E[F(x^5)-F(x^*)]=244,334,099.53179267\ldots, \]
while the right side of Corollary6, with zero inherent error and \(\|x^0-x^*\|^2=1\), is
\[ \rho^5\frac{2\rho-\varrho} {\alpha(1-\varrho/\rho)((1+\beta)\gamma-24(1+\beta)\gamma^2)} =201,800.12260815\ldots. \]
Even substituting the larger conventional hard-thresholding constant \(1+2\sqrt{k^*/(k-k^*)}=5001/5000\) satisfies the parameter conditions and yields only291,189.92661497. The counterexample does not depend on that typography.

The failure is convergence itself, not just an insufficient initial constant. Write \(K=(N-2)/200\) and \(\eta=1/200\). The first step is deterministically \(u_1=1-\eta\). On the event that every subsequent sampled component is component1,

\[ u_{j+1}=(1+K)u_j-(K+\eta)u_{j-1}. \]
At step2, \(u_2=-b\), where \(b=\eta K+2\eta-1>0\). At step3, the negative magnitude is at least(1+K)b. Thereafter, if consecutive negative magnitudes are v_j≥2v_(j−1)>0, then
\[ v_{j+1}=(1+K)v_j-(K+\eta)v_{j-1} \ge(K/2)v_j\ge2v_j. \]
The prefix event through iteration t has probability \(N^{-(t-1)}\). Hence, for every t≥2,
\[ \mathbb EF(x^t)\ge\frac{b^2}{4N} \left(\frac{K^2}{4N}\right)^{t-2}, \qquad \frac{K^2}{4N}=624.999975\ldots>1. \]
This lower bound tends to infinity, contradicting geometric convergence to the zero optimum gap.

The proof's missing control is visible directly: at the initial error e1, the average squared component gradient is \(N/4\), whereas \(4\rho_s^+(F(x^0)-F(x^*))=1\). A one-sided upper curvature bound cannot control this squared-gradient variance. The proximal branch separately imposes individual convexity (PDF6) and gradient Lipschitzness (PDF18); those are not global assumptions for the hard-thresholding branch.

The positive_target_sparsity_embedding entry in unpublished audit files contains exact fractions for all expectations, parameter conditions and bounds. The certificate also checks a separate3-dimensional, k*=0 fixture by full vector hard-thresholding path enumeration; it violates the bound at iteration5 and has a divergent lower bound with growth factor277.7777666. The positive-sparsity embedding above avoids relying on that boundary case. These are independent mathematical implementations, with no historical author-code attribution claim.

Reason for rejection. Geometric convergence of AsySGHT-qM is explicitly one of the paper's three principal contributions in the abstract, contribution list PDF7, and conclusion PDF48–49. It fails even without asynchronous interference and with exact, freshly updated memories. Enlarging a constant cannot fix a divergent expectation. Requiring individual convexity removes allowed component functions; replacing Eq7 by an absolute restricted gradient-Lipschitz condition changes the relevant curvature from1 to N/2−1, an unbounded factor, and materially changes the allowed step/rate guarantee. The paper as written therefore does not establish this central convergence contribution. This construction does not claim that the separate proximal/general-SGD results or the plotted logistic experiments fail.

Discovery method. While tracing the hard-thresholding variance estimate, noticed that the component assumption bounds curvature only from above, but the proof uses a squared-gradient bound requiring control of negative curvature.

Verification method. Read the full53-page paper and its complete proofs, then rechecked rendered assumptions, algorithms and theorem formulas. Verified restricted eigenvalues and every parameter condition; checked exact path expectations and an independent second-moment recursion. Proved the infinite rare-path lower bounds by induction. Independently checked the positive-sparsity embedding proposed during a second review, including both interpretations of the hard-thresholding constant.

Two additional reviewers performed bounded independent checks against the original PDF and completed their helpers with exit code0. The root review independently enumerated256 positive-sparsity vector paths through iteration8, checked a separate moment matrix, and verified the all-time rare-path induction. The Fine review independently checked128 three-dimensional paths, moments,80 rare prefixes, and the positive-sparsity embedding. Both supported the mathematical contradiction and rejection assessment. These were issue checks, not additional full-paper reviews. Their records are root-bounded-qa.{json,md,log} and fine-bounded-qa.{json,md,log} in the evidence directory above.

Confidence. High: explicit finite quadratics, exact initialized memories, exact probabilities, rational path expectations and an infinite-path induction establish the contradiction. The rejection assessment concerns the advertised hard-thresholding convergence contribution and makes no empirical attribution claim.

findings.title: The default hierarchical model has no normalized posterior
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-514__I01 — The default hierarchical model has no normalized posterior
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF6 Eqs7–8, PDF7 global-shrinkage prior and Eqs9–11, PDF8 Section3.1/Eqs12–18, and PDF33 Eqs79–83. The main affected claim is the exact-posterior/KL variational-inference construction in Section3.1. The default global update is PDF10 Eqs28–29.

**Claim.** BISN treats the offdiagonal precision-matrix entries as normal variables with local and global shrinkage parameters. For each edge,

\[
 K_{jk}\mid\lambda_{jk},\omega\sim N(0,(\omega\lambda_{jk})^{-1}),
 \qquad p(\lambda_{jk})=\frac1{\pi\sqrt{\lambda_{jk}}(1+\lambda_{jk})}.
\]

The diagonal entries have flat priors and the default global prior is \(p(\omega)\propto1/\omega\). Section3.1 then claims to approximate the exact joint posterior \(p(L,D,\lambda,\omega\mid X)\) by minimizing KL divergence, equivalently maximizing its evidence lower bound. The prior is repeated explicitly in AppendixB/Eq83. The footnote on PDF7 offers an optional informative prior; it does not replace or restrict the default construction.

**Error and evidence.** The default posterior has infinite total mass. This is a failure of posterior propriety, not merely use of an improper prior whose posterior might still be proper.

Consider two variables and the four observed rows

\[
 X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&0\\0&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

They have mean zero and full-rank empirical covariance \(I_2/2\). For
\(K=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&b\end{pmatrix}\), the exact zero-mean Gaussian likelihood is

\[
 L(K)=(2\pi)^{-4}(ab-c^2)^2e^{-(a+b)}.
\]

Express the joint density in precision-matrix coordinates. Apart from the fixed positive multiplier attached to the flat priors, its density is

\[
 L(K)\sqrt{\frac{\omega\lambda}{2\pi}}
 e^{-\omega\lambda c^2/2}
 \frac1{\pi\sqrt\lambda(1+\lambda)}\frac1\omega,
\]

integrated against \(da\,db\,dc\,d\lambda\,d\omega\) on the positive-definite cone. Restrict integration to

\[
 1\le a,b,\lambda\le2,\qquad \omega\ge4,
 \qquad |c|\le\omega^{-1/2}.
\]

Every matrix in this region is strictly positive definite, since \(ab-c^2\ge3/4\). On this region,

\[
 L(K)\ge(2\pi)^{-4}\frac9{16}e^{-4},\quad
 \sqrt{\frac{\omega\lambda}{2\pi}}e^{-\omega\lambda c^2/2}
 \ge\frac{\sqrt\omega}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-1},\quad
 p(\lambda)\ge\frac1{3\pi\sqrt2}.
\]

The allowed c interval has length \(2/\sqrt\omega\), which cancels the normal density's \(\sqrt\omega\) factor. Tonelli's theorem therefore gives the following lower bound on the evidence/normalizing integral:

\[
 Z\ge C\int_4^\infty\frac{d\omega}{\omega}=\infty,
 \qquad
 C=(2\pi)^{-4}\frac9{16}e^{-5}
       \frac2{3\pi\sqrt2\sqrt{2\pi}}>0.
\]

Thus there is no probability distribution to use as the claimed exact joint posterior. In fact, the problem is not specific to this data set: for any finite two-variable data set, the Gaussian likelihood has a strictly positive minimum on the compact positive-definite region \(a,b\in[1,2], |c|\le1/2\). The same tail argument applies. Increasing sample size does not resolve it.

The LDL transformation does not remove the divergence. On the displayed region its parameters are \(D_{11}=a>0\), \(L_{21}=c/a\), and \(D_{22}=b-c^2/a>0\). Its Jacobian determinant is \(a\), exactly as Eq11 predicts. Changing the integral back to K coordinates introduces the inverse factor \(1/a\), so these factors cancel. The argument already stays strictly inside the positive-definite cone. Eqs9,13,79 and83 include no additional \(\omega\)-dependent truncation normalizer or cutoff that could change this tail.

 Its outputs in unpublished audit files include1,000 exact rational region/LDL checks, direct quadrature of the restricted marginal and30 successive logarithmic omega intervals whose mass approaches a strictly positive constant. Those calculations corroborate the analytic lower bound; the assertion of infinite mass follows from the displayed integral, not a finite numerical approximation.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's main contribution is a tuning-free **Bayesian** sparse-network inference method, justified as a tractable approximation to the exact posterior. Under its default model, that posterior does not exist for even ordinary full-rank Gaussian data. Consequently the claimed KL target and finite data-evidence interpretation cannot justify the main inference procedure or its adaptive posterior shrinkage. This affects the model underlying every application, rather than an auxiliary theorem constant or a pathological approximation setting.

A proper global prior or a finite truncation would define a different hierarchical model and change the global-shrinkage update. For example, a proper Gamma prior with shape/rate \(a_0,b_0>0\) changes the variational global shape from \(p(p-1)/4\) to \(a_0+p(p-1)/4\), and adds \(b_0\) to its rate. That changes the adaptive shrinkage feeding the local parameters and graph selection. The paper supplies neither such a default model nor validation of its resulting outputs. It needs a substantive model/inference revision before the claimed Bayesian contribution can be accepted.

This finding does not assert that the numerical graph estimates must be inaccurate, that the unnormalized finite mean-field functional cannot be computed, that its supremum is necessarily infinite, or that the separate generic conditional DRSG convergence theorem is false. The LDL algebra, positive definiteness of variational draws and potential utility of the algorithm as a heuristic may remain. They do not supply the missing exact posterior.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the hierarchy underlying automatic sparsity selection, I noticed that the global log-uniform precision prior places infinite mass on arbitrarily strong shrinkage, while the Gaussian likelihood remains positive near diagonal precision matrices.

**Verification method.** Read all54 original pages and all AppendicesA–H, rechecked the prior, factorization, variational target and repeated appendix prior in the original rendered PDF, and constructed the explicit lower bound above. Checked every positivity and measure/Jacobian condition with exact rational arithmetic and independent quadrature. A second reviewer independently inspected the original prior pages and reproduced the divergent-tail certificate. The released author code was inspected for a hidden proper-prior term or cutoff; its global shape/update contains neither. Its first commit is after the journal publication month, so code inspection is corroboration and is not used to attribute a specific historical experiment.

**Confidence.** High. The evidence is an explicit positive lower bound on the actual normalizing integral, with a legal finite full-rank data set, correct LDL measure, original-page verification and independent mathematical confirmation. The rejection assessment is confined to the central default posterior-inference claim.

findings.title: The NOAA PPCA baseline omits conditional-mean centering, creating the reported predictive advantage
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-595__I01 — The NOAA PPCA baseline omits conditional-mean centering, creating the reported predictive advantage
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF23, Table4 and Section5.2; PDF24, the comparison of PPCA and GPPCA accuracy and interval coverage; PDF37–38, AppendixD's PPCA protocol. The formula against which the implementation can be checked is the paper's Gaussian conditional mean in Eq24, PDF11. Cited repository `MengyangGu/GPPCA`, commit `bc0c64f31cbe754b9a18ad82b33220846ba40572` dated2019-12-14, file `Real_example_2/2019_Sep_NOAA_gridded_temp_GPPCA_shared_cov_month_interpolation.R`, lines418–450, especially445.

**Claim.** On24,000 held-out NOAA temperatures, Table4 compares PPCA and GPPCA using the same50 or100 latent factors, with either estimated measurement variance or variance fixed at0.1. It reports lower RMSE for GPPCA in every corresponding comparison and, with fixed measurement variance, approximately nominal95% coverage for GPPCA versus substantially lower coverage for PPCA. Section5.2 attributes the improvement to GPPCA's treatment of temporal correlation and linear trend. AppendixD says the PPCA training matrix is centered, PPCA loadings are estimated, the predictive distribution is obtained similarly to Eq24, and the empirical mean is added back.

**Error and evidence.** For a Gaussian PPCA model partitioned into observed coordinates1 and unobserved coordinates2, let training means beμ1,μ2 and covariance blocksC11,C21,C22. Its conditional predictor must be

\[
\widehat y_2=\mu_2+C_{21}C_{11}^{-1}(y_1-\mu_1).
\]

This is exactly the subtraction appearing in the paper's Eq24. The code computes the covariance from centered training data, but then uses

```r
pred_ppca_conditional_mean = Useful_block %*% output_partial_obs +
  matrix(row_mean_output[index_testing_loc], ...)
```

Here `Useful_block=C21 C11^{-1}`, and `output_partial_obs` contains the raw observed temperatures. The code has not subtracted `row_mean_output[-index_testing_loc]`. Consequently it adds the spurious termC21 C11^{-1}μ1 to every prediction at the held-out coordinates. Restoring the mean of the predicted variables does not remove this term.

A small exact example already demonstrates the error: take training mean(1,2), covariance[[2,1],[1,2]], and observed first coordinatey1=1. This is a valid rank-one PPCA covariance, with loading(1,1) and noise variance1. Its correct conditional second-coordinate mean is2; the implemented predictor gives2.5.

The practical consequence can be checked on the released data and split, rather than inferred from that example. The repository's NOAA RDS was downloaded at the pinned commit and verified against Git blobSHA1 `83713a6469cc45da602e27cad53c02b8b0f7facc`. Using `set.seed(1)` and R's `Rejection` sampling reproduces the original code's four PPCA RMSE, coverage and interval-length triples to their recorded precision, including its in-file higher-precision comments. In the following table, the corrected run changes only the conditional mean by subtracting `Useful_block %*% μ1`; the fitted covariance, factor count, noise choice, split and interval widths are identical.

| Factors; measurement variance | Published PPCA RMSE, independently reproduced | PPCA RMSE after centering fix | Published GPPCA RMSE | PPCA95% coverage: original→corrected | Published GPPCA coverage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|50; estimated|0.6203871994|0.3854466188|0.386|0.677208→0.887000|0.870|
|100; estimated|0.6024701351|0.3091523482|0.320|0.525125→0.891167|0.772|
|50; fixed0.1|0.6173094929|0.3842721954|0.385|0.765458→0.932500|0.933|
|100; fixed0.1|0.5852149243|0.3045533117|0.314|0.819000→0.976250|0.977|

The fixed-variance comparisons avoid any question about how PPCA's noise estimator was implemented. For100 factors, the original inflated RMSE0.5852 falls to0.3046, below GPPCA's reported0.314; its coverage rises from81.9% to97.625%, essentially the same as GPPCA's97.7%. At50 factors the apparent coverage deficit similarly disappears. The unchanged interval lengths are1.321160506 and1.396626647, respectively. The omitted mean term has RMS0.4867064 and0.5011674 in these fixed-variance runs, large enough to dominate the original error. Thus the baseline's poor calibration here does not support the claimed modeling advantage.

**Reason for rejection.** A central empirical contribution is improved prediction and uncertainty quantification for correlated outputs relative to PPCA, the method GPPCA is designed to generalize. The NOAA study is the paper's large real-data demonstration of that contribution. Its PPCA comparison implements a different, biased predictor; the released artifacts reproduce the published poor baseline values, and a one-term correction removes or reverses the claimed advantage in every matched RMSE comparison. The paper's explanation that the observed accuracy and fixed-noise coverage gains establish the benefit of temporal correlation/trend is therefore unsupported by this experiment. This is a demonstrated invalid headline comparison, not a request for additional experiments. The covariance identities, constrained likelihood construction, other simulation results and DIAMOND application are not refuted by this finding; they do not make the paper's real-data comparative contribution valid as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Eq24 and AppendixD to the published NOAA driver, noticed that the PPCA covariance used centered training data but its conditional-mean multiplication used uncentered observations.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered PDF11/23/24/37/38 and the pinned source; derived the conditional mean directly; verified source/data Git hashes; executed the unchanged original PPCA matrix expressions in native R; reproduced all four reported baseline metric triples; then changed only the missing mean subtraction and recomputed the same held-out metrics. Checked the older `Rounding` sampling convention separately as a robustness control, without treating it as the matching historical split.

The independent parent check regenerates the split and SVD, conditions through the latent-factor posterior rather than the covariance-block inverse, and confirms both fixed-noise cases to 1e−10. Its scope is this issue, not a second full-paper review.

 This execution uses only base-R linear algebra and the released data. It does not require running the GPPCA optimizer or external GP packages. GPPCA values above are the paper's reported values, not a claimed fresh full-pipeline rerun. No final-run manifest is available, but the prepublication driver, exact dataset and exact higher-precision matches of all four baseline triples provide direct attribution of the defective comparison.

**Confidence: High.** The missing subtraction follows directly from Gaussian conditioning and is visible in authenticated source. Native reproduction matches the published baseline values and shows the consequence of the isolated correction on the same held-out observations.

The omitted mean term has RMS0.4867064 and0.5011674 in these fixed-variance runs, large enough to dominate the original error. Thus the baseline's poor calibration here does not support the claimed modeling advantage.

Reason for rejection. A central empirical contribution is improved prediction and uncertainty quantification for correlated outputs relative to PPCA, the method GPPCA is designed to generalize. The NOAA study is the paper's large real-data demonstration of that contribution. Its PPCA comparison implements a different, biased predictor; the released artifacts reproduce the published poor baseline values, and a one-term correction removes or reverses the claimed advantage in every matched RMSE comparison. The paper's explanation that the observed accuracy and fixed-noise coverage gains establish the benefit of temporal correlation/trend is therefore unsupported by this experiment. Verification method. GPPCA values above are the paper's reported values, not a claimed fresh full-pipeline rerun. No final-run manifest is available, but the prepublication driver, exact dataset and exact higher-precision matches of all four baseline triples provide direct attribution of the defective comparison.

findings.title: The MVU rate uses a bound for a different distance matrix
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-720__I01 — The MVU rate uses a bound for a different distance matrix
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 16, Section 5.2, Corollary 6 and equations (38)–(40), especially equation (39). The claimed rate is interpreted in the numerical experiment on PDF page 18 and compared with Isomap on pages 20–21.

**Claim.** For a manifold isometric to a convex domain, with positive reach, a sufficiently dense sample, a connected radius graph, and the stated smallness condition on

\[
\xi=c_0(r/\tau)^2\vee c_1(a/r)^2,
\]

Corollary 6 claims RMS Procrustes error at most a constant times \(\sqrt d\,\rho^3\xi/\omega^2\) for the output of Maximum Variance Unfolding followed by dimension-\(d\) PCA. In particular, it claims linear dependence on \(\xi\), matching the Isomap guarantee and yielding the discussed \((\log n/n)^{1/d}\) rate when the geometric parameters are fixed.

**Error and evidence.** The proof replaces the returned MVU squared-distance matrix by the graph squared-distance matrix. They are different objects:

- \(\Delta_{ij}=g_{ij}^2\) is the true intrinsic squared distance.
- \(\Gamma_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}\) is the shortest-path graph distance.
- \(\Lambda_{ij}=\|z_i-z_j\|^2\) is the squared distance between the returned MVU/PCA coordinates.

Equation (35) bounds \(\max_{ij}|\gamma_{ij}^2-g_{ij}^2|\). Equation (39) instead asserts

\[
|\Lambda-\Delta|_\infty
=\max_{ij}|\gamma_{ij}^2-g_{ij}^2|
\le12\rho^2\xi.
\]

The equality has no justification and is false. MVU does not return graph distances: it optimizes over Euclidean distance matrices, while graph squared distances need not be Euclidean. The triangle inequality and the PCA contraction give only \(\Lambda_{ij}\le\gamma_{ij}^2\). Consequently, the graph estimate controls the **positive** part of \(\Lambda_{ij}-\Delta_{ij}\); it does not control the negative part needed by this absolute-value maximum.

This distinction is also explicit in the cited primary source. Its Theorem 2 characterizes MVU as an \(L^1\) approximation to graph squared distances over a constrained Euclidean-distance class; its Theorem 3 supplies an average \(L^1\) error bound, not the pointwise bound used in (39). See [Paprotny and Garcke (2012), PDF pages 5–7](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v22/paprotny12/paprotny12.pdf).

The printed identification can fail under the paper's own geometric conditions, not merely for an arbitrary unrelated matrix. Take the full grid

\[
\{(i/K,j/K):0\le i,j\le K\}\subset[0,1]^2,
\qquad r=K^{-1/2},\quad K\ge3.
\]

The flat convex domain has infinite reach, the covering radius is \(a=1/(\sqrt2 K)\), and \(\xi=O(1/K)\). Its half-width stays positive, so all smallness conditions hold for sufficiently large \(K\).

Every MVU optimizer is congruent to the original flat grid. To verify this, for any feasible embedding \(p(I,J)\), variance tensorization for independent uniform grid indices gives

\[
\operatorname{Var}(p)
\le E_J\operatorname{Var}_I(p\mid J)
 +E_I\operatorname{Var}_J(p\mid I)
\le2\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\operatorname{Unif}\{0,1/K,\ldots,1\}\right).
\]

The second inequality follows from the axis-neighbor edge constraints and the triangle inequality along each row and column. The original grid attains the bound. Equality forces an additive embedding, straight unit-length coordinate directions, and orthogonal directions because both diagonal edge directions are also constrained. Thus PCA in dimension 2 preserves the optimizer and \(\Lambda=\Delta\).

However, the grid pair \((0,0),(1,(K-1)/K)\) has no interior grid point on its straight segment, since \(\gcd(K,K-1)=1\), and no direct radius edge. Every graph path is strictly longer than its Euclidean distance. Therefore the left side of the printed equality is zero and the right side is strictly positive. This example disproves the identification; it does **not** disprove the corollary's upper bound, which trivially holds on this particular example.

The error matters because (39) is the only supplied step giving the extra power of \(\xi\). Even granting the preceding \(L^1\) bound (37),

\[
|\Lambda-\Delta|_1\le9\rho^2 n^2\xi,
\]

a valid bounded-diameter estimate gives \(|\Lambda-\Delta|_\infty=O(\rho^2)\), hence

\[
\|\Lambda-\Delta\|_F=O(n\rho^2\sqrt\xi),
\]

instead of the \(O(n\rho^2\xi)\) bound in (40). Applying the paper's classical-scaling result through this route yields \(O(\sqrt\xi)\) coordinate error under a corresponding smallness condition. A separate argument exploiting optimality and/or geometric rigidity would be needed to obtain the stronger claimed rate; neither the supplied proof nor the cited result provides one.

For an additional reproducible check that the missing norm implication is substantive, let \(n-1\) points be equally spaced on \([-1,0]\), with one point at 1, and obtain a second Euclidean configuration by moving only the last point to 0. Its squared distances all decrease. The distance-matrix difference has \(L^1\) norm \(4(n-1)\) but maximum absolute entry 3. At \(\xi=1/n\), it satisfies the stated type of \(O(n^2\xi)\) average bound and the one-sided upper bound, while violating the proposed \(O(\xi)\) maximum bound for large \(n\). This is a norm-implication check, **not an MVU optimum or a counterexample to Corollary 6**.

**Reason for rejection.** A named contribution is a new finite-sample performance guarantee for MVU with the same rate as Isomap. The sole proof of that guarantee uses an invalid substitution; the valid available estimates yield a materially weaker rate, halving the discussed sample-size exponent. Removing this contribution, weakening its rate, or supplying a new substantive argument is required. Numerical slopes do not establish the missing universal guarantee. This leaves a central advertised theoretical contribution unsupported as written and warrants changing accept to reject. The Procrustes, classical-scaling and Isomap results are not refuted by this finding.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the transfer of the graph-distance estimate into the MVU proof, noticed that the symbol on the left of (39) refers to the optimizer's output while the right refers to graph shortest paths.

**Verification method.** Re-read all 37 original pages, including the full proof section and appendices; inspected rendered page 16; checked the relevant primary-source theorems; derived the valid one-sided and norm bounds; and constructed the exact flat-grid certificate and separate Euclidean norm-implication fixtures. Independent bounded review confirmed the matrix distinction and the missing two-sided bound. Small-grid SDP calculations agree with the analytic certificate; their solver status is retained as `optimal_inaccurate`, so they are diagnostic support rather than a certified numerical proof. The argument above supplies the exact evidence. Theoretical checks and scripts are in unpublished audit files and an unpublished audit file.

**Confidence.** High in the invalid proof step and the resulting absence of a proof for the stated rate. No confidence claim is made that Corollary 6 is false; a different proof might establish it. Rejection rests on the unsupported central guarantee in the paper as written.

papers.preface_markdown: The complete 19-page paper, including both appendices, was read. The two findings concern separate conditional-probability errors: an omitted derivative of a conditional feature distribution in the hinge-loss analysis, and an invalid cancellation of a residual-feature cross term after additional conditioning in the regression analysis. The paper contains no original empirical experiment section.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 14–15, Theorem 9 and its proof; the conditional marginal is defined immediately above the theorem on page 14. Related central claims appear in the abstract and Section 5, PDF pages 1 and 16.

**Claim.** For normalized hinge-loss SGD, when the current and optimal unit parameter vectors have positive cosine \(c\), the conditional expected cosine improvement decreases with global difficulty \(\Psi\) throughout \(\Psi>1-c\), to first order in the step size. The theorem imposes no independence between difficulty and the remaining feature coordinates.

**Error and evidence.** The proof defines \(f(x_2)\) as the marginal conditional on \(x_1=1-\Psi\), then differentiates its integral while treating this conditional density as independent of \(\Psi\). That omitted term can reverse the conclusion.

Here is a continuous feature distribution satisfying the optimization and update conditions. Independently draw

\[
a\sim\operatorname{Unif}[1/4,1/2],\qquad
d\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1/100,1/100],\qquad
y\in\{-1,1\}\text{ equiprobably}.
\]

Use raw features \( (ya,y(8a-3+d))\) and the paper's augmented vector

\[
x=(ya,y(8a-3+d),1),\quad
\bar w=(1,0,0),\quad w_t=(3/5,4/5,0).
\]

Both parameter vectors have norm one. Also \(E[yx]=(3/8,0,0)\). For every unit vector \(w\),

\[
E[\max(1-yx\cdot w,0)]\ge 1-E[yx]\cdot w
=1-\tfrac38w_1\ge\tfrac58.
\]

At \(\bar w\), every margin equals \(a<1\), and the expected loss equals \(5/8\). Thus \(\bar w\) is the unique global minimizer for the stated norm constraint. It also minimizes the regularized convex objective with multiplier \(\lambda=3/16\): its gradient is \(-E[yx]+2\lambda\bar w=0\).

Global difficulty is \(\Psi=1-a\in[1/2,3/4]\), entirely inside the theorem's promised regime \(\Psi>1-3/5=2/5\). Write \(b=8a-3+d\). For example, at \(\Psi=3/5\) and \(7/10\), all current margins are below one, so every example receives update (23). The exact normalized cosine gain is

\[
G(a,d;\eta)=
\frac{3/5+\eta a}
{\sqrt{1+2\eta((3/5)a+(4/5)b)+\eta^2(a^2+b^2+1)}}-\frac35.
\]

Its first-order coefficient, averaged over \(d\), is

\[
E_d[G]/\eta
=\frac{16}{25}a-\frac{12}{25}(8a-3)+O(\eta)
=-\frac{44}{25}+\frac{16}{5}\Psi+O(\eta).
\]

The slope is **positive** \(16/5\), opposite to Theorem 9. At the two difficulties, the leading coefficients are \(4/25\) and \(12/25\).

This is not caused by retaining a large second-order term. For \(0<\eta\le1/100\), \(a\in[1/4,1/2]\) and \(|d|\le1/100\), the derivative of the fraction with respect to \(a\) has the sign of

\[
H-(3/5+\eta a)[7+\eta(a+8b)],
\]

where \(H\) is the expression inside its square root. Uniformly, \(H\le1.022388\), whereas the subtracted product is at least \(4.15152\). Hence the gain strictly increases with \(\Psi\) wherever these updates are active, including a neighborhood of both example difficulties. At \(\eta=1/1000\), quadrature of the exact expression gives conditional gains approximately **0.0001596242** at \(\Psi=0.6\) and **0.0004797355** at \(\Psi=0.7\). The analytic sign argument establishes the result independently of quadrature.

**Reason for rejection.** A central contribution is the claimed theoretical justification for prioritizing globally easier examples in hinge-loss learning. Its main theorem is false even for a continuous, bounded feature distribution with an explicitly verified global optimizer. Repair requires a substantive restriction on the conditional feature distribution, rather than an algebraic correction preserving the stated theorem. The surviving regression result under its separate independence assumption does not establish this claimed hinge-loss guarantee.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the Leibniz differentiation, noticed that the proof's conditional feature density changes when the conditioning difficulty changes.

**Verification method.** Re-read the full paper and inspected rendered pages 14–15; constructed the distribution above, proved its optimizer exactly, derived the exact normalized update and a uniform finite-step derivative certificate, and checked its two conditional gains numerically. Independent bounded root review confirmed the original assumptions, optimizer and finite-step reversal using a different exact polynomial comparison.

**Confidence.** High. The original theorem's conditions and the optimizer are explicitly verified, and the reversal occurs already in its first-order term and persists for arbitrarily small positive steps.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 9, final displayed conditional-progress expression after Lemma 4; PDF page 10, equation (18) and the proof of Theorem 5; PDF page 11, Corollary 5.1. Related local-difficulty claims appear in the abstract and Section 5.

**Claim.** Corollary 5.1 states that, for any \(c>0\), if the function \(\nabla\) defined on page 10 is \((c-1/c)\)-Lipschitz, then expected regression SGD progress is nondecreasing in local difficulty \(\Upsilon\) whenever \(\Upsilon\ge c\Psi\). The analysis invokes Assumption 1 and neglects second-order step-size terms.

**Error and evidence.** The residual-feature cross term cancels when conditioning only on global difficulty, as in equation (16). It need not cancel after also fixing the current loss. Page 9 reuses the canceled formula under this additional conditioning. The resulting equation (18) has the wrong first-order expression. This invalidates the stated Lipschitz sufficient condition, as the following full-support continuous example demonstrates.

Define the continuous function

\[
n(U)=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le U\le2,\\
3(U-2)/8,&2\le U\le10/3,\\
21/2-3U,&10/3\le U\le11/3,\\
-1/2,&U\ge11/3.
\end{cases}
\]

It is globally 3-Lipschitz and takes values in \([-1/2,1/2]\). Define an even feature density \(f(u)=g(|u|)/Z\), with

\[
g(t)=1\quad(0\le t\le3),\qquad
g(t)=g(t-2)\frac{1+n(t-1)}{1-n(t-1)}\quad(t>3),
\]

and \(Z=2\int_0^\infty g(t)\,dt\). This recursion is an explicit positive continuous function. For \(t\ge14/3\), \(g(t)=g(t-2)/3\), so \(Z\) is finite and every polynomial moment exists. Thus \(f\) is a continuous, positive density on all of \(\mathbb R\).

Draw raw feature \(u\sim f\) and label \(y\sim N(0,1)\) independently; use \(x=(u,1)\), \(\bar w=(0,0)\), and \(w_t=(-1,0)\). Assumption 1 holds exactly. The least-squares optimizer is uniquely \(\bar w=0\), since \(E[xy]=0\) and \(E[xx^T]\) is positive definite. The distance parameter is \(\lambda=1\). Condition on global difficulty \(\Psi=|y|=1\).

By evenness and the defining recursion, the paper's function satisfies, for every \(U>0\),

\[
\nabla(U)=\frac{f(U+1)-f(U-1)}{f(U+1)+f(U-1)}=n(U).
\]

Choose \(c=10/3\). Its allowed Lipschitz constant is \(c-1/c=91/30>3\), so the corollary's hypothesis holds globally. The point \(U=7/2\) is strictly above \(c\Psi\).

Directly applying the actual update (7), and averaging the four conditional possibilities for the feature and residual signs, gives the **exact** progress

\[
\frac{\Delta(1,U)}{4\eta}
=U^2+U n(U)-\eta U^2[U^2+2+2U n(U)].
\]

In particular, the first-order expression is \(U^2+U\nabla(U)\), rather than equation (18)'s \(1+U^2+2U\nabla(U)\). At \(U=7/2\), \(n(U)=0\) and \(n'(U)=-3\), so

\[
\frac1{4\eta}\frac{\partial\Delta(1,U)}{\partial U}

findings.title: Outer validation outcomes are used for supervised feature selection
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-772-01 — Outer validation outcomes are used for supervised feature selection
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p25, Section4.1 and Table5; p26, Section4.2.1; Figures12–14 on pp28–30; Tables10–12 on pp56–57; Table8 and recommendations on p35. Original rendered pages25,26,35 were inspected. The released implementation has the same order in `analysisMaster.R` and `FeatureSelection/FeatureSelection.R`.

**Claim.** The paper compares six survival predictors using five-fold cross-validation and derives model recommendations for unseen patients. Section4.2.1 reports that MTLR performs best on six of eight datasets for concordance/L1-loss and seven of eight for integrated Brier score. Table8 gives recommendations by dimensionality and censoring, including the high-dimensional DBCD and DLBCL datasets. These comparative conclusions are explicit contributions on PDF pp4 and37.

**Error and evidence.** The supervised screening step precedes the outer training/test split. On p25, the paper says it passes each feature through a univariate Cox filter, keeps features with p<=.10, and then partitions the data into five folds. A Cox significance test depends on survival time and event/censoring labels. Consequently every held-out patient’s outcome helps decide which inputs train the model used to predict that patient.

The historical authored source confirms the procedure. In prepublication commit `0c148ef944994cc6a7508483120ec06e9212c879` of [haiderstats/ISDEvaluation](https://github.com/haiderstats/ISDEvaluation/tree/0c148ef944994cc6a7508483120ec06e9212c879), `analysisMaster` calls `validateAndClean`, then `FeatureSelection(..., type="UniCox")`, then `createFoldsAndNormalize`, and only then enters the per-fold fitting loop. The unchanged `uniCox` fits `coxph(Surv(time,delta) ~ feature)` on its supplied whole dataset and retains p<.1. The fold constructor sorts by `(delta,time)` and assigns patients round-robin. Training-based normalization is separate and does not resolve outcome-dependent screening. All20 source blobs were checked against exact Git SHA1, with SHA256 recorded.

Formally, with outer test fold F and supervised gate G, the reported prediction uses A(D_{-F}, G(D_{all})). The deployment procedure must use a gate fitted without test outcomes: A(D_{-F}, G(D_{-F})). The former lets the validation outcome enter both predictor construction and evaluation. Inner cross-validation for model hyperparameters occurs after this leakage.

The flaw was reproduced using original high-dimensional matrices recovered from the primary [Survlab dataset page](https://user.it.uu.se/~kripe367/survlab/download.html), with URLs and hashes preserved:

| Native check | DBCD | DLBCL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Patients / genes |295 /4919 |240 /7399 |
| Whole-data genes selected |2330 |1770 |
| Published Table5 selected count |2330 |1771 |
| Frozen outer fold1 size |59 |48 |
| Genes after only held-out outcome pairs are permuted |1882 |1440 |
| Original selected genes removed / previously excluded genes added |660 /212 |656 /326 |

For DBCD the native selector reproduces Table5’s2330 genes exactly. Fix the original fold1, retain every training row and every patient’s predictor values bit-for-bit, and use `set.seed(772); pi=sample(idx)` to permute only held-out `(time,delta)` pairs. The selected model inputs change by872 genes. For example, gene `g8` has whole-data Cox p=.09200269 originally and p=.3551267 after the held-out-only permutation; its training-only p=.29962604 never changes. Gene `g21` changes .03487866→.4465263, with training-only p=.32154113. This cannot occur for a training-only feature gate. DLBCL independently shows the same dependence; its one-feature discrepancy from the historical printed selected count is retained explicitly rather than presented as an exact replication.

A direct prediction check used the unchanged authored `MTLR` wrapper and the historical CRAN MTLR0.2.1 package. Hold the training labels, held-out predictors, held-out labels passed to prediction, normalization procedure and supported fixed regularization C1=100 constant. Change only the feature gate induced by the intervention above. DBCD fold1 survival predictions change by a maximum absolute probability .0949669 and mean .01399550. Thus validation outcomes affect actual predictions through the demonstrated gate. This fixed-C1 check establishes dependence; it is not a rerun of historical internal hyperparameter tuning.

An independent reviewer rechecked original pp4/25/26/35/37, the source chain, all20 Git blobs and both original matrix hashes. A different held-out-only permutation, seed18772, changes12 of the first60 gene gates with the same59 held-out patients and all training data unchanged; `g8` p becomes .479778. The native checks completed successfully under R4.4.3 and survival3.8.12.

**Reason for rejection.** The comparative evaluation and dataset-specific model recommendations are main contributions. Their reported five-fold evidence does not estimate out-of-sample performance for a deployable supervised pipeline, because the validation outcomes fit the feature gate. Feature-free KM does not receive this channel, and the feature-based methods need not benefit equally. The high-dimensional model comparisons and their practical recommendations therefore lack valid validation evidence as written. Repair requires moving selection inside each outer training fold and repeating the model tuning, fitting and evaluation; it cannot be achieved by editing a displayed formula or relabeling a column while retaining the conclusions. This warrants reject for the paper as written. The evidence does **not** establish a particular corrected ranking reversal or falsify the separate D-calibration expectation theorem.

**Discovery method.** The ordering in Section4.1 first raised suspicion while tracing how the outer validation folds were formed. The released master analysis and Cox selector supplied a specific implemented outcome channel.

**Verification method.** Full-paper and appendix review; original rendered-page recheck; historical source and original-data hash verification; native unchanged univariate Cox screening on real datasets; held-out-only paired-label intervention with exact training-data equality assertions; historical native MTLR prediction dependence; and independent different-seed replication.

 Original matrices/converted numeric CSVs: an unpublished audit file. Full certificate entrypoint: an unpublished audit file. Minimal different-seed check: `Rscript 18772`. Fixed-C1 prediction check: an unpublished audit file. Native feature-selection summaries, per-gene p-value certificates, exact perturbation rows, selected-gene lists and survival-curve arrays are retained in the evidence directory.

**Limits.** No matched historical end-to-end rerun of all eight datasets, model versions, tuning grids and calibration tests was completed. Corrected historical scores and rankings are therefore not quantified. Native DLBCL screening differs from the printed count by one feature. Neither limit resolves the explicit outer-outcome leakage or DBCD’s exact published-count reproduction.

**Confidence: High.** The error is explicit in the PDF and code, reproduced on the original DBCD with the exact published selected count, and confirmed by an independent intervention that holds training data fixed. Actual historical-model predictions depend on the leaked gate.

findings.title: The proposed dual solves a different objective on the stated class
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-790__I01 — The proposed dual solves a different objective on the stated class
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 4, Section 2.1, equation (4) and the following convexity/uniqueness assertion; PDF page 5, Section 2.2, equation (5), Lemma 1, equation (6), and the primal recovery formula; PDF page 28, Section 7.1.1, first equality in the proof of Lemma 1. The RCD/AP methods in Section 3 optimize that purported dual.

**Claim.** Each set function is assumed normalized, meaning F(∅)=0, and nonnegative. The paper explicitly includes monotone submodular functions, permits x,a∈R^N, and takes W positive diagonal. It claims that P(x)=∥x−a∥²_W+Σ_r f_r(x)² is strongly convex with a unique minimizer; equation (5) asserts f_r(x)²=max_{φ_r≥0}(φ_r f_r(x)−φ_r²/4). Lemma 1 claims that minimizing g(y,φ)=∥Σ_r y_r−2Wa∥²_{W⁻¹}+Σ_r φ_r² over y_r∈φ_r B_r, φ_r≥0 is a dual formulation of this problem, recovering its solution as x=a−W⁻¹Σ_r y_r/2.

**Error and evidence.** A nonnegative normalized set function need not have a nonnegative Lovász extension on R^N. The maximization in equation (5) equals max{f_r(x),0}². It drops the square penalty wherever the extension is negative.

Take N=2, R=1, W=I, a=(−1,−1), and

    F(∅)=0; F({1})=F({2})=F({1,2})=1.

This is the rank function of the rank-one uniform matroid: it is normalized, nonnegative, monotone and submodular. Both elements are incident. All 16 subset-pair submodularity inequalities and every nested-set monotonicity inequality hold. Its base polytope is B=conv{(1,0),(0,1)}, and equation (2) gives f(x)=max{x₁,x₂}. At x=a the extension is −1, so the left side of equation (5) is 1, whereas the right side is max_{φ≥0}(−φ−φ²/4)=0.

The original objective is

    P(x)=(x₁+1)²+(x₂+1)²+max{x₁,x₂}².

On x₁≥x₂ this is the diagonal quadratic (x₁+1)²+(x₂+1)²+x₁²; its unconstrained minimizer (−1/2,−1) belongs to that region and has value 1/2. The other region gives the second global minimizer (−1,−1/2), also with value 1/2. Their midpoint (−3/4,−3/4) has value 11/16>1/2. Thus the asserted convexity and uniqueness fail under the stated assumptions.

For the purported dual, feasibility means y₁,y₂≥0 and φ=y₁+y₂. Its objective is

    g(y,φ)=(y₁+2)²+(y₂+2)²+(y₁+y₂)².

Its unique minimum over this cone is y=0, φ=0, with value 8. The prescribed recovery returns x=a=(−1,−1), for which P(x)=1, an objective gap of 1/2 from the true minimum. Starting from the printed zero initialization, either the RCD or AP cone projection for this single-block instance remains zero, because it projects the negative vector 2a onto a cone with nonnegative y. Hence arbitrarily accurate solution of the proposed dual, and the corresponding convergence guarantees, do not solve the stated primal problem even to accuracy ε<1/2. This is an exact wrong optimization problem, not only an unproved exchange of min and max.

The failure is not restricted to an isolated tie or scale. With F(S)=t for every nonempty S, W=wI and a=(−s,−s), any positive w,s,t satisfy the assumptions. The two original minima are (−ws/(w+t²),−s) and its coordinate swap, with value wt²s²/(w+t²). The cone solution still recovers a, giving value t²s² and a strictly positive gap t⁴s²/(w+t²). Exact rational checks verify 64 such parameter triples.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's first two stated contributions are a new dual formulation for general QDSFM and linearly convergent methods for that problem. On an explicitly included monotone submodular function, the claimed convex primal is nonconvex, its minimizer is not unique, the central transformation is false, and the algorithms optimize a different objective and return a provably suboptimal solution. Restoring validity requires changing the objective to squared positive parts, restricting the vector domain, or materially narrowing the set-function class. In particular, imposing F(V)=0 excludes every nonzero monotone normalized function, contrary to the claimed generality. This invalidates the central general optimization contribution as written and warrants changing accept to reject. The graph/hypergraph cut applications have F(V)=0 and are not refuted by this example; their survival does not repair the false general formulation and guarantees.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the nonnegative-square conjugacy used to pass from the primal to the cone dual, I checked whether nonnegativity of F implies the asserted nonnegativity of its Lovász extension on the paper's unrestricted signed domain.

**Verification method.** Re-derived equation (2), the base polytope and the nonnegative scalar conjugate exactly. Solved both primal regions and the proposed cone problem with rational arithmetic, checked the midpoint violation, and verified all submodularity/monotonicity assumptions. Executed 64 positive rational variants and 49 graph-cut controls; the latter confirm that the issue disappears in the zero-endpoint cut subclass. Re-read all 49 original pages and inspected the rendered equations on pages 4, 5 and 28 for a domain, symmetry, or F(V)=0 restriction. No general restriction resolves it; Table 1 concerns the specific application subclass. The page-35 proof of Lemma 24 explicitly allows F(V)≥0 rather than requiring zero. No empirical failure or code behavior is needed for the mathematical counterexample.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample satisfies every relevant stated assumption, all objective values and optima are exact rational numbers, and the failure directly concerns the central equivalence rather than a numerical approximation or a missing proof step. The scope is the general formulation; no conclusion is drawn that the cut-specific experiments are false.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 1(i), PDF page 7; its assumptions C1–C7, PDF page 22; the normalization for the power-one statistic, PDF page 24; and Appendix C's opening argument using C4 and Bernstein blocking, PDF pages 26–28. The resulting normal calibration is used on PDF pages 8 and 25–26.

**Claim.** Under C1–C7 and the null, each fixed finite-power statistic, jointly over a fixed candidate set, has the stated Gaussian limit. In particular, whenever the candidate set contains 1,

$$
\frac{L(1)-\psi(1)}{\omega(1)}\ \Longrightarrow\ N(0,1),
\qquad
\psi(1)=0,\qquad
\omega^2(1)=\frac1n\sum_{j,l=1}^p\sigma_{jl}+o(p/n).
$$

Here \(L(1)=n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-\widehat\mu_{0i})\sum_jX_{ij}\), and \(\Sigma\) is the covariance of the scores computed using the true null mean.

**Error and evidence.** C4 controls sums of pairwise covariances. It does not provide the joint dependence control needed for the claimed central limit theorem. The following bounded logistic-null example satisfies the stated assumptions but has a degenerate limit for the displayed statistic.

For positive integers \(k\), let

$$
m=3k,\qquad n=2^{2k},\qquad p=2^{3k}-1,\qquad q=n.
$$

For observation \(i\), draw \(A_i\) uniformly from the binary vector space \(\mathbb F_2^m\). Index the \(p\) features by its nonzero vectors \(v\), and set

$$
X_{iv}=(-1)^{A_i\cdot v}.
$$

The dot product is taken modulo two. Independently draw \(Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(3/4)\) and \(q-1\) independent Rademacher nuisance covariates. Include an intercept as the first nuisance covariate, so

$$
Z_i=(1,Z_{i2},\ldots,Z_{iq}),\qquad
\vartheta^0=(\log 3,0,\ldots,0),\qquad \beta=0.
$$

Observations are IID at each sample size. Every feature has mean zero, and Walsh orthogonality gives

$$
E[X_{iv}X_{iw}]=\mathbf1_{\{v=w\}},\qquad
\sum_{v\ne0}X_{iv}=
\begin{cases}
p,&A_i=0,\\
-1,&A_i\ne0.
\end{cases}
$$

Consequently \(\Sigma=(3/16)I_p\), and the paper's normalization is
\(\omega^2(1)=(3/16)p/n+o(p/n)\), which tends to infinity.

Let \(E_n=\{A_1,\ldots,A_n\ne0\}\). A union bound gives

$$
\Pr(E_n^c)\le \frac{n}{p+1}=2^{-k}\longrightarrow0.
$$

On \(E_n\), for **any fitted logistic probabilities**, including those obtained from TLP,

$$
L(1)=-\frac1n\sum_i(Y_i-\widehat\mu_{0i}),\qquad |L(1)|\le1.
$$

It follows that \(L(1)/\omega(1)\to0\) in probability, contradicting the claimed standard normal limit. This does not rely on failure of nuisance selection or on a particular tuning choice. With the oracle intercept MLE, the residuals sum to zero and \(L(1)=0\) exactly on \(E_n\). Using the known true mean also gives the same degenerate asymptotic conclusion. Optional sample recentering of the features does not remove the example: on \(E_n\), it makes every feature-row sum zero.

The assumptions can be checked individually:

- **C1:** \(\Sigma=(3/16)I_p\); all off-diagonal correlations are zero.
- **C2:** \(S_{iv}=(Y_i-3/4)X_{iv}\) has zero third moment because \(E[X_{iv}^3]=0\). Also \(|S_{iv}|\le3/4\) and \(S_{iv}^2/\sigma_{vv}\le3\), giving the required uniform exponential moment.
- **C3:** Only the intercept is active, so \(q_0=1\) and the selected nuisance matrix is uniformly bounded. All conditional feature means given that matrix are zero; \(P_0\) is empty.
- **C4:** The two normalized absolute covariance sums equal \(3/16\) and 1, respectively.
- **C5:** \(pq_0^4/n^2\to0\), \(q_0=1\), and \(q=n\) is below the allowed exponential bound eventually. More precisely, any wrong model with at most one nuisance covariate has maximum Hellinger affinity \(\cos(\pi/12)<1\) with the true intercept model. Thus \(C_{\min}=-\log\cos(\pi/12)>0\). For a wrong Rademacher predictor with success probability parameter \(b\), its average affinity is
  \[
  \frac{\sqrt3+1}{4}\big(\sqrt b+\sqrt{1-b}\big)\le\cos(\pi/12).
  \]
  The empty model attains the same maximum.
- **C6:** The conditional response variance is \(3/16\), and \(n^{-1}\widetilde Z^\top W\widetilde Z=3/16\) exactly.
- **C7, first condition:** Write \(G(\vartheta)=-\log(1-h^2(\vartheta,\vartheta^0))\). The logarithmic derivative of Bernoulli Hellinger affinity with respect to the logistic linear predictor is a positive weighted average of \((1-\mu)/2\) and \(-\mu/2\). Its absolute value is at most \(1/2\). Since every \(|Z_{ij}|\le1\), \(G\) is \(1/2\)-Lipschitz in the coefficient \(\ell_1\) norm. Hence
  \[
  G(\vartheta)\ge G(\vartheta_{\tau+})-\tfrac12q\tau,
  \]
  as required with \(d_1=1,d_2=1,d_3=1/2\).
- **C7, entropy condition:** A one-covariate Bernoulli family can be parameterized by \(u=\arcsin\sqrt b\in[0,\pi/2]\). Its square-root densities are uniformly Lipschitz in \(u\), so monotone endpoint brackets on a mesh of width proportional to \(t\) have Hellinger bracket width at most \(t\). For the true intercept family, a Hellinger ball of radius \(2\epsilon\) confines \(u\) to an interval of length \(O(\epsilon)\). For every wrong Rademacher family, the minimum squared Hellinger distance to the truth is \(1-\cos(\pi/12)>0\). Whenever its local class is nonempty, \(\epsilon\) is bounded below by a positive constant, so the whole compact angle interval also has length \(O(\epsilon)\). Therefore the bracketing number is at most \(1+C\epsilon/t\), and the stated entropy bound holds for a uniform constant \(c_0\). Empty support gives a singleton class and entropy zero. Even taking the union over the \(q\) singleton supports adds only \(\log q\), which is absorbed by the stated \((\log q)^2\) factor.

The alpha-mixing condition C9 is imposed for the alternative-power analysis, not for Theorem 1. Adding that condition to the null theorem would substantially restrict the asserted covariance-based extension; it is not among C1–C7.

**Reason for rejection.** The main theorem justifying analytic normal p-values and the joint adaptive calibration is false on a legal bounded canonical-GLM null, including a component in the default candidate set. More accurate nuisance estimation cannot repair it: the failure persists for the oracle and known true mean. The proposed replacement of stronger dependence assumptions by C4 is insufficient. A materially stronger joint dependence or Lindeberg assumption, and a new proof/calibration analysis, are needed. This invalidates a central theoretical contribution of the paper as written and warrants rejection. This finding does not assert that every reported simulation or the ADNI results are numerically false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Appendix C, noticed that the known-mean normal limit was imported from an alpha-mixing argument after only a pairwise moment condition had been imposed. An initial concern about ordinary nuisance-feature correlation was discarded because C3 addresses it. Pairwise-independent Walsh features then gave an exact obstruction to the claimed extension.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original theorem, assumptions, normalization and proof on rendered PDF pages 7, 22, 24 and 26. Derived the complete counterexample and all assumption checks above. An independent script enumerates Walsh systems through 511 features and verifies their exact means, covariance and row sums, then checks the explicit asymptotic family. A native R check evaluates the score and the authored variance helper without modifying it. Independent bounded root QA checks the counterexample and C7 separately. The remainder of the paper, appendices, experiments and available implementation were also reviewed; no additional issue is inferred merely from unavailable historical artifacts.

**Confidence.** High. The contradiction follows from an exact row-sum identity and a probability bound tending to one, not a numerical approximation. All null assumptions, including the Hellinger conditions, have explicit checks; the conclusion holds for any bounded logistic fitted probabilities.

 The authored code is pinned to commit 7bdedfb9981993467bb744e6e3a9e99aec80ebbf. The native check exercises the score and mathematical moment helpers; missing mvtnorm prevented a full analytic p-value run. No historical simulation or ADNI rerun is claimed.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 22–29, Section 4.1: generating models (1)–(3), Tables 1–6, and the simulation of setting (G) on page 27 with results in Table 8. The comparisons and signal-regime interpretations on pages 24–27 depend on these experiments.

**Claim.** The reported change-point frequencies are obtained from the specified dynamic stochastic block models. Their Bernoulli edge probabilities and the tabulated signal `Fn = ||Ed_z(Lambda) - Ed_w(Delta)||_F²` support comparisons of the three estimators under the stated signal and clustering conditions. The graph model has zero diagonal and probabilities in [0,1].

**Error and evidence.** Several specified models have probabilities outside [0,1]. This is a finite-parameter problem in the reported experiments, independent of asymptotic notation.

1. In reallocation model (1), the between-community probability is `q = 3/5 - n^(-delta)m^(-lambda)`. For the six Table 1–6 settings `(m,n,lambda) = (60,60,0), (500,20,0), (500,100,0), (60,60,1/20), (500,20,1/20), (500,100,1/20)`, eight of the eighteen combinations with `delta = 1/20, 1/10, 1/4` have q<0. They are the first two delta values in each lambda=0 table and delta=1/20 in Tables 4 and 5. An exact rational certificate, avoiding rounding, is

   `q < 0  iff  (3/5)^20 n^(20 delta) m^(20 lambda) < 1`.

   For example, Table 1's first setting has q approximately -0.21478. Model (3) repeats the same infeasible delta=1/20 entry in its connection matrix.

2. Connectivity model (2) specifies `Delta = Lambda + n^(-1/4)m^(-lambda) J_2`, with Lambda's diagonal entries 0.6 and J_2 the all-ones matrix. Table 2 uses n=20, lambda=0, giving diagonal block probabilities `0.6 + 20^(-1/4) = 1.0728708... > 1`. These are probabilities of edges between distinct nodes in the same block, not graph self-loops.

3. Setting (G) on page 27 specifies `p1² = 0.8`, `p2 = p1 + 1/sqrt(20)`, and `Delta = p2 I_2`. Exactly, `1/sqrt(20) = p1/4`, hence `p2 = sqrt(5)/2 > 1` (equivalently, p2²=5/4). The post-change edge probability itself is p2. Thus the claimed Table 8 post-change Bernoulli model does not exist.

The reported signal calculations further prevent treating this as an isolated harmless parameter typo. For Table 1's reallocation model, the balanced contiguous and alternating partitions differ on exactly 1,800 ordered node pairs. Therefore the printed law gives

`Fn = 1800 * 60^(-1/10) = 1195.246247...`,

matching the reported 1195.246. Clipping the negative q to zero would instead give `Fn = 1800 * (0.6)^2 = 648`; it changes the model and signal-regime interpretation. This calculation does not assert that clipping was used historically.

There is also a direct model/table mismatch in the connectivity column even for the legal Table 1 configuration. With the stated no-self-loop convention, model (2) gives

`Fn = m(m-1) n^(-1/2) m^(-2 lambda)`.

For Tables 1, 2 and 3 this equals approximately 457.013, 55,789.896 and 24,950, whereas the reported values are 2,390.49, 185,283.6 and 157,739.3. Each reported value is instead reproduced by `m² n^(-1/10)`. The gap includes a different exponent and cannot be accounted for by the diagonal convention alone. These are repeated manifestations of one unreconciled experimental specification, counted as one issue.

**Reason for rejection.** The central finite-sample validation compares estimators and explains their success or failure using these models and signals. Several claimed experiments cannot be generated by the stated Bernoulli laws, and their reported signal values are tied to infeasible or different formulas. Consequently that comparative contribution is unsupported as written. Specifying legal generators and regenerating or reconciling the results is necessary; a preserving typesetting correction has not been established. This does not assert misconduct, a particular historical implementation, a reversal of any corrected ranking, or falsity of the general change-point theory.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the empirical comparisons to their generating laws, the negative off-diagonal probability stood out. Checking the other experimental settings then exposed probabilities above one and inconsistent signal values.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original definitions and all relevant tables; inspected the rendered model and table pages. Used exact rational inequalities for the entire parameter grid, constructed the 60-node matrices directly, and recomputed their Frobenius signal. An independent reader repeated the parameter, signal and rendered-page checks; NumPy also rejects the invalid probability. A separate 720-case comparison of cumulative and direct least-squares criteria passed on legal graphs. Those controls are not reproductions of the historical experiments. Journal, author and repository searches did not recover authenticated original drivers, random seeds or result arrays, so the historical generating procedure remains unknown.

**Confidence.** High. The impossible probabilities have exact algebraic certificates, the original rendered specifications were checked, and independent calculations reproduce the signal mismatch. The conclusion concerns the reported experimental specification and its evidentiary consequence, not unobserved historical code.

**Exact location.** PDF page 10, Theorem 8 and Remark 10/(A1); Algorithm I and Definition 7/(2.8) on page 9; proof in Section 7.1, pages 33–34. The dependency affects the guarantees in Theorems 11–13, page 11, through the misclassification control discussed in Remark 35/(A9), pages 43–44.

**Claim.** Under nonsingularity (NS), for every candidate split b,

`M_b = O_P{ K/(n nu²) [tau m + |tau-b| J²] }`,

where `J² = ||P-Q||_F²`, `P=Ed_z(Lambda)`, `Q=Ed_w(Delta)`, and nu is the minimum nonzero singular value of P and Q. Algorithm I takes the K eigenvectors of largest absolute eigenvalue from each temporal sum, then applies fixed-factor approximate K-means. Remark 10 uses this theorem to assert that (A1), together with SNR-DSBM, makes the required clustering error negligible. Definition 7 weights each incorrectly labelled node by the reciprocal true community size; for balanced communities of size h its value is the number of mistakes divided by h.

**Error and evidence: exact family.** Let even integers s tend to infinity, and choose

`K=s, m=s^8, n=s^12, tau=1/4, b=3/4, c*=1/8, q=1/2`.

Partition the nodes into K² cells indexed by `(z,w)`, each containing s^6 nodes. Both z and w have K balanced communities of size `h=m/K=s^7`; every pair of communities from the two partitions intersects in h/K nodes. Let Z and W be their unnormalized membership matrices and set

`Lambda = Delta = q(J_K-I_K)`,  
`P = q(11' - ZZ')`, `Q = q(11' - WW')`.

These are legal undirected Bernoulli models: within-block probability zero, between-block probability 1/2. The graph diagonals are exactly zero. Lambda and Delta have eigenvalues q(K-1) and -q, so (NS) holds. P and Q each have rank K and `nu=qh`; there is no rank or self-loop convention issue. The specified change and candidate times are integers.

The centered Z and W subspaces are orthogonal. The expected first temporal sum divided by n is

`E(B1/n) = P/4 + Q/2`.

Its nonzero eigenvalues are:

| Subspace | Eigenvalue | Multiplicity |
|---|---:|---:|
| Constant vector | `3 qh(K-1)/4` | 1 |
| W contrasts | `-qh/2` | K-1 |
| Z contrasts | `-qh/4` | K-1 |

Therefore the K largest absolute eigenvectors span exactly W. Their row vectors take K distinct values; grouping by w has K-means objective zero. Every finite multiplicative approximation must also have zero objective and return w up to permutation. Because z and w are independent balanced partitions, any relabeling matches exactly m/K nodes. Hence the population error relative to z is `M(z,w)=K-1`.

Meanwhile,

`J² = 2 q² m² (K-1)/K²`,

so Theorem 8's claimed rate equals

`K³/(4 n q² m) + K(K-1)/n`,

which tends to zero. The error grows with K instead.

**The counterexample also holds for the actual sampled graphs.** Write `E = B1/n - E(B1/n)`. Independence across times and Bernoulli variances give

`E||E||_F² <= 3m²/(16n)`.

The relevant eigenspace gap is `g=qh/4`, so

`E||E||_F²/g² <= 12K²/n -> 0`.

The separated eigenspace perturbation bound therefore gives an aligned empirical eigenvector error tending to zero in squared Frobenius norm. The W row prototypes have squared separation 2/h. The deterministic approximate-K-means argument bounds the number of incorrectly recovered W labels by a constant times h times that eigenvector error. Thus, in Definition 7's normalization, `M(w, zhat_b)=o_P(1)`. Balanced-class overlap then yields

`M(z, zhat_b) >= K-1-o_P(1)`.

Since M_b is the maximum of the two segment errors, the other segment cannot repair this contradiction. This is an asymptotic counterexample to the stochastic theorem, not merely a population calculation or a low-probability noiseless sample.

**The downstream assumptions do not exclude the family.** With rho=q,

`K m rho/nu² = 2s^(-5) -> 0`,  
`m sqrt(n) rho/nu² = 2`.

Thus both parts of (A1) hold. Sparse-DSBM holds, and `nJ²/(K²rho)` and `nJ²/(m²rho)` both diverge, satisfying SNR-DSBM and even SNR-ER. But the misclassification control needed downstream has the opposite behavior: using the established error, its squared scale has population value

`n²(K-1)² rho²/J² = s^10(s-1)/2 -> infinity`.

Consequently (A1) does not imply the claimed negligible error through Theorem 8/Remark 10. The proof on pages 33–34 suppresses the fixed-split population mixture bias by an inappropriate 1/n factor; temporal replication removes sampling noise but cannot turn the W mixture eigenspace into Z.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's central contribution includes guarantees for clustering at every candidate time under the explicit signal and (A1) conditions. The supporting clustering theorem is false under those very conditions, and the asserted implication that supplies the main proofs' required error control also fails. Recovering those guarantees requires a new localization or mixture-bias argument, or materially changed conditions; changing a constant does not fix the uniform assertion. This establishes a false Theorem 8 and a central dependency gap. It does **not** establish that Theorem 11's final change-point rate is itself false: localization might still validate that conclusion by a different argument.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the clustering bound into (A1) and the change-point proof, the 1/n factor multiplying misspecification error suggested that increasing time replication was incorrectly being treated as removing population bias at a wrong split.

**Verification method.** Re-read Algorithm I, Definition 7, Theorem 8, Remark 10, their full proof and the downstream assumptions in the original PDF, including full rendered pages 9, 10, 33 and 34. Derived the balanced orthogonal-partition construction, exact spectrum, signal, assumption checks and sampling-noise extension. Five compressed population matrices independently verified the top-K projector and zero W-clustering cost; no astronomically large graph was simulated. An independent reader checked 24 additional quotient matrices, six rational family fixtures, and the complete analytic stochastic argument. All saved controls exited successfully.

**Confidence.** High. The original theorem and its assumptions were checked against a legal, explicit family; the spectrum and rates are exact and sampling perturbations vanish. Independent verification confirmed the counterexample and central dependency. The report deliberately confines the false-theorem claim to Theorem 8.

findings.title: The named consensus Monte Carlo baseline uses mixture pooling
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-817-01 — The named consensus Monte Carlo baseline uses mixture pooling
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp20–24, Section6.1, Figures6–7; pp40–41, AppendixB.1–B.2 and Figure15; p30, Section7. Original rendered pp22–24/30/40 were checked. The implementation cited on p40 is `gelman/ep-stan`, release v1.3: `experiment/fit.py` lines540–674, especially641–646; `experiment/plot_paper.py` lines148–158 and195–201.

**Claim.** The hierarchical-logistic experiment has 64 groups, 20 observations per group, 16 predictors and 34 shared parameters. The paper claims EP outperforms Scott et al. consensus Monte Carlo across the tested partition counts K=2,4,8,16,32,64. Figures6–7 compare error and computation time; AppendixB.2/Figure15 also compares marginal Gaussian KL. The conclusion repeats this empirical advantage. This is a substantial named-method comparison supporting the framework's practical contribution.

**Error and evidence.** The released baseline does not implement consensus Monte Carlo aggregation. AppendixB.1 expressly points to [ep-stan v1.3](https://github.com/gelman/ep-stan/releases/tag/v1.3). Its annotated tag `4bbcf359ca2cad074e8096a5c09c838a619fa952` points to commit `6684cfddb29bfc300dbab0496672ef03368c4cb1`, dated2018-02-20. The tag describes the version used for the arXiv v3 experiments. All48 released blobs were recovered and checked against exact Git SHA1, with SHA256 also recorded.

`fit.py` lines540–598 correctly allocates the Gaussian prior natural parameters as Q0/K and r0/K, and line638 appends each shard's shared-parameter draws. It then executes:

```python
samp = np.concatenate(samples, axis=0)
nsamp = samp.shape[0]
samp.mean(axis=0, out=m_s_cons[i])
samp -= m_s_cons[i]
samp.T.dot(samp, out=S_s_cons[i])
S_s_cons[i] /= nsamp - 1
```

This estimates the moments of an equally weighted mixture of subposteriors. Lines661–674 save these moments in `res_c_*.npz`. The paper plotting script selects model `m4b`, matching the described model and priors, loads `m_s_cons`/`S_s_cons` at148–158, and computes the named baseline's MSE and Gaussian KL at195–201. Thus the faulty operation enters the expressly cited figure-generation path.

In contrast, the primary [Scott et al. consensus paper](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/41849.pdf), PDF pp6–7, Eq3–5/Figure2, combines independent draws by

`theta_g = (sum_k W_k)^(-1) sum_k W_k theta_kg`, with `W_k = Sigma_k^(-1)`.

Even its equal-weight variant averages draws across shards; it does not concatenate them. Original rendered pages6–7 of that primary paper were checked.

An exact proper-prior example demonstrates that this distinction affects both means and uncertainty. Take prior N(0,10), K=2, and likelihood precisions1/5 and19/20, with likelihood centers0 and200/19. Each fractional prior has precision1/20. The two subposteriors are therefore N(0,4) and N(10,1). Their product is the true posterior N(8,4/5). Equal-size concatenation converges to the equal mixture, whose mean is5 and variance is `(4+1)/2 + ((0-5)^2+(10-5)^2)/2 = 55/2`. Correct Scott weights1/5 and4/5 give mean8 and variance `(1/5)^2*4+(4/5)^2*1=4/5`. All priors and likelihoods are proper Gaussian factors; no degeneracy or violated assumption is used. An independent reviewer derived this certificate and verified the same source path.

The error also persists with increasing Monte Carlo sample size. For K identical subposteriors N(mu,K*Sigma), their product and correct consensus are N(mu,Sigma), whereas concatenation retains covariance K*Sigma. The Gaussian KL from the true product to the pooled distribution is exactly `(d/2)*(log(K)+1/K-1)`, which does not tend to zero as sampling increases.

The native diagnostic executes the **unchanged AST** of the six source lines above and the unchanged authored `kl_mvn`, using independent Gaussian subposterior fixtures. With seed18817, 50000 draws per shard, d=4 and correlated Sigma, all K=2/4/8/16/32/64 checks pass. For K=64, pooled covariance diagonal ratios are63.9381,63.9893,63.9755,64.0814, versus correct-consensus ratios1.00503,1.00215,.995811,.998886. Native KL is6.348863 versus .000143774 after correct averaging; the exact limiting wrong KL is6.349016. This fixture isolates the implemented aggregation and does not claim to reproduce the original hierarchical-logistic scores.

**Reason for rejection.** The published comparison is against a named competing distributed method, but the cited implementation evaluates an intrinsically different and systematically overdispersed operation. Its performance curves consequently do not establish the claimed advantage over consensus MC. Replacing the aggregation requires recomputing the baseline moments, errors and time/error curves. Relabeling it as a mixture would withdraw the claimed named-method comparison. Because this comparison is a substantial principal empirical contribution and is repeated as a conclusion, its invalidation warrants changing accept to reject for the paper as written. The separate EP framework may remain useful; no particular corrected historical ranking reversal is asserted.

**Discovery method.** The concatenation first stood out while tracing the paper's central consensus comparison through the explicitly linked experimental release.

**Verification method.** Full paper and appendix review; original rendered equation/figure/citation checks; exact Git provenance for all48 blobs; source-to-plot tracing; primary consensus-definition check; native execution of the unchanged aggregation and KL on Gaussian controls; and independent original-page/source review plus the proper-prior unequal-Gaussian derivation above.

 the aggregation test needs NumPy/SciPy, not Stan.

**Limits.** Original result arrays and a complete historical PyStan2.17 run were not recovered. No corrected historical scores, exact ranking reversal, or full timing replay are claimed. The source is the release expressly cited for these experiments; the evidence does not assert access to unseen historical output files. The native Gaussian controls are implementation certificates, not a substitute historical benchmark. The independent two-point finite-sample source diagnostic is also not presented as Gaussian data.

**Confidence: High.** The precise named-algorithm substitution is present in the expressly cited, hash-verified source, directly feeds its comparison plotting path, and fails exact proper-prior Gaussian checks. Native unchanged-source and independent checks agree; remaining limits concern the corrected historical numerical outcomes.
