findings.title: Released entropy regularizer rewards the context-only failure it is claimed to prevent
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-856__I01 — Released entropy regularizer rewards the context-only failure it is claimed to prevent
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp.12–14, Section5.3, equations(12)–(16) and Remark5; PDF pp.20–22, Sections6.2.2–6.2.3, Figure8 and the conclusion that high predictive performance indicates meaningful signal in explanatory features. Released linked source `cen/models/cen.py`, lines30,55–62; `cen/layers/contextual_dense.py`, lines128–165; `cen/regularizers/entropy.py`, lines22–71. The classification YAMLs, including `cen/configs/model/mnist/cen_convex_pxl.yaml` and `cen/configs/model/imdb/cen_convex_tpc.yaml`, enable this regularizer without overriding the model's softmax output activation.

**Claim.** Section5.3 identifies the central failure: a contextual encoder can encode the class directly in its generated explanation and ignore X. The proposed remedy approximately maximizes H(Y|theta), so that accurate predictions must use X. Section6.2.2 attributes its explanation-contribution experiment to this regularization mechanism and concludes that the explanations are meaningful rather than spurious. The abstract lists valid instance-specific explanations and systematic detection of misleading explanations as central advantages.

**Error and evidence.** The released classifier first computes p=softmax(logits) and passes p as `outputs` to the regularizer. The regularizer computes its cross-entropy target as softmax(outputs), applying softmax a second time, while its other argument is the logarithm of a once-softmaxed averaged prediction. Consequently even when all explanatory kernels are zero, the returned negative cross-entropy is not negative conditional entropy. Its gradient can have the opposite sign.

An exact two-class example needs no approximation to P(X|C). Let C be a balanced one-hot binary context, let X be identically zero, and generate logits (b,0) for context0 and (0,b) for context1. Generate Y from these probabilities to satisfy the paper's generative assumption exactly; the contextual classifier then has accuracy sigmoid(b), and X conveys no information. All explanatory feature kernels are zero and the only predictive information is the contextual bias. This is an allowed affine CEN and is also realized by the convex dictionary CEN with zero kernels and two groups of class-specific biases; finite selector weights suffice. Gaussian perturbations of X cannot affect any prediction because the kernels are zero.

Writing p=1/(1+exp(-b)), the intended negative model conditional entropy is

`p log p + (1-p) log(1-p)`.

Ignoring only the explicitly documented epsilon smoothing for this display, the actual returned term is

`-[q log p + (1-q) log(1-p)]`, where `q=exp(p)/(exp(p)+exp(1-p))`.

At b=4, the original implementation returns −1.122425, whereas the correct negative entropy is −0.0900948. The derivative with respect to b is −0.2298315 in the original implementation and +0.0706508 for the correct quantity. Minimizing the implemented term therefore increases confidence in the context-only class bias instead of discouraging it. At b=40 the original term is −3.715564 with the source's epsilon=1e-6, while true negative entropy is about −1.7e-16. A genuine binary negative entropy lies in [−log2,0], so this cannot be a different unbiased estimate of the same quantity. Without epsilon the implemented objective tends to minus infinity as b grows, because 1-q tends to 1/(1+e)>0. With epsilon it saturates at a value much smaller than the maximal-entropy loss.

Executed the untouched original TensorFlow2.3.4 regularizer at eight bias values and differentiated both quantities. Executed the untouched original `build_model` and full `ContextualAffineDense` layer with the default softmax activation: it returns probabilities(0.98201376,0.01798621) and regularization loss−1.122425. The actual convex dictionary variant, with16dictionary entries and finite selector weights±10, returns the same counterexample result. Four fresh200-step scalar contextual-bias optimizations, using the original regularizer with coefficients0.02,0.1,1,10, retain100% classification accuracy with zero information in X; larger entropy coefficients increase the final contextual bias and spuriously claimed entropy. These are bounded mathematical/implementation demonstrations, not a reproduction of the paper's dataset curves.

**Historical source chain.** JMLR's official paper page links `https://github.com/alshedivat/cen`. findings.title: Invalid dual-certificate bound breaks the proof of the central adversarial recovery guarantee
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-881__I01 — Invalid dual-certificate bound breaks the proof of the central adversarial recovery guarantee
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.32, Appendix C, auxiliary inequality 4 in the proof of Lemma 26; Lemma 26 on p.31; Lemma 14 and equations (12)–(13) on p.15; its proof on pp.32–33; Theorem 13 on p.14 and the near-half-corruption consequence on p.16. The same error affects the deterministic certificate statement in Lemma 11, p.13.

**Claim.** The paper constructs the good-measurement dual coefficients as

`λ_G = −J_G⁺(J_B λ_B + d)`, with `λ_B = μs`, `s_j ∈ {−1,+1}`.

It claims that its singular-value conditions ensure `||λ_G||∞ < μ` and the other certificate inequality. Lemma 14 asserts this with probability at least `(1−δ)²` for a standard Gaussian design, for every μ in interval (13). The bad support is random, but the corruption values may be chosen to be maximally harmful after observing the design (p.15). Theorem 13 invokes this lemma as its proof of conic recovery; p.16 uses the resulting condition to allow a corruption fraction approaching one half with sufficiently informative prior knowledge.

**Error and evidence.** Appendix C uses

`||J_G⁺J_B||∞ ≤ ||J_G⁺J_B||₂`.

The paper explicitly defines the matrix infinity norm as the maximum absolute row sum (p.5). This comparison is false. A valid general comparison costs a factor `sqrt(|B|)`, which is missing from the first certificate bound and the lower endpoint of the claimed μ interval.

An exact counterexample to the general Lemma 26 is `J_G=[3]`, `J_B=[1,1,1,1]`, `d=1`, `α=10`, and `s=(1,1,1,1)`. Its hypotheses are `3>2` and `(3−2)(30−1)=29>16`. Its asserted interval is `[1,29/16]`. At `μ=3/2`, the prescribed coefficient is `λ_G=−7/3`, violating `|λ_G|<μ`.

The error persists under the Gaussian assumptions used for the main stochastic result. Take

`l=2, |G|=100000, |B|=45000, δ=.05, ε=.1, α=10⁶, d=(0,1)`.

Let `J_G,J_B` have independent standard normal entries and choose the permitted adversarial signs `s_j=sign((J_B)₁j)`. A uniformly random independent bad support can be relabeled into this fixed partition by Gaussian exchangeability. Set `Δ_t=τ/√t` as permitted in the lemma. Direct substitution gives `τ=53.9168157`, equation (12)'s left side `316.227766` and right side `260.960299`; interval (13) is approximately `[.01982370,9.192188]`, containing μ=1.

Here is an analytical probability check. Write `Q=J_GJ_Gᵀ`, `v₀=J_Bs`, and `S=Σ_j |(J_B)₁j|`, so `||v₀||≥S`. Consider the following events:

1. `S≥.75|B|`. The complementary probability is at most `.00352175`, by Chebyshev's inequality using the mean `√(2/π)` and variance `1−2/π` of an absolute standard normal.
2. `||Q/|G|−I||₂≤.05`. Apply the bound `P(|χ²_G/G−1|>t)≤2exp(−Gt²/8)` at `t=.025` to the four directions `e₁,e₂,(e₁+e₂)/√2,(e₁−e₂)/√2`. These bound every Gram entry within `.025`, hence its operator error within `.05`. The total exceptional probability is at most `.00323717`.
3. Every good column has norm at most 6. Since its squared norm is `χ²₂`, a union bound gives exceptional probability at most `|G|exp(−18)=.00152300`.
4. Some good column has absolute projection at least 3.5 onto `v₀/||v₀||`. Conditional on `J_B`, the direction is fixed and the projections are independent standard normals. The normal tail bound `P(|Z|≥z)≥2φ(z)z/(z²+1)` bounds the exceptional probability by `9.50×10⁻²¹`.

These events have joint probability at least `.99171809`, by a union bound; independence between the events is unnecessary. On them,

`||Q⁻¹−I/|G|||₂ ≤ .05/(.95|G|)`

and therefore

`||J_GᵀQ⁻¹v₀||∞ ≥ (3.5−6·.05/.95)·.75|B|/|G| > 1.07467`.

For every μ in interval (13), the additional `d/μ` term can change a coordinate by at most

`6/(.95|G|·.01982369585) < .00319`.

Thus the prescribed certificate satisfies `||λ_G(μ)||∞/μ > 1.07148` **simultaneously for every μ in the printed interval**, with probability greater than `.9917`. Lemma 14 instead bounds failure probability by `1−(1−.05)²=.0975`. This is an analytical contradiction, not a conclusion inferred from failed solver runs or a finite simulation.

The certificate failure can also be embedded in the paper's actual quadratic SDP model. Set `x=e₁`, prior `x̂=(1,h)` with `h=10⁻⁹`, and `M=I−x̂x̂ᵀ/||x̂||²`. Let `M_r=[[J₁r,J₂r],[J₂r,0]]`, so `M_rx` is exactly the required Gaussian column. Then `d=Mx=(h²,−h)/(1+h²)` and take `μ=||d||`. Rescaling by `||d||` leaves the same probability argument; its small positive first component only strengthens the lower bound. The actual information parameter exceeds `10⁶` whenever `max_r||M_r||≤500`, an event whose complement has a negligible Gaussian tail bound. All required Jacobian ranks and prior-measurement nondegeneracy conditions hold almost surely.

Uniform SSC/SSS assumptions do not repair the related deterministic certificate assertion either. In dimension 2, let `J_G` contain one column `(3,0)`, 3300 columns `(.1,0)`, and 4000 columns `(0,.1)`, and let `J_B` contain 25 columns `(1,0)`. The squared SSC minimum at level 7301 is 34, and the squared SSS maximum at level 25 is 33: removing any 25 columns leaves first-coordinate energy at least `67−(9+24)=34`, and second-coordinate energy at least `40−.25=39.75`. Take the valid rational constants `γ=29/5`, `Γ=23/4`, `α=10⁶`, `d=(0,1)`, and μ=21. Lemma 11's condition and interval hold, as does Theorem 10's numerical threshold. Nevertheless the prescribed coefficient for the `(3,0)` column is `−(25/14)μ`, again violating its required infinity bound.

**Reason for rejection.** The error invalidates the supplied certificate proof for the central conic recovery guarantee, including the advertised regime approaching half corrupted measurements. Theorem 13 explicitly depends on the false Gaussian lemma and gives no alternative certificate or recovery proof. Replacing the invalid norm comparison by the valid factor requires, through this argument, `σ_min(J_G)>√|B| σ_max(J_B)`; at leading Gaussian order this requires `|G|>|B|²`, which loses the near-half-corruption regime. Restricting the corruption signs to be independent of the design would also change the paper's adversarial model. Preserving the claimed result therefore requires a different argument, rather than correcting a constant while leaving the central proof intact. This loss of support for a central theoretical contribution warrants rejection as written. **This finding does not show that another certificate cannot exist or that the primal recovery conclusions are false.**

**Discovery method.** While tracing how singular values bound individual dual coefficients, noticed that a maximum row-sum norm had been replaced by a spectral norm.

**Verification method.** Read the entire 36-page paper and Appendices A–C; rechecked the original rendered theorem, lemma, norm definition, and proof equations. Verified the exact general and uniform-SSC witnesses, derived the analytical Gaussian probability contradiction and its uniform μ extension, and ran 64 direct Gaussian checks. An independent reviewer rechecked the PDF and derivation and ran 12 fresh instances of the actual quadratic embedding; all violated the certificate bound throughout the interval while satisfying the spectral events. Separately, 96 native original MATLAB helper fixtures and 24 independently transcribed conic recovery controls passed; these do not repair the invalid main proof.

**Confidence.** High. The incorrect norm step, exact certificate counterexamples, and Gaussian probability contradiction are independently reproducible and satisfy the relevant assumptions. The conclusion is confined to the failed certificate and unsupported main proof. The historical empirical figures and the truth of the primal recovery theorem have not been refuted.

 Results, derivation constants, native controls and independent QA: an unpublished audit file. The relevant files are `targeted-checks.json`, `genton-bounded-qa.json`, `genton-bounded-qa.log`, `native-controls.json`, and `conic-controls.json`.

findings.title: Admissible sparse corruptions create strict spurious local minima
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-18-884__I01 — Admissible sparse corruptions create strict spurious local minima
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 22, hypotheses on PDF page 23 and conclusions on PDF page 24; Theorem 23 on PDF page 24; the central deterministic guarantee in Theorem 5 on PDF page 5. The defective degree-counting step is Appendix H, equation (110), PDF page 45. Theorem 35 on PDF page 30 and the probabilistic proof on PDF page 26 invoke the deterministic descent argument.

**Claim.** For the symmetric objective

\[
F(u)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega}|u_i u_j-X_{ij}|+
\frac n2\sum_i(u_i-1)_+^4,\qquad u\geq0,
\]

Theorem 22 asserts absence of spurious local minima, a unique global minimum at the positive true factor \(u^*\), and unique positive D-stationarity. Its assumptions include measurements strictly exceeding \(c(u^*_{\min})^2\), normalization \(u^*_{\max}=1\), clean minimum degree greater than \((48/c^2)\kappa(u^*)^4\) times corrupted maximum degree, and a measurement graph without bipartite components. Theorem 23 supplies an analogous stationary-point guarantee for the asymmetric problem, with a connected clean bipartite graph, quartic regularization, and balancing penalty \(\alpha|\|u\|^2-\|v\|^2|\), for \(\alpha>0\). Theorem 5 advertises benign landscapes and recovery in both cases.

**Error and evidence: a symmetric counterexample.** Let \(n=100\), \(k=50\), \(A=\{1,\ldots,50\}\), and \(B=\{51,\ldots,100\}\). Set \(u^*=\mathbf1_{100}\), \(c=99/100\), \(\beta=1\), and \(\lambda=n/2=50\). Measure both orientations of these edges:

- Clean: all edges between \(A\) and \(B\), and the internal edge \(\{1,2\}\), with value 1.
- Corrupted: a perfect matching within each part, with value 4 on every matched edge. In \(A\), use \(\{1,3\},\{2,4\},\{5,6\},\ldots,\{49,50\}\); in \(B\), use consecutive pairs. Thus no corrupted edge coincides with the clean internal edge.

No other edges are measured; unmeasured matrix entries may be set to 1. These are finite symmetric matrices with no self-loops. Every relevant assumption holds:

1. The true factor is strictly positive, normalized, and has \(\kappa(u^*)=1\).
2. All measurements are at least 1, strictly above \(.99\). The nonzero noise values are 3.
3. The clean graph has minimum degree 50; every vertex has corrupted degree 1. Hence
   \[
   50>\frac{48}{(.99)^2}=\frac{480000}{9801}\approx48.9746.
   \]
4. The clean and total graphs are connected and non-bipartite: vertices 1, 2 and any vertex of \(B\) form a clean triangle. This meets even Theorem 5's stronger clean-graph non-bipartiteness condition. Replacing the total graph by the clean graph in Theorem 22 would not fix the counterexample.

First, the true factor is a **strict local minimum** of the specified objective. For a perturbation direction \(h\), define

\[
S(h)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in B}|h_i+h_j|,\qquad T(h)=|h_1+h_2|.
\]

At \(u^*=\mathbf1\), the quartic regularizer has zero first derivative. Each vertex has exactly one bad neighbor, so the ordinary directional derivative is

\[
F'(u^*;h)=2S(h)-2\sum_i h_i+2T(h).
\]

Because \(\sum_{i\in A,j\in B}(h_i+h_j)=k\sum_i h_i\),

\[
F'(u^*;h)\geq 2(1-1/k)S(h)+2T(h).
\]

If \(S(h)=0\), then \(h_i=a\) on \(A\) and \(h_j=-a\) on \(B\). Then \(T(h)=2|a|\), so the lower bound is strictly positive for every nonzero \(h\).

This first-order argument also gives an explicit neighborhood, so it does not confuse stationarity with local minimality. Write \(M=\|h\|_\infty\). Comparing entries through any vertex of \(B\) gives

\[
M\leq\tfrac12 T(h)+\tfrac32 S(h),
\qquad F'(u^*;h)\geq\frac{98}{75}M.
\]

There are 5,102 ordered measurements. For \(M<10^{-4}\), every corrupted residual stays negative, each quadratic product remainder has absolute value at most \(M^2\), and the regularizer is nonnegative. Therefore

\[
F(u^*+h)-F(u^*)\geq
\left(\frac{98}{75}-5102M\right)M>0
\quad (0<M<10^{-4}).
\]

Nevertheless, this strict local minimum is **not global**. Along the positive feasible curve

\[
u_i(t)=\begin{cases}t&i\in A,\\t^{-1}&i\in B,\end{cases}
\qquad 1<t<2,
\]

all clean cross-part products remain 1. The clean internal edge contributes \(2(t^2-1)\); the bad matchings contribute \(k(4-t^2)+k(4-t^{-2})\); and the regularizer contributes \(k^2(t-1)^4\). Thus

\[
F(u(t))-F(u^*)=
2(t^2-1)-50(t^2+t^{-2}-2)+2500(t-1)^4.
\]

At the rational point \(t=11/10\),

\[
F(u^*)=300,\qquad
F(u(t))-F(u^*)=-\frac{13943}{12100}\approx-1.152314<0.
\]

This is a strict spurious local minimum under the paper's own definition: it is a local minimum with a feasible point of strictly lower objective value. It contradicts both Theorem 22's absence claim and its asserted global recovery at the true factors.

The failure also persists if measurements are counted only once in the upper triangle: the same point is a strict local minimum, and the objective gap at \(t=11/10\), with the same prescribed regularizer, is \(-5459/12100<0\). The counterexample does not depend on doubling symmetric measurements.

**An asymmetric counterexample to the same guarantee.** Set \(m=n=100\), split both rows and columns into two groups of 50, and let all true factors equal 1. Clean measurements are the two diagonal \(50\times50\) blocks, together with the bridge \((r_1,c_{51})\). Corrupted measurements are perfect matchings in both off-diagonal blocks: match \(r_{i+1}\) to \(c_{51+((i+1)\bmod50)}\) and \(r_{51+i}\) to \(c_{1+i}\), for \(0\leq i<50\). Give clean entries value 1 and bad entries value 4. The clean bridge is not corrupted. The clean bipartite graph is connected with minimum degree 50, every bad degree is 1, and the same \(c=.99\), \(\kappa=1\), and normalized balanced truth satisfy Theorem 23. Use its prescribed \(\lambda=(m+n)/2=100\), and any \(\alpha>0\).

For the symmetrized objective, let

\[
u(t)=(t\mathbf1_{50},t^{-1}\mathbf1_{50}),\qquad
v(t)=(t^{-1}\mathbf1_{50},t\mathbf1_{50}).
\]

The balancing penalty vanishes identically. Direct substitution gives

\[
F(w(t))-F(w^*)=
2(t^2-1)-100(t^2+t^{-2}-2)+10000(t-1)^4.
\]

Here \(F(w^*)=600\), and at \(t=11/10\) the difference is \(-13459/6050\approx-2.224628\).

The true factors are again a strict local minimum. Let \(S\) sum \(|h_{u_i}+h_{v_j}|\) over the two clean diagonal blocks, let \(T=|h_{u_1}+h_{v_{51}}|\), and let \(H=\sum_i h_{u_i}-\sum_j h_{v_j}\). The same degree identity yields

\[
F'(w^*;h)\geq2(1-1/k)S+2T+2\alpha|H|.
\]

If all three terms vanish, the two blocks permit reciprocal modes \(a,b\); the bridge forces \(a=b\); the norm-balance derivative forces \(a=b=0\). Hence the bound is positive on every nonzero direction. Continuity on the unit sphere gives uniform positive linear growth, and the finite absolute-quadratic objective has a uniform quadratic remainder. This establishes a strict local minimum with an explicit lower feasible objective. The balancing penalty and clean connectivity therefore do not preserve the claimed asymmetric landscape.

The quartic regularizer is coercive, so a global minimum is attained. It is distinct from the true factors by the strict objective gap, and distinct from the origin, whose objective is 10,802. Connectedness and positive measurements exclude a nonzero boundary local minimum: a zero coordinate adjacent to a positive coordinate has a strictly decreasing feasible coordinate direction, while its balance and quartic terms have zero first derivative. Thus there is another positive global, hence D-min-stationary, point, contradicting Theorem 23's explicit stationary-point classification.

**Why the degree argument fails.** High clean degree can come almost entirely from measurements invariant under a reciprocal scaling. In the symmetric example, all dense cross-part measurements are invariant; in the asymmetric example, all diagonal-block measurements are invariant. Only the few odd-cycle or bridge constraints identify the relative scale. Equation (110) lower-bounds their clean directional contribution using the full clean degree, overlooking cancellation between the extreme-ratio sets \(T_1\) and \(T_2\). The corrupted distinguishing constraints can dominate even when their maximum degree is tiny. Connectivity/non-bipartiteness gives qualitative identifiability in the clean problem, but does not give the required quantitative resistance to corruptions.

No fixed change to the numerical multiplier 48 repairs this defect. Enlarging the blocks increases the clean-to-bad degree ratio without adding distinguishing clean constraints. In the simpler variant retaining only two bad internal edges, the same reciprocal curve decreases the objective at the truth to first order while the regularizer grows only to fourth order; this persists for arbitrarily large blocks. A valid deterministic theorem needs additional control on informative constraints, or a materially different objective or argument.

**Reason for rejection.** Both symmetric and asymmetric deterministic recovery and landscape guarantees are central advertised contributions. The specified objectives have strict spurious local minima in admissible instances, and the claimed true global solutions have strictly higher objective values than explicit feasible alternatives. These are false main results, rather than merely missing proof details. Their use as building blocks also leaves the subsequent supplied arguments unsupported at that step. The counterexamples do not by themselves refute a high-probability statement under independent random sampling or any particular historical empirical curve; those claims are not reported as separately false. The exact failure of the central deterministic guarantees warrants rejection as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Appendix H's degree-based lower bound, I examined reciprocal-scaling directions that leave dense clean sets unchanged. This exposed the difference between vertex degree and the number of constraints informative about that direction. Matching corruptions then supplied a strict spurious-local-minimum construction.

**Verification method.** Read all 51 original PDF pages, including Appendices A–J, and rechecked the definitions, Assumption 1, regularizers and theorem statements against rendered pages 5, 22–24 and 43–45. Enumerated the finite graphs, checked every degree/connectivity/bipartiteness condition, and evaluated the full objectives with exact rational arithmetic. Re-derived the all-direction local growth proofs and exact zero subgradient certificates. Independent review checked the original PDF and additional block sizes, rational perturbations and directional identities. Review continued through the experiments and other proofs; historical simulation arrays and the authors' modified implementation were unavailable and are not needed for these objective counterexamples.

The strict-local-minimum proofs cover every nonzero direction and control the nonlinear remainder, and all relevant paper assumptions hold with strict margins. findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 4, PDF page 14, Equation (30); its proof in Appendix A.2, PDF pages 43–44, starting at Equation (124). Consequences claimed on PDF pages 16 and 22, Discussion page 32, and Table 1/page 33. Abstract policies are defined on PDF page 10, Definition 3; general real-valued features replace the one-hot assumption starting on PDF page 12, Section 4.2.

**Claim.** For arbitrary real-valued state features, a LAM with reward error `εr` and expected next-feature error `εp` permits linear predictions of the value and Q-value of every abstract policy, with error at most `(εr + γ εp ||vπ||)/(1−γ)`. Thus zero errors imply exact value and Q-value representation for every such policy. The paper uses this conclusion to claim that LSFM reward-predictive features generalize across all policies, including optimal policies, without changing the representation. This is a principal distinction from value-predictive features in the paper's comparison.

**Error and evidence.** Predicting expected rewards for every fixed action sequence does not preserve the value of policies that condition later actions on the observed latent state. The following finite MDP satisfies the paper's assumptions and has exact reward-predictive LAM and LSFM models, yet contradicts both the zero-error value guarantee and the claimed preservation of optimal control.

Take discount `γ=1/2`, states `A,B,C,D,E,Z`, and actions `a,b,c`. Write `e1,e2,e3` for the standard basis of `R³`. Set

| State | Feature | Next state under either a or b | Reward a | Reward b | Next state under c | Reward c |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | e1 | C | 0 | 0 | Z | 3/4 |
| B | e1 | D or E, each with probability 1/2 | 0 | 0 | Z | 3/4 |
| C | (e2+e3)/2 | C | 1/2 | 1/2 | Z | 0 |
| D | e2 | D | 1 | 0 | Z | 0 |
| E | e3 | E | 0 | 1 | Z | 0 |
| Z | 0 | Z | 0 | 0 | Z | 0 |

Rewards are deterministic given state and action and bounded by one. The feature matrix has full column rank, feature norms are at most one, and every policy specified below depends only on the feature vector. There is no missing-data, reward-noise, unboundedness, or feature-rank issue.

For actions a and b use

```
M = [[0, 1/2, 1/2],
     [0,   1,   0],
     [0,   0,   1]],
w_a = (0,1,0)^T,    w_b = (0,0,1)^T.
```

For action c use `M_c=0` and `w_c=(3/4,0,0)^T`. At every state and action, `E[φ(s′)|s,a]=φ(s)^T M_a` and `r(s,a)=φ(s)^T w_a`, using the paper's row-feature convention. In particular, the deterministic transition A→C and the randomized transition B→D/E have the same expected next feature. Hence `εr=εp=0`. Induction proves that the model predicts the expected reward at every horizon for every fixed action sequence exactly.

This also is an exact LSFM for the uniformly random target policy used in Section 4.2. Set

```
F_bar = [[1, 1/4, 1/4],
         [0, 3/2,   0],
         [0,   0, 3/2]],
F_a = F_b = [[1, 3/8, 3/8],
             [0, 7/4,   0],
             [0,   0, 7/4]],
F_c = I.
```

Then `F_bar=(F_a+F_b+F_c)/3` and `F_j=I+γ M_j F_bar` for every action. The same exact transition identities give `εψ=0` and `Δ=0`. Even the unstated contraction condition needed elsewhere in the appendix is satisfied: `γ max_j ||M_j||_F = sqrt(5/2)/2 < 1`.

Now consider the abstract policy that selects a at A,B,C,D, b at E, and c at Z. It respects `φ(A)=φ(B)` and is therefore allowed by Definition 3. Its values, with the Bellman/return convention used in the proof and Equation (34), are

```
Vπ(C)=1, Vπ(D)=Vπ(E)=2,
Vπ(A)=1/2, Vπ(B)=1, Vπ(Z)=0.
```

Since `φ(A)=φ(B)`, every linear predictor gives the same prediction at A and B. It cannot equal both 1/2 and 1, whereas Theorem 4's right-hand side is exactly zero. Indeed, any decoder of the feature vector, even nonlinear, must have maximum error at least 1/4 on A and B. Equation (1) earlier in the paper prints an extra factor γ; following that convention rescales both values and still gives the same contradiction. The failure does not depend on this indexing inconsistency.

The loss of control information is also concrete. In this same MDP the optimal values of a/b at A are 1/2, versus 3/4 for c, so A uniquely prefers c. At B the optimal values of a/b are 1, versus 3/4 for c, so B prefers a or b. Because the sets of optimal actions are disjoint and the features at A and B are identical, **no abstract policy can be optimal at both states**. Thus exact LSFM reward prediction can discard information necessary for optimal control even before any transfer or approximation error.

The invalid first step of the proof is Equation (124). It silently requires the existence of a coefficient vector whose feature prediction satisfies the policy Bellman equation, although the assumptions establish closure only under each fixed action's linear reward/expected-feature map. Mixing actions according to a state-dependent policy need not preserve that linear space. Subsequent bounds on one-step errors cannot establish the missing existence statement. The explicit counterexample shows that this is a false theorem, rather than merely an incomplete derivation.

**Reason for rejection.** The central general-real-feature connection between exact LSFM reward prediction, all-policy value prediction, and optimal control is false. Table 1's advertised all-policy property and the policy/optimal-control conclusions on pages 22 and 32 fail even at zero model error. Restricting to one-hot/bisimulation features would restore the earlier, narrower setting that Section 4.2 explicitly relaxes; restricting to fixed action sequences would remove the feedback-policy/optimal-control conclusion. Neither is a routine constant or proof correction preserving the paper's claimed distinction. The finite experiments cannot establish this false general guarantee. This warrants rejecting the paper as written, while leaving its separate fixed-action-sequence prediction and one-hot bisimulation results unrefuted.

**Discovery method.** Compared the open-loop reward-prediction definition with the claimed extension to arbitrary feedback policies. The paper's own Figure 4 distinguishes a deterministic intermediate state from a mixture with the same expected feature; allowing subsequent actions to respond differently at the mixture components suggested the counterexample.

**Verification method.** Read all 53 PDF pages, all of Appendices A–C, and the experiment protocols. Rechecked Definition 3, Theorem 4, Equation (124), and the policy claims against the original rendered pages. The reproducible helper uses exact rational arithmetic to verify every transition, reward, successor-feature, and Bellman identity. It checks six discount choices for the five-state value witness, 90 open-loop state/horizon/reward checks, and the six-state optimal-control extension. An unchanged matrix-LSFM class from the related author's August 2020 repository also gives exactly zero reward, SF, and total loss for the six-state construction under TensorFlow 2.3.4 compatibility mode. That repository identifies a distinct related paper, so this native check is not presented as an authentication or rerun of JMLR's historical figures.

An independent reviewer checked the original definition, theorem and proof pages, reconstructed the exact matrices, and solved all 243 deterministic abstract policies in the six-state example. None is optimal at both A and B; the disjoint optimal-action sets also exclude randomized abstract policies.

**Confidence: High.** A finite exact counterexample meets all relevant stated assumptions and forces unequal true values and disjoint optimal actions at identical features. The result does not rely on numerical optimization, unavailable historical data, or an unproved assertion about the theorem's falsity.

 Source provenance is retained in `source-provenance.json`.

This also is an exact LSFM for the uniformly random target policy used in Section 4.2. Set

F_bar = [[1, 1/4, 1/4],
         [0, 3/2,   0],
         [0,   0, 3/2]],
F_a = F_b = [[1, 3/8, 3/8],
             [0, 7/4,   0],
             [0,   0, 7/4]],
F_c = I.

Then F_bar=(F_a+F_b+F_c)/3 and F_j=I+γ M_j F_bar for every action. The same exact transition identities give \(\epsilon \psi =0\) and \(\Delta =0\). Even the unstated contraction condition needed elsewhere in the appendix is satisfied: \(\gamma \max _{j} \lVert M_{j}\rVert _{F} = \operatorname{sqrt}(5/2)/2 < 1\).

Now consider the abstract policy that selects a at A,B,C,D, b at E, and c at Z. It respects \(\phi (A)=\phi (B)\) and is therefore allowed by Definition 3. Its values, with the Bellman/return convention used in the proof and Equation (34), are

Vπ(C)=1, Vπ(D)=Vπ(E)=2,
Vπ(A)=1/2, Vπ(B)=1, Vπ(Z)=0.

Since \(\phi (A)=\phi (B)\), every linear predictor gives the same prediction at A and B. It cannot equal both 1/2 and 1, whereas Theorem 4's right-hand side is exactly zero. Indeed, any decoder of the feature vector, even nonlinear, must have maximum error at least 1/4 on A and B. Equation (1) earlier in the paper prints an extra factor γ; following that convention rescales both values and still gives the same contradiction. The failure does not depend on this indexing inconsistency.

The loss of control information is also concrete. In this same MDP the optimal values of a/b at A are 1/2, versus 3/4 for c, so A uniquely prefers c. At B the optimal values of a/b are 1, versus 3/4 for c, so B prefers a or b. Because the sets of optimal actions are disjoint and the features at A and B are identical, no abstract policy can be optimal at both states. Thus exact LSFM reward prediction can discard information necessary for optimal control even before any transfer or approximation error.

The invalid first step of the proof is Equation (124). It silently requires the existence of a coefficient vector whose feature prediction satisfies the policy Bellman equation, although the assumptions establish closure only under each fixed action's linear reward/expected-feature map. Mixing actions according to a state-dependent policy need not preserve that linear space. Subsequent bounds on one-step errors cannot establish the missing existence statement. The explicit counterexample shows that this is a false theorem, rather than merely an incomplete derivation.

Reason for rejection. The central general-real-feature connection between exact LSFM reward prediction, all-policy value prediction, and optimal control is false. Table 1's advertised all-policy property and the policy/optimal-control conclusions on pages 22 and 32 fail even at zero model error. Restricting to one-hot/bisimulation features would restore the earlier, narrower setting that Section 4.2 explicitly relaxes; restricting to fixed action sequences would remove the feedback-policy/optimal-control conclusion. Neither is a routine constant or proof correction preserving the paper's claimed distinction. The finite experiments cannot establish this false general guarantee. This warrants rejecting the paper as written, while leaving its separate fixed-action-sequence prediction and one-hot bisimulation results unrefuted.

Discovery method. Compared the open-loop reward-prediction definition with the claimed extension to arbitrary feedback policies. The paper's own Figure 4 distinguishes a deterministic intermediate state from a mixture with the same expected feature; allowing subsequent actions to respond differently at the mixture components suggested the counterexample.

Verification method. Read all 53 PDF pages, all of Appendices A–C, and the experiment protocols. Rechecked Definition 3, Theorem 4, Equation (124), and the policy claims against the original rendered pages. The reproducible helper uses exact rational arithmetic to verify every transition, reward, successor-feature, and Bellman identity. It checks six discount choices for the five-state value witness, 90 open-loop state/horizon/reward checks, and the six-state optimal-control extension. An unchanged matrix-LSFM class from the related author's August 2020 repository also gives exactly zero reward, SF, and total loss for the six-state construction under TensorFlow 2.3.4 compatibility mode. That repository identifies a distinct related paper, so this native check is not presented as an authentication or rerun of JMLR's historical figures.

An independent reviewer checked the original definition, theorem and proof pages, reconstructed the exact matrices, and solved all 243 deterministic abstract policies in the six-state example. None is optimal at both A and B; the disjoint optimal-action sets also exclude randomized abstract policies.

Confidence: High. A finite exact counterexample meets all relevant stated assumptions and forces unequal true values and disjoint optimal actions at identical features. The result does not rely on numerical optimization, unavailable historical data, or an unproved assertion about the theorem's falsity.

findings.title: The accelerated MSE theorem admits estimators with infinite MSE at every sample size
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-102-I01 — The accelerated MSE theorem admits estimators with infinite MSE at every sample size
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 19, Section 4.4, Theorem 4, equation (23) and Remark 5; proof in Appendix A.3, PDF pages 41–42, especially equations (50)–(51). The reciprocal-moment mistake also occurs in Theorem 2, page 12, and Appendix A.2, pages 40–41. These are instances of one underlying error.

**Claim.** Theorem 4 considers three independently generated valid AIS normalizing-constant estimators. It assumes that their individual weight variances obey

$$
\operatorname{Var}(w^+_{1,n})\le s^+_1n^{-a},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(w^-_{1,k})\le s^-_1k^{-b},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(w_{2,m})\le s_2m^{-c},
$$

for positive constants. It concludes an expected squared-error bound for their ratio, with an asymptotically dominated remainder. Remark 5 consequently claims MSE $O(M^{-2})$ when $N=K=M$ and $a=b=c>1$. Neither the theorem nor its proof imposes a lower-tail or inverse-moment condition on the denominator estimator.

**Error and evidence.** Vanishing variance of a positive denominator does not control the moments of its reciprocal. The following proper Bayesian model satisfies the stated hypotheses and makes the expected squared error infinite for every finite $M$.

Let $X\sim\mathcal N(0,2)$ and $Y\mid X=x\sim\mathcal N(x,2)$, where the second argument denotes variance, and observe $Y=0$. Write $\phi$ for the standard normal density and $C=(8\pi)^{-1/2}$. Then

$$
\gamma_2(x)=p(x,Y=0)=C\phi(x),\qquad E_2=C,
$$

and the posterior is $\phi$. Choose the bounded nonconstant target

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}2,&x\ge0,\\-1,&x<0.\end{cases}
$$

Thus $E^+_1=C$, $E^-_1=C/2$, and $\mu=1/2$. Use the two normalized half-normal proposals

$$q^+_1(x)=2\phi(x)\mathbf1_{x\ge0},\qquad
q^-_1(x)=2\phi(x)\mathbf1_{x<0}.$$

Every numerator weight is respectively exactly $C$ and $C/2$. The two numerator estimates therefore have variance zero for every positive sample size. Their normalizing constants are strictly positive; this construction does not use a zero-mass target or an undefined proposal.

For denominator sample $m$, use the normalized full-support proposal

$$
q_m(x)=(1-\epsilon_m)\phi(x)+\epsilon_m h(x),\qquad
\epsilon_m=(m+1)^{-2},\qquad h(x)=\frac1{\pi(1+x^2)}.
$$

Draw the denominator samples independently, also independently of both numerator estimators. This is a deterministic proposal-update schedule satisfying the theorem's convergence and weight-variance hypotheses. In particular, $q_m$ converges to the exact optimal proposal $\phi$ in total variation. Every importance weight $w_{2,m}=C\phi(X_m)/q_m(X_m)$ is positive, unbiased for $C$, and uniformly bounded above by $4C/3$. All its positive moments are finite. Moreover,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(w_{2,m})}{C^2}
&=\int\frac{\phi(x)^2}{q_m(x)}\,dx-1\\
&\le\frac1{1-\epsilon_m}-1
=\frac1{m(m+2)}\le\frac1{m^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence Theorem 4 applies with $a=b=c=2$, $s_2=C^2$ and, for example, $s^+_1=s^-_1=C^2>0$. For $N=K=M$ its displayed bound and dominated remainder predict vanishing finite MSE. The actual estimator is

$$\widehat\mu_M=\frac{C/2}{\widehat Z_{2,M}},\qquad
\widehat Z_{2,M}=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M w_{2,m}.$$

Fix any finite $M$. Define

$$A_M=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M(m+1)^2,\qquad t_R=1+(R+1)^2.$$

For $R\ge1$, the event $B_R=\{X_m\in[R,R+1]\text{ for every }m\le M\}$ has probability at least

$$\Pr(B_R)\ge\frac1{((M+1)!)^2\pi^M t_R^M},$$

because $q_m\ge\epsilon_m h$ and $h(x)\ge(\pi t_R)^{-1}$ on that interval. On $B_R$,

$$
\frac{\widehat Z_{2,M}}C
\le b_R:=A_M\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,t_R e^{-R^2/2},
$$

using $\phi(x)\le(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-R^2/2}$ and $q_m(x)\ge\epsilon_m/(\pi t_R)$. For all sufficiently large $R$, $b_R\le1/2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(\widehat\mu_M-1/2)^2]
&\ge\frac{\Pr(B_R)}{16b_R^2}\\
&\ge\frac{e^{R^2}}
{8 A_M^2\pi^{M+1}((M+1)!)^2t_R^{M+2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last expression tends to infinity as $R\to\infty$ for each fixed $M$. Therefore

$$\boxed{\mathbb E[(\widehat\mu_M-\mu)^2]=\infty\quad\text{for every finite }M.}$$

This is an analytic tail bound, not an inference from an unstable simulation. The estimator may still converge in probability; that does not imply MSE convergence. No asymptotically dominated finite remainder in (23) can absorb an infinite expected squared error at every sample size.

Appendix A.3 first expands the reciprocal denominator and then takes expectations in (50) and variances in (51), declaring discarded products/remainders dominated without a condition controlling small denominator values. The counterexample identifies exactly why this step fails even with bounded ordinary importance weights, independent samples and faster-than-$1/m$ variance decay. The assertion on page 42 that adaptive weights are independent is also generally too strong; martingale uncorrelatedness can justify the component variance sum, but does not repair the reciprocal-moment failure shown here.

**Reason for rejection.** Theorem 4 and Remark 5 are the paper's central theoretical justification for its new TAAIS claim of faster-than-Monte-Carlo MSE rates, emphasized in the abstract, introduction and Sections4.4–4.5. Under their own sufficient conditions the method can instead have infinite MSE at every budget. Restoring an expected-error guarantee requires substantive denominator lower-tail/inverse-moment assumptions or a modified guarded estimator and a new proof; convergence to the optimal proposal and decay of ordinary weight variance alone do not suffice. The counterexample uses a standard heavy-tailed defensive mixture, so the missing restriction materially changes the admitted proposal class. The exact-oracle decomposition in Theorem 1 and possible empirical gains remain valid, but they do not establish the advertised general accelerated expected-MSE guarantee. This loss of a principal theoretical contribution warrants rejection of the paper as written. No failure of a particular historical experiment is alleged.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the reciprocal Taylor expansions used to convert component-variance decay into ratio MSE, I checked whether the proof controlled inverse moments. I then used a Gaussian target and a vanishing Cauchy mixture to isolate the missing lower-tail control.

**Verification method.** I re-read Theorem 4/Remark 5 and complete Appendices A.2–A.3 in the original PDF and inspected rendered pages 19, 40, 41 and 42; no resolving inverse-moment condition appears. The exact construction above checks every stated condition and yields the divergent tail lower bound. The independent helper verifies 1000 rational variance identities, 200 numerator-weight fixtures, seven numerical chi-square variance checks and 21 finite tail-bound evaluations; it exits 0. These numerical checks supplement the analytic proof. The full paper review continued after finding this issue.

Independent bounded verification also reconstructed a different numerator target and a faster-decaying defensive-mixture schedule, checked the original assumptions and reached the same infinite-MSE conclusion. Its exact calculations and finite controls all passed. This was independent bounded verification, rather than a second full-paper review.

**Confidence.** High. The assumptions, bounded weight-variance estimate and infinite-MSE lower bound are explicit and analytic; the conclusion is independent of implementation, numerical tail sampling, and interpretation of finite empirical curves.

Paper: Asymptotic Consistency of \(\alpha\)-{R}ényi-Approximate Posteriors ID: 2020__accepted__v21-19-161

Review coverage: All 42 PDF pages, including the entire Appendix A and references. All seven contact sheets and individual original pages 9, 10, 13, 14, 17, 33, and 34 inspected. Checking continued after finding the counterexample.

findings.markdown:
### Exact location and claim

Theorem9, PDF14, asserts consistency of every global α-Rényi minimizer under Assumptions1–4. Theorem14, PDF17, asserts the analogous reverse-KL consistency. Assumption4, PDF9, requires arbitrarily concentrated log-concave **good sequences**, not log-concavity of the whole family; PDF10 expressly distinguishes the good sequence from the minimizer. Proposition8, PDF13, and its proof PDF31–34 supply the claimed vanishing divergence used in both main theorems. The invalid asymptotic replacement is PDF33 following Equation56: the Laplace approximation treats the n-dependent factor qbar_n^(1−alpha) as if it were fixed on the same n^(−1/2) scale.

## Fixed counterexample family and model

Let Xi independently follow N(theta,1), theta∈R, with theta0=0 and proper prior pi(theta)=exp(−|theta|)/2. Write m=sample mean. The exact posterior is

 r[m,n](theta) = Z_n(m)^(−1) exp[−n(theta−m)^2/2−|theta|].

Set eta=10^(−6), g=N(10,1). Fix, once and for all, Q as the union of (i) every Laplace(location,scale) distribution, (ii) every Dirac distribution, and (iii) every mixture

 (1−eta) r[mu,1/v] + eta*g,  mu∈[−1,1], 0<v≤1.

Here r[mu,t] is the explicitly given two-parameter density proportional to exp[−t(theta−mu)^2/2−|theta|]. Q does not depend on the sample or sample size. The posterior-matching choice mu=m,v=1/n belongs to Q whenever |m|≤1, an event that holds eventually almost surely.

## Every assumption is satisfied

Assumption1: the prior is continuous, positive at0, bounded by1/2, and has first absolute moment1. Assumption2: the normal likelihood has exact LAN with I(0)=1 and rate sqrt(n); its MLE is m, converging to0 almost surely. Assumption3: every required Dirac is present.

For **every** M>0, choose qbar_n=Laplace(m,b_n), b_n=sqrt[M/(2n)]. Its mean is exactly the MLE, variance is exactly M/n, and it is log-concave. There is a deterministic global posterior/qbar bound, so no random-threshold interpretation of Assumption4 is needed. Put u=theta−m and

 Ztilde_n(m)=integral exp[−nu²/2−|m+u|+|m|]du.

The triangle inequality and integration over |u|≤1/sqrt(n) give Ztilde≥2exp(−3/2)/sqrt(n). Completing the square then yields, for **all theta,m and n≥1**,

 r[m,n](theta)/qbar_n(theta)
 ≤ b_n sqrt(n) exp[3/2+(1+1/b_n)^2/(2n)]
 ≤ sqrt(M/2) exp[3/2+(1+sqrt(2/M))²/2] = M_r(M) < infinity.

Thus any fixed compact ball containing0 meets Assumption4(3), with n1=n2=n3=n_M=1, and all remaining good-sequence properties hold exactly. Posterior consistency and local normality also hold here; the counterexample does not exploit a globally inconsistent likelihood.

## Uniform gap separating all Laplace members

Let P=N(0,1) and any L=Laplace(a,b). Its total-variation distance from P is at least delta=1/250.

If |a|≥.1, the event (−infinity,a] gives distance at least Phi(.1)−.5>.0398>delta. If |a|<.1, the two-sided Laplace tails at t=.5,1,1.5 have the form C exp(−t/b), so L(|X|>1)^2=L(|X|>.5)L(|X|>1.5). The standard normal tails violate that identity by

 P(|X|>1)^2−P(|X|>.5)P(|X|>1.5) > .018 > 4delta=.016.

Each event probability differs by at most TV, so a product difference can change by at most4TV. Hence TV(P,L)>delta. The companion helper certifies these constants with200-bit Arb intervals; this is a uniform analytic bound over every location and scale, not a finite optimizer search. Location/scale invariance gives the same bound for N(m,1/n).

Uniformly in m, the exact posterior r[m,n] has TV distance at most8/sqrt(n) from N(m,1/n), for n≥4. To verify this, let Z~N(0,1), a=1/sqrt(n), and w(Z)=exp[−|m+aZ|+|m|]. Then exp(−a|Z|)≤w≤exp(a|Z|), E w≥1−a, and E|w−1|≤4a because E|Z|exp(|Z|)<4. Therefore TV=E|w/Ew−1|/2≤E|w−1|/Ew≤8a.

For n≥16,000,000, every Laplace L consequently satisfies TV(r[m,n],L)≥delta/2. Pinsker and Rényi monotonicity give

 D2(r[m,n]||L) ≥ KL(r[m,n]||L) ≥ 2(delta/2)^2 = 1/125000 = .000008.

## Every global minimizer is inconsistent

The matching fixed-weight mixture q=(1−eta)r[m,n]+eta*g satisfies q≥(1−eta)r[m,n], hence

 D2(r[m,n]||q) ≤ −log(1−eta) < .000001000001 < .000008,

and the same upper bound holds for KL. Diracs have infinite divergence from this continuous posterior. Thus, eventually almost surely, **every** global D2 or reverse-KL minimizer in Q belongs to the fixed-weight mixture class.

The minima exist. Compactify its parameters by adding v=0, where the Gaussian-Laplace factor r[mu,1/v] converges weakly to delta_mu. Divergence is lower semicontinuous. At v=0 the continuous part is eta*g, so either divergence equals its divergence to g minus log eta, and is at least−log eta, much larger than the matching candidate. On v>0 ordinary dominated convergence applies (q≥eta*g and r[m,n]^2/g integrable for n≥1). Therefore the compactified minimum lies at v>0, in the stated Q. These standard arguments can alternatively be checked directly by Fatou for D2.

Every such minimizer has q(|theta|>1)≥eta*g(|theta|>1)>eta/2=5×10^(−7), uniformly in n. Since P(|m|≤1) tends to1, these minimizers cannot converge weakly to delta0, even in probability. Theorems9 and14 are false for a family satisfying every stated hypothesis.

## Direct diagnosis of the proof

Even the good sequence used by the paper's zero-bound argument need not have vanishing divergence. For alpha2, I1 and M=2/e, choose the above good Laplace sequence. In local normal coordinates its scale is c=1/sqrt(e). Its limiting D2 is

 log[(c/sqrt(pi))*exp(1/(4c²))*(1+erf(1/(2c)))] > .1,

whereas the zero-divergence inference in Theorem9 fixes this variance constant and claims an asymptotic upper bound0. Proposition8 itself existentially chooses a variance-bound constant for a sequence; this diagnostic concerns the proof's specific subsequent choice, rather than an assertion that every interpretation of Proposition8's quantifier is false. The n-dependent Laplace factor changes on exactly the same scale as the concentrating Gaussian and cannot be removed from the integral at its value at the mode. Log-concavity and a variance upper bound do not repair this operation.

## Reject threshold, discovery, verification and limits

The main advertised contribution is sufficient-condition consistency for alpha>1 and the reverse-KL extension. The exact admissible counterexample falsifies both conclusions and the common vanishing-divergence argument. Repair requires substantively stronger approximation-family assumptions, such as vanishing attainable divergence or structural restrictions on all candidate distributions; a corrected constant or proof line cannot establish the theorem as written.

Discovery: the proof moves from a bounded good-sequence divergence to zero divergence by choosing a variance constant, despite allowing non-Gaussian log-concave shapes. Verification: original assumptions/proof and all appendices rechecked; explicit model/fixed family; global deterministic assumption bounds; uniform TV separation certified with Arb; exact divergence comparisons and minimizer existence. The executable also evaluates representative good-sequence integrals. No empirical learning claim or historical figure replay is used. **Confidence: High.** The analytic construction satisfies every stated assumption and forces every attained minimizer to retain fixed contamination. A second reviewer independently rechecked the original assumptions/theorems/proof and minimum-attainment argument, and ran 20 posterior-normal integral checks and 100 global-ratio checks with actual exit status 0. This confirms a false central theorem, rather than an unfilled proof gap.

 The analytic argument above establishes the uniform bounds and minimizer failure independently of finite numerical sampling.

Exact location and claim

Theorem9, PDF14, asserts consistency of every global α-Rényi minimizer under Assumptions1–4. Theorem14, PDF17, asserts the analogous reverse-KL consistency. Assumption4, PDF9, requires arbitrarily concentrated log-concave good sequences, not log-concavity of the whole family; PDF10 expressly distinguishes the good sequence from the minimizer. Proposition8, PDF13, and its proof PDF31–34 supply the claimed vanishing divergence used in both main theorems. The invalid asymptotic replacement is PDF33 following Equation56: the Laplace approximation treats the n-dependent factor qbar_n^(1−alpha) as if it were fixed on the same n^(−1/2) scale.

Fixed counterexample family and model

Let Xi independently follow N(theta,1), theta∈R, with theta0=0 and proper prior pi(theta)=exp(−|theta|)/2. Write m=sample mean. The exact posterior is

\[ r[m,n](\theta)=Z_n(m)^{-1}\exp\!\left[-\frac{n(\theta-m)^2}{2}-|\theta|\right]. \]

Set eta=10^(−6), g=N(10,1). Fix, once and for all, Q as the union of (i) every Laplace(location,scale) distribution, (ii) every Dirac distribution, and (iii) every mixture

(1−eta) r[mu,1/v] + eta*g, mu∈[−1,1], 0<v≤1.

Here r[mu,t] is the explicitly given two-parameter density proportional to exp[−t(theta−mu)^2/2−|theta|]. Q does not depend on the sample or sample size. The posterior-matching choice mu=m,v=1/n belongs to Q whenever |m|≤1, an event that holds eventually almost surely.

Every assumption is satisfied

Assumption1: the prior is continuous, positive at0, bounded by1/2, and has first absolute moment1. Assumption2: the normal likelihood has exact LAN with I(0)=1 and rate sqrt(n); its MLE is m, converging to0 almost surely. Assumption3: every required Dirac is present.

For every M>0, choose qbar_n=Laplace(m,b_n), b_n=sqrt[M/(2n)]. Its mean is exactly the MLE, variance is exactly M/n, and it is log-concave. There is a deterministic global posterior/qbar bound, so no random-threshold interpretation of Assumption4 is needed. Put u=theta−m and

Ztilde_n(m)=integral exp[−nu²/2−|m+u|+|m|]du.

The triangle inequality and integration over |u|≤1/sqrt(n) give Ztilde≥2exp(−3/2)/sqrt(n). Completing the square then yields, for all theta,m and n≥1,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{r[m,n](\theta)}{\bar q_n(\theta)}&\le b_n\sqrt{n}\,\exp\!\left[\frac{3}{2}+\frac{(1+1/b_n)^2}{2n}\right]\\ &\le\sqrt{\frac{M}{2}}\,\exp\!\left[\frac{3}{2}+\frac{(1+\sqrt{2/M})^2}{2}\right]=M_r(M)<\infty. \end{aligned} \]

Thus any fixed compact ball containing0 meets Assumption4(3), with n1=n2=n3=n_M=1, and all remaining good-sequence properties hold exactly. Posterior consistency and local normality also hold here; the counterexample does not exploit a globally inconsistent likelihood.

Uniform gap separating all Laplace members

Let P=N(0,1) and any L=Laplace(a,b). Its total-variation distance from P is at least delta=1/250.

If |a|≥.1, the event (−infinity,a] gives distance at least Phi(.1)−.5>.0398>delta. If |a|<.1, the two-sided Laplace tails at t=.5,1,1.5 have the form C exp(−t/b), so L(|X|>1)^2=L(|X|>.5)L(|X|>1.5). The standard normal tails violate that identity by

P(|X|>1)^2−P(|X|>.5)P(|X|>1.5) > .018 > 4delta=.016.

Each event probability differs by at most TV, so a product difference can change by at most4TV. Hence TV(P,L)>delta. The companion helper certifies these constants with200-bit Arb intervals; this is a uniform analytic bound over every location and scale, not a finite optimizer search. Location/scale invariance gives the same bound for N(m,1/n).

Uniformly in m, the exact posterior r[m,n] has TV distance at most8/sqrt(n) from N(m,1/n), for n≥4. To verify this, let Z~N(0,1), a=1/sqrt(n), and w(Z)=exp[−|m+aZ|+|m|]. Then exp(−a|Z|)≤w≤exp(a|Z|), E w≥1−a, and E|w−1|≤4a because E|Z|exp(|Z|)<4. Therefore TV=E|w/Ew−1|/2≤E|w−1|/Ew≤8a.

For n≥16,000,000, every Laplace L consequently satisfies TV(r[m,n],L)≥delta/2. Pinsker and Rényi monotonicity give

D2(r[m,n]||L) ≥ KL(r[m,n]||L) ≥ 2(delta/2)^2 = 1/125000 = .000008.

Every global minimizer is inconsistent

The matching fixed-weight mixture q=(1−eta)r[m,n]+eta*g satisfies q≥(1−eta)r[m,n], hence

D2(r[m,n]||q) ≤ −log(1−eta) < .000001000001 < .000008,

and the same upper bound holds for KL. Diracs have infinite divergence from this continuous posterior. Thus, eventually almost surely, every global D2 or reverse-KL minimizer in Q belongs to the fixed-weight mixture class.

The minima exist. Compactify its parameters by adding v=0, where the Gaussian-Laplace factor r[mu,1/v] converges weakly to delta_mu. Divergence is lower semicontinuous. At v=0 the continuous part is etag, so either divergence equals its divergence to g minus log eta, and is at least−log eta, much larger than the matching candidate. On v>0 ordinary dominated convergence applies (q≥etag and r[m,n]^2/g integrable for n≥1). Therefore the compactified minimum lies at v>0, in the stated Q. These standard arguments can alternatively be checked directly by Fatou for D2.

Every such minimizer has q(|theta|>1)≥eta*g(|theta|>1)>eta/2=5×10^(−7), uniformly in n. Since P(|m|≤1) tends to1, these minimizers cannot converge weakly to delta0, even in probability. Theorems9 and14 are false for a family satisfying every stated hypothesis.

Direct diagnosis of the proof

Even the good sequence used by the paper's zero-bound argument need not have vanishing divergence. For alpha2, I1 and M=2/e, choose the above good Laplace sequence. In local normal coordinates its scale is c=1/sqrt(e). Its limiting D2 is

log[(c/sqrt(pi))exp(1/(4c²))(1+erf(1/(2c)))] > .1,

whereas the zero-divergence inference in Theorem9 fixes this variance constant and claims an asymptotic upper bound0. Proposition8 itself existentially chooses a variance-bound constant for a sequence; this diagnostic concerns the proof's specific subsequent choice, rather than an assertion that every interpretation of Proposition8's quantifier is false. The n-dependent Laplace factor changes on exactly the same scale as the concentrating Gaussian and cannot be removed from the integral at its value at the mode. Log-concavity and a variance upper bound do not repair this operation.

Reject threshold, discovery, verification and limits

The main advertised contribution is sufficient-condition consistency for alpha>1 and the reverse-KL extension. The exact admissible counterexample falsifies both conclusions and the common vanishing-divergence argument. Repair requires substantively stronger approximation-family assumptions, such as vanishing attainable divergence or structural restrictions on all candidate distributions; a corrected constant or proof line cannot establish the theorem as written.

Discovery: the proof moves from a bounded good-sequence divergence to zero divergence by choosing a variance constant, despite allowing non-Gaussian log-concave shapes. Verification: original assumptions/proof and all appendices rechecked; explicit model/fixed family; global deterministic assumption bounds; uniform TV separation certified with Arb; exact divergence comparisons and minimizer existence. The executable also evaluates representative good-sequence integrals. No empirical learning claim or historical figure replay is used. Confidence: High. The analytic construction satisfies every stated assumption and forces every attained minimizer to retain fixed contamination. A second reviewer independently rechecked the original assumptions/theorems/proof and minimum-attainment argument, and ran 20 posterior-normal integral checks and 100 global-ratio checks with actual exit status 0. This confirms a false central theorem, rather than an unfilled proof gap.

The analytic argument above establishes the uniform bounds and minimizer failure independently of finite numerical sampling.

findings.title: The fixed trace penalty makes the main consistency theorem false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-181-I01 — The fixed trace penalty makes the main consistency theorem false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Proposition1 and Equation(10), PDF page14; the objective in Equation(3) and its constraints, PDF page5; the fixed choice λn3=1 and conditions(A)–(E), PDF page13. The invalid proof step is AppendixA, PDF pages26–27, especially the assertion that I4≥0 at the bottom of page27. The related algorithm drops the relevant term in Step6, PDF page9.

**Claim.** For the estimators minimizing the proposed joint objective, Proposition1 asserts

\[
\max\{\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta_0\|_F,
\|\widehat X-ZZ^\top\|_F\}
=O_p\!\left(\max\left\{
\sqrt{(p_n+s_n)\log(p_n)/n},
\sqrt{p_n^2/(nK_n)-p_n/n}\right\}\right)
\]

under(A)–(E) and the three additional tuning/growth conditions in the proposition. The paper expressly fixes λn3=1. The claimed objective contains `tr(SΘ) − log det Θ + λn3 tr(XΘ)`; both other penalties omit diagonal entries, and every feasible X has Xii=1.

**Error and evidence.** At every joint local minimum of that objective, varying just Θii is feasible for sufficiently small variations because Θ is positive definite. Neither the off-diagonal lasso penalty nor the off-diagonal group penalty changes. Consequently,

\[
0=S_{ii}-(\widehat\Theta^{-1})_{ii}
+\lambda_{n3}\widehat X_{ii},
\qquad
(\widehat\Theta^{-1})_{ii}=S_{ii}+1. \tag{A}
\]

This identity already obstructs convergence to the true inverse covariance. It holds whatever communities the procedure estimates; it also holds for objective(4), since its extra log-determinant depends only on X.

Here is a sequence satisfying every stated condition. Let

\[
p_n=2\lfloor n^{1/4}\rfloor,\quad K_n=p_n/2,\quad s_n=p_n,
\quad\lambda_{n1}=\lambda_{n2}=\sqrt{\log(p_n)/n},
\quad\lambda_{n3}=1.
\]

Partition the nodes into pairs, use those pairs as the known true communities, and take independent Gaussian observations with block diagonal precision matrix whose repeated block is

\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/4\\-1/4&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}16/15&4/15\\4/15&16/15\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The true ZZᵀ consists of all-ones two-by-two blocks. Check the hypotheses explicitly:

- The eigenvalues of Σ0 are4/5 and4/3; those of ZZᵀ are0 and2. Thus(A) holds with τ1=1/2, τ2=2, τ3=3.
- Each pair supplies two nonzero off-diagonal entries, so the paper's definition gives sn=pn. All true nonzero entries have magnitude at least1/4, satisfying(E).
- Penalty derivatives in(B) are bounded by a constant times λn1+λn2, hence have the required order `(pn/sn+1) sqrt(log(pn)/n)`.
- Kn=pn/2 gives(C), and(D) becomes pn/n→0. All communities have exactly the same size.
- Proposition1(i) holds with equality in order; (ii) holds with ζ=2 because `2pn(log pn)²/n→0`; (iii) holds by construction. All required pn,sn,Kn tend to infinity, and λn1,λn2 tend to zero.

The asserted rate therefore tends to zero. But S11→16/15 in probability, while(A) forces `(Θhat⁻¹)11=S11+1`. If the claimed Frobenius convergence of Θhat were true, bounded eigenvalues of Θ0 and continuity of matrix inversion would instead force `(Θhat⁻¹)11→16/15`. These conclusions contradict each other.

The contradiction can be made quantitative. Write `d=||Θhat−Θ0||op`. On the event `|S11−16/15|≤1/2`, the norm of `Θhat⁻¹−Σ0` is at least1/2. If d<3/8, then

\[
\|\widehat\Theta^{-1}-\Sigma_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le(8/3)(4/3)d=(32/9)d.
\]

Thus d≥9/64; if d≥3/8 the same lower bound already holds. Since the event has probability tending to1,

\[
\Pr\!\left(\|\widehat\Theta-\Theta_0\|_F\ge9/64\right)\longrightarrow1.
\]

This excludes every local or global minimizing estimator claimed by the proof, rather than merely one unfortunate optimization trajectory.

For intuition, even supplying the true communities and taking the population covariance does not help. As the other penalties vanish, the precision-block optimizer is

\[
(T^{-1}+\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top)^{-1}
=\begin{pmatrix}31/40&-19/40\\-19/40&31/40\end{pmatrix},
\]

with Frobenius error9/20 per block. Independent convex optimization of the stated block problem at five penalty levels confirms the diagonal identity and the nonvanishing error; this numerical check supplements the exact argument.

The appendix's assertion that `I4=tr(ΘX)−tr(Θ0ZZᵀ)≥0` is false: set `ΔV=0` and `ΔU=−tE11`, for small positive t. This is a feasible precision perturbation and gives I4=−t. The Gaussian likelihood has zero population first derivative at Θ0, and both off-diagonal penalties remain unchanged, so this first-order descent cannot be dominated by the quadratic likelihood remainder. An upper order bound on I4 does not establish its sign.

**Reason for rejection.** The abstract and introduction identify theoretical justification for joint graph/community estimation as a central contribution and the distinction from the criticized two-step alternatives. The main joint convergence theorem is false under its own complete hypotheses. The sparsistency and community-recovery arguments rely on the missing convergence result. This is a fixed population bias, not a loose constant or a missing proof detail. Merely omitting the diagonal from the trace penalty would still leave a nonvanishing within-pair off-diagonal score if X converged to ZZᵀ. A vanishing coupling or a different population target and new theory would be required.

Step6's explicitly stated approximation deletes λn3X from the precision update, and the recovered original software does the same. Such an update is not the minimization problem used in Proposition1; it cannot establish the false theorem about the stated objective. The report does not infer that a particular published simulation number is false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the joint consistency proof, I noticed that the nonvanishing trace perturbation was asserted to have a favorable sign without a sign argument. Differentiating in a diagonal coordinate exposed a deterministic contradiction.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the rendered original objective, constraints, λn3=1 convention, all assumptions, Proposition1 and the complete appendix proof. Constructed the growing Gaussian pair-block sequence above and checked every condition. Independently derived the KKT identity, inverse-norm lower bound and population optimizer; tested five convex subproblems. A second reviewer separately read the relevant original pages, verified all assumptions, reproduced the exact obstruction and checked40 diagonal finite differences. The rest of the full32-page paper and the recovered nine-page external supplement were also reviewed.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample is analytic, satisfies all the theorem's stated conditions, and applies to every local minimizer. It does not depend on numerical solver accuracy, unavailable historical outputs, or inferred experimental misconduct.

findings.title: Incompatible generated-error correlation invalidates the central smoothed-estimator variance/rate analysis
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-246__I01 — Incompatible generated-error correlation invalidates the central smoothed-estimator variance/rate analysis
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 11–12, Section 2.4, generated derivative-noise covariance and Assumption 5, Theorem 2 variance and the optimized MSE rate immediately below it; PDF 35–36 AppendixH PartII, especially Eq37. The same unverified correlation transfer is reused for Theorem 4/PDF 18 and AppendixN/PDF 42.

**Claim.** The paper says its derivative pseudo-observations have shrinking stationary short-range correlations satisfying Assumption 5, and uses an existing local-polynomial correlated-noise theorem to obtain

Var[rhat'(u0)|U] = [3 sigma²(n+1)²/(k(k+1)(2k+1))] [(1+rho_c)/(h(n−2k))] R(K*_0) {1+o_P(1)},

where rho_c is a finite constant and Assumption 5 requires n integral|rho_n(x)|dx uniformly bounded and mass concentrated on distances of order 1/n. For odd p, it then gives h=O(n^(-2/(5p+6))), k=O(n^((3p+4)/(5p+6))) and conditional MSE O_P(n^(-(4p+4)/(5p+6))). In particular p=1 gives k of ordern^(7/11), h of ordern^(-2/11), and MSE O_P(n^(-8/11)). The p=1 local-linear smoother is explicitly allowed. All smoothness premises below are satisfied by the cubic regression r(u)=u³, for which B=6 and r-third=6 are positive, so the advertised joint optimal-tuning constants are nondegenerate.

**Error and exact certificate.** The error variables are not an arbitrary exogenous short-range noise process. Each pseudo-observation reuses2k original errors, and nearby pseudo-observations share them over k ranks. A bandwidth theorem for correlation concentrated within one rank cannot simply be applied to this triangular array as k→infinity. The abstract conditional theorem under Assumption 5 is not claimed false here; the generated-error application and the advertised optimized rate are the demonstrated failures.

An exact lower bound refutes the claimed application without approximating the covariance. Take iid U_i~Uniform(0,1), iid independent e_i~N(0,1), r(u)=u³, target u0=1/2. Use the paper's original weights 9 and estimator 8, and smooth only its interior pseudo-observations by the original local-linear intercept 12. Choose the legitimate compact symmetric bimodal probability kernel

K(t)=(15/4)t²(1−t²)1(|t|<1).

It is nonnegative, bounded, symmetric, continuous, Lipschitz at0, has compact support and K(0)=0. Thus it also satisfies the special kernel feature used for bandwidth selection. Set k=floor(n^(7/11)), h=n^(-2/11), as in the paper's optimized p=1 rates.

Write the final estimate as sum_t b_t Y_t, conditional on the ordered U. For each raw pseudo-observation i, define d_ij=U_(i+j)−U_(i−j), D_i=sum_(j=1)^k d_ij². Substitution of weights 9 gives raw coefficients a_i,i+j=d_ij/D_i and a_i,i−j=−d_ij/D_i, with all others zero. Consequently

sum_t a_it=0 and sum_t a_it U_t=sum_j d_ij²/D_i=1.

The local-linear intercept weights l_i in12 sum to one exactly, whenever its Gram matrix is nonsingular. Hence b_t=sum_i l_i a_it satisfies sum_t b_t=0 and sum_t b_t U_t=1. In particular sum_t b_t(U_t−u0)=1.

Only rows with |U_i−u0|<h enter because K is compactly supported. Every coefficient in such a row lies at most k ranks from i. Uniform-order-statistic concentration gives max_i|U_i−i/(n+1)|=O_P(n^-1/2), so each such rank displacement is at most k/(n+1)+O_P(n^-1/2)=o_P(h), since k/n=n^-4/11 and h=n^-2/11. With probability tending 1, every nonzero b_t therefore lies within 2h ofu0. The number of design points in that interval is Binomial(n,4h), so with probability tending 1 is at most 5nh. The kernel Gram matrix is nonsingular with probability tending 1 since nh→infinity.

Cauchy–Schwarz now gives the entirely conditional bound

1=(sum_t b_t(U_t−u0))² <= (sum_t b_t²) sum_(t:b_t nonzero)(U_t−u0)² <= (sum_t b_t²) 20nh³.

Because original errors are independent with variance 1, the actual conditional variance is sum_t b_t², so it is at least1/(20nh³) with probability tending 1. At the paper's claimed bandwidth this is Omega_P(n^-5/11). Conditional MSE is at least conditional variance for every regression function. In particular r(u)=u³ has B=sup|r-second|=6 and r-third=6, so both bias terms used to derive the paper's joint optimal tuning have fixed positive constants. It cannot be O_P(n^-8/11): n^(8/11)MSE is bounded below by n^(3/11)/20 on an event whose probability tends1. This is a diverging rate discrepancy, not a missing constant.

The same event and bound can be made uniform over every u0 in [1/4,3/4], so the contradiction also applies directly to the paper's conditional MISE optimization. Let D_n be the sup norm between the empirical CDF and the uniform CDF. D_n=O_P(n^-1/2)=o_P(h). This bounds the number of design points in every length4h interval simultaneously by n(4h+2D_n)≤5nh, and bounds every k-rank displacement by k/n+2D_n=o_P(h). For each target, the kernel Gram matrix is nonsingular because both subintervals [u0−h/2,u0−h/4] and [u0+h/4,u0+h/2] contain observations with strictly positive kernel weights, uniformly with probability tending 1. Integrating the conditional variance lower bound over [1/4,3/4] gives conditional MISE≥1/(40nh³)=Omega_P(n^-5/11), which is incompatible with the advertised n^-8/11 MISE rate. Independent bounded review checked this uniform integrated strengthening.

For these k,h, k→infinity, k/n→0,h→0,nh→infinity, and the printed smoothed consistency condition n k^-3 h^-1→0 holds. The raw estimator by itself is not consistent for k=n^(7/11); the printed joint optimized-smoothed-rate paragraph nevertheless explicitly specifies this rate and Theorem 2 does not impose the raw n²/k³→0 condition. If one adds that raw consistency requirement, the advertised p=1 optimizer is itself excluded and the claimed optimization is still not proved. No hidden assumptions6/7 are defined among the listed five assumptions onPDF 11–12.

Regular-spacing autocorrelation illustrates why the transfer fails: for raw derivative coefficients proportional to j at rank offsets±j, the limiting correlation at displacement c*k is 1−(3/2)c+c³/4 for0<=c<=2. It stays positive, e.g..85025 atc=.1. Spatial range is k/n, so n integral|rho_n| grows at least a positive multiple ofk, rather than staying bounded. The rigorous rate certificate above uses random design and does not depend on using equispaced design as a counterexample. Exact random-design covariance controls are supplemental evidence, not the proof of the asymptotic contradiction.
