findings.title: The fixed-domain argmax argument does not establish the central estimator law or test calibration
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-264-I01 — The fixed-domain argmax argument does not establish the central estimator law or test calibration
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 1, PDF 6–7, especially condition 4 and Equation 13; Theorem 2, PDF 7, Equation 14; Proposition 3, PDF 8; Appendix A, PDF 17 first proof paragraph and PDF 20 Equations 29–30/application of the argmax theorem. The estimator is defined by Equations 7–11 on PDF 6. The central advertised significance-test interpretation occurs in the abstract and PDF 2/10/16.

**Claim.** With the stated smooth regression model, bounded Sobolev parameter ball
\[
\Theta=\{f:\|f\|_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor+2}\le B\},
\]
and approximate neural-network maximization
\[
L_n(f_n)\ge\sup_{f\in\Theta_n}L_n(f)-o_P(1),
\]
Theorem 1 asserts
\[
r_n(f_n-f_0)\Rightarrow h^*,\qquad
r_n=(n/\log n)^{(d+1)/(2(2d+1))},
\]
where \(h^*\in\Theta\) maximizes a centered Gaussian process with covariance \(4\sigma^2P(st)\). Its hypotheses include condition 4: the centered empirical criterion evaluated at \(f_n\) is at least its supremum over local perturbations \(f_0+h/r_n\), \(h\in\Theta\), up to \(o_P(1)\). Theorem 2 and Proposition 3 transfer this to finite null distributions for the scaled population and empirical squared-gradient statistics, supplying the proposed test's calibration.

**Error and evidence.** The proof applies an argmax theorem on the fixed compact index domain \(\Theta\) to \(h_n=r_n(f_n-f_0)\), without establishing that \(h_n\) belongs to that domain or is compactly localized where the criterion convergence is proved. PDF 17 asserts an estimator rate from a citation despite Equation 10's unrestricted \(o_P(1)\) optimization error, then treats a norm rate as tightness in an infinite-dimensional function space. Neither inference supplies the missing fixed-domain localization. Condition 4 is only a lower bound: values attained outside the index ball can exceed its supremum by arbitrarily much and still satisfy that condition.

The following explicit diagnostic verifies that this is a substantive missing premise, including verification of condition 4. It satisfies every numbered hypothesis of Theorem 1 and the literal parameter/estimator constraints 7/10/11, yet its scaled error and null statistics diverge.

Take \(d=3\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}([-1,1]^3)\), independently \(\epsilon\sim N(0,1)\), and \(Y=\epsilon\), so \(f_0=0\) and the variable 1 null is true. Set \(B=c=\tilde c=1\), choose logistic activation, and write
\[
g(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-x_1}},\quad K_n=\lceil\log n\rceil,
\quad r_n=(n/\log n)^{2/7},\quad t_n=r_n^{-1/2},
\]
\[
Z_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)\epsilon_i,
\qquad f_n=t_n\operatorname{sign}(Z_n)g.
\]
Set \(\operatorname{sign}(0)=1\). This estimator uses only observed \((X_i,Y_i)\). It is a single sigmoid unit with incoming weight 1 and outgoing weight of magnitude \(t_n<1\), padded with zero output weights to \(K_n\) units. Thus it belongs to Equation 11. The dimension condition \(K_n^{7/3}\log K_n=O(n)\) holds. The design density is 1/8, positive and bounded, and the errors have the required independence and finite positive variance.

For \(x_1\in[-1,1]\), \(1/4<g<3/4\), \(g'\ge3/16\), and \(|g'|,|g''|,|g'''|\le1/4\). Only coordinate 1 derivatives are nonzero. Consequently \(\|g\|_3^2\le3/4<1\), so all \(f_n\) belong to the exact Sobolev ball. These are smooth one-unit functions; no singular noise, vanishing design density or high-frequency derivative perturbation is involved.

Here are direct checks of the two maximization conditions. Write \(G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P)\). On a bounded three-dimensional cube, evaluation on \(H^3\) has a uniformly bounded Riesz representer \(k_x\). Therefore the Hilbert-valued sum \(U_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\epsilon_i k_{X_i}\) has bounded second moment, and
\[
\sup_{h\in\Theta}|P_n(\epsilon h)|
\le \|U_n\|_{H^3}/\sqrt n=O_P(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Since
\[
L_n(h)-L_n(0)=P_n(\epsilon h)-\tfrac12P_nh^2,
\]
while \(|L_n(f_n)-L_n(0)|\le t_n|P_n(\epsilon g)|+t_n^2P_ng^2/2=o_P(1)\), the actual nonnegative gap \(\sup_{h\in\Theta_n}L_n(h)-L_n(f_n)\) tends to 0 in probability. Equation 10 is satisfied.

The right side of condition 4 before its remainder is
\[
T_n=\sup_{h\in\Theta}\{2G_n(h\epsilon)-r_n^{-1}G_n(h^2)\}=O_P(1).
\]
For completeness, this bound does not assume Theorem 1. \(H^3\) on this cube is a multiplication algebra: \(\|h^2\|_{H^3}\le C_{\rm alg}\|h\|_{H^3}^2\). The analogous centered evaluation sum \(V_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_i(k_{X_i}-Ek_X)\) also has bounded second moment. Hence
\[
T_n\le2\|U_n\|_{H^3}+(C_{\rm alg}/r_n)\|V_n\|_{H^3}=O_P(1).
\]
The left side of condition 4 is exactly
\[
A_n=r_nG_n(2f_n\epsilon-f_n^2)
=2\sqrt{r_n}|Z_n|-G_n(g^2)\ \longrightarrow\ +\infty
\quad\text{in probability}.
\]
Indeed, conditional on the design, \(Z_n\) is normal with variance \(P_ng^2\in[1/16,9/16]\), so its density near 0 is uniformly bounded; \(G_n(g^2)=O_P(1)\). Thus \(R_n=(T_n-A_n)_+=o_P(1)\), and \(A_n\ge T_n-R_n\) for every sample. This verifies the exact inequality and remainder required in condition 4.

Nevertheless, for every sample,
\[
\|r_n(f_n-f_0)\|_{L^2(P)}
=\sqrt{r_n}\|g\|_{L^2(P)}\ge\sqrt{r_n}/4\to\infty.
\]
For \(\mu=P\), the two null statistics satisfy
\[
r_n^2\lambda_1^n=r_nP[(g')^2]\ge9r_n/256\to\infty,
\qquad
r_n^2\hat\lambda_1^n=r_nP_n[(g')^2]\ge9r_n/256\to\infty.
\]
The claimed limit from an \(h^*\in\Theta\) is bounded by \(P[(\partial_1h^*)^2]\le B^2=1\). The displayed divergence therefore cannot have that limit. A test using the intended scaled statistic and the claimed fixed finite null quantile rejects this true null with probability tending 1. This is a diagnostic of the stated asymptotic/optimizer conditions, not a claimed rerun of the historical Adam experiments. PDF 10 also omits the scaling in its displayed rejection rule; the argument concerns the intended scaled rule required by Theorem 2.

There is a separate background wording issue that must be kept explicit. PDF 6 asserts whole-ball density of the fixed-cap neural-network sieves by universal approximation. The construction above verifies all explicit numbered theorem hypotheses and the literal sieve constraints; it is not presented as verifying that extra global fixed-cap density assertion if it is interpreted as an independently imposed premise. Density does not supply the missing rate/localization: the same estimator and supremum bounds apply to any dense sieve family containing the one sigmoid. The principal finding is the unsupported central argmax step; the diagnostic shows why its explicit estimator conditions are insufficient.

The actual local least-squares objective also contains the population term removed by centering:
\[
r_n\sqrt n\{P_n l_{f_0+h/r_n}-P_n l_{f_0}\}
=2G_n(h\epsilon)-r_n^{-1}G_n(h^2)
-\frac{\sqrt n}{r_n}P(h^2).
\]
Its final coefficient diverges because \(r_n=o(\sqrt n)\). A valid local-argmax analysis must account for this drift and its changing domain. The centered process convergence in the paper does not establish that the actual estimator maximizes the asserted limiting process.

**Reason for rejection.** The new contribution is a statistically justified significance test, rather than only a gradient importance score. Theorem 1 is the sole foundational estimator law; Theorem 2, Proposition 3 and the quantile-based test are derived from it. Its proof lacks the domain/tightness/local-objective argument that would connect fitted networks to the claimed null law. The explicit admissible-estimator diagnostic can even yield divergent true-null statistics while satisfying the numbered conditions. Changing a displayed constant or quoting a norm rate does not resolve this: a stronger estimator specification, valid localization and a fresh derivation establishing the correct limit/calibration are required. As written, the paper does not establish its central theoretical testing guarantee; this warrants changing accept to reject. This report does not assert that no corrected neural-network significance test can exist, or that the historical numerical rankings have been independently disproved.

**Discovery method.** Tracing Appendix A's use of the argmax theorem exposed the unproved membership/tightness of the scaled error in its fixed index ball. Comparing the weak optimization tolerance with the centered, one-sided condition 4 suggested an oversized but consistent one-unit noise fit.

**Verification method.** Read the full original paper and rechecked definitions/conditions/proof on rendered PDF 6/7/17/20/21. Constructed the estimator above; checked every explicit numbered hypothesis, network and Sobolev bound, Equation 10 and especially condition 4 analytically. Independently derived its diverging norm and both gradient statistics. A reproducible Python helper checks 640 direct criterion identities, 100 local-loss/drift identities and quadrature derivative/Sobolev moments. The full supremum/condition 4 proof is analytic, not inferred from a finite simulated function grid. Independent root review examined the original conditions and the same localization failure.

**Confidence.** High for the central proof failure and the exact diagnostic under the explicit numbered/estimator conditions. The algebra gives a deterministic lower bound for both scaled null statistics; condition 4 is separately proved rather than assumed. The fixed-cap density interpretation and absence of a historical TensorFlow rerun are explicitly limited, so the finding is stated as a central unsupported proof/calibration result rather than an unqualified all-background-assumption counterexample.

 The recorded computational checks are independent mathematical controls, not author-code execution.

\[ r_n^2\lambda_1^n=r_nP[(g')^2]\ge9r_n/256\to\infty, \qquad r_n^2\hat\lambda_1^n=r_nP_n[(g')^2]\ge9r_n/256\to\infty. \]
The claimed limit from an \(h^*\in\Theta\) is bounded by \(P[(\partial_1h^*)^2]\le B^2=1\). The displayed divergence therefore cannot have that limit. A test using the intended scaled statistic and the claimed fixed finite null quantile rejects this true null with probability tending 1. This is a diagnostic of the stated asymptotic/optimizer conditions, not a claimed rerun of the historical Adam experiments. PDF 10 also omits the scaling in its displayed rejection rule; the argument concerns the intended scaled rule required by Theorem 2.

There is a separate background wording issue that must be kept explicit. PDF 6 asserts whole-ball density of the fixed-cap neural-network sieves by universal approximation. The construction above verifies all explicit numbered theorem hypotheses and the literal sieve constraints; it is not presented as verifying that extra global fixed-cap density assertion if it is interpreted as an independently imposed premise. Density does not supply the missing rate/localization: the same estimator and supremum bounds apply to any dense sieve family containing the one sigmoid. The principal finding is the unsupported central argmax step; the diagnostic shows why its explicit estimator conditions are insufficient.

The actual local least-squares objective also contains the population term removed by centering:

\[ r_n\sqrt n\{P_n l_{f_0+h/r_n}-P_n l_{f_0}\} =2G_n(h\epsilon)-r_n^{-1}G_n(h^2) -\frac{\sqrt n}{r_n}P(h^2). \]
Its final coefficient diverges because \(r_n=o(\sqrt n)\). A valid local-argmax analysis must account for this drift and its changing domain. The centered process convergence in the paper does not establish that the actual estimator maximizes the asserted limiting process.

Reason for rejection. The new contribution is a statistically justified significance test, rather than only a gradient importance score. Theorem 1 is the sole foundational estimator law; Theorem 2, Proposition 3 and the quantile-based test are derived from it. Its proof lacks the domain/tightness/local-objective argument that would connect fitted networks to the claimed null law. The explicit admissible-estimator diagnostic can even yield divergent true-null statistics while satisfying the numbered conditions. Changing a displayed constant or quoting a norm rate does not resolve this: a stronger estimator specification, valid localization and a fresh derivation establishing the correct limit/calibration are required. As written, the paper does not establish its central theoretical testing guarantee; this warrants changing accept to reject. This report does not assert that no corrected neural-network significance test can exist, or that the historical numerical rankings have been independently disproved.

Discovery method. Tracing Appendix A's use of the argmax theorem exposed the unproved membership/tightness of the scaled error in its fixed index ball. Comparing the weak optimization tolerance with the centered, one-sided condition 4 suggested an oversized but consistent one-unit noise fit.

Verification method. Read the full original paper and rechecked definitions/conditions/proof on rendered PDF 6/7/17/20/21. Constructed the estimator above; checked every explicit numbered hypothesis, network and Sobolev bound, Equation 10 and especially condition 4 analytically. Independently derived its diverging norm and both gradient statistics. A reproducible Python helper checks 640 direct criterion identities, 100 local-loss/drift identities and quadrature derivative/Sobolev moments. The full supremum/condition 4 proof is analytic, not inferred from a finite simulated function grid. Independent root review examined the original conditions and the same localization failure.

Confidence. High for the central proof failure and the exact diagnostic under the explicit numbered/estimator conditions. The algebra gives a deterministic lower bound for both scaled null statistics; condition 4 is separately proved rather than assumed. The fixed-cap density interpretation and absence of a historical TensorFlow rerun are explicitly limited, so the finding is stated as a central unsupported proof/calibration result rather than an unqualified all-background-assumption counterexample.

The recorded computational checks are independent mathematical controls, not author-code execution.

findings.title: The central contrast guarantee fails for allowed weight functions
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-290__I01 — The central contrast guarantee fails for allowed weight functions
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 7, Proposition 2 and Eq. 4; PDF 30–32, Appendix A, Lemmas17/18 and the proof of Proposition 2. Consequences concern Corollary 3 on PDF 8 and the first theoretical contribution identified on PDF 4.

**Claim.** For the two-class stochastic tree model of Sections 2.1–2.2, with leaf weight0 and `w(T_i)>0`, Proposition 2 states that `Delta_i(x)=0` exactly when the edited vertexx is the root. If `rho>H/2`, it additionally claims, with probability at least `G_rho(h)`,

`Delta_i(x) >= P_rho(0) C_i,h`,

where `C_i,h=[K(T_i,T_i)−max_{height(u)=h}K(T_i[u],T_i[u])]/#leaves(T_i)`. The kernel permits nonnegative weights depending on subtree identity; no restriction to height-only weights is stated in this theorem.

**Error and evidence.** Write `L` for a leaf, `S_d` for a star with d leaf children, and parentheses for a root with the listed children. Take

`T_0=(S_3,L,L)`, `T_1=(S_2,L)`,

`tau_0=L`, `tau_1=(L)`, `tau_2=((L))`.

Extend `tau_h` as a unary chain of heighth if needed. These trees satisfy every structural assumption:

1. Both prototypes have height2. Within each, its two nonleaf subtrees have distinct heights and are nonisomorphic.
2. Every original nonleaf in class0 has root degree3; every original nonleaf in class1 has root degree2. Hence their only shared subtree is a leaf.
3. After any permitted subtree replacement, every remaining nonleaf vertex outside the inserted chain keeps its original root degree3 or2, respectively. Such subtrees still cannot be shared across classes. This verifies the third assumption for all 35 pairs of edit locations.
4. No positive-height unary chain is an original subtree of either prototype.

Set `rho=3/2`, `H=2`. The edit-height probabilities are `P(0)=1/16`, `P(1)=6/16`, `P(2)=9/16`; vertices of the selected height are sampled uniformly as required.

First give weight1 to the two exact prototype trees and0 to every other subtree. This defines a valid positive semidefinite subtree kernel and gives both required root weights1. Edit the unique height1vertex of `T_0`, producing `A_0=(tau_1,L,L)`. This query contains neither full prototype. Consequently `K(A_0,T)=0` for every tree T, so `Delta_0(x)=0` althoughx is not the root. This directly contradicts the first assertion.

The lower-bound failure persists with **strictly positive weights on every nonleaf subtree**. Give weight1 to `T_0,T_1`, weight `epsilon=1/100` to every other nonleaf, and0 to leaves. For `A_0`, its unary-chain feature has the same expected count in each class, so its contribution cancels. Its remaining feature is its own root, present in class0 with probability `6/16` and absent in class1. Thus exactly

`Delta_0(x)=(6/16)epsilon=3/800`.

But `K(T_0,T_0)=1+epsilon`, the height1subtree self-kernel isepsilon, and `T_0` has five leaves. Hence `C_0,1=1/5`, and the claimed bound is

`P(0) C_0,1=1/80 > 3/800`.

This also refutes the probabilistic statement: the inequality is met only by unedited class0queries, with total probability `1/16`, whereas `G_rho(1)=7/16`. An arbitrarily small positiveepsilon makes the discrepancy arbitrarily large in ratio.

The exact failed proof step is Appendix A's `u=v` case of Lemma 17. Editing a subtree also changes the identities of its ancestor subtrees. The proof retains their old weights in `K(T_i,T_i)` while removing only the edited vertex and descendants. Arbitrary subtree weights give no equality between old and changed-ancestor weights. In the zero-weight example, Lemma 17 predicts self-kernel1 for `A_0`, whose actual self-kernel is0. Neither Lemma 18 nor Proposition 2 can follow from that identity.

**Reason for rejection.** This invalidates the paper's central general-weight separation guarantee, its strict-positive-contrast assertion and the guarantee used for the subsequent sample-size argument. That theory is explicitly the first main contribution and motivates learning subtree-dependent weights. Positivity does not repair the theorem; a height-only restriction would remove the arbitrary identity-dependent setting needed for that contribution. Repair requires a different bound accounting for changed ancestors or a materially restricted theorem, not a correction preserving the advertised result. The paper's computational framework and empirical examples do not establish this false guarantee.

**Discovery method.** Traced how arbitrary weights were handled in the edited-tree self-kernel identity and noticed that changed ancestors retained their original weights.

**Verification method.** Constructed the explicit two-tree model; checked all 35 structural edit pairs and all finite outcomes with exact rational arithmetic; independently reproduced the construction in a second audit implementation. Rechecked original PDF 3–8/30–32, including full rendered3/7/8/31. The unchanged prepublication treex kernel independently returns the zero query row in the root-only example;7,776 additional ordered/unordered kernel-pair controls agree with direct subtree counting.

**Confidence: High.** The contradiction uses exact finite probabilities, meets all stated structural assumptions, persists when every nonleaf weight is positive, and has independent mathematical and native-code checks.

findings.title: Positive leaf weight can improve the claimed separation/sample-size criterion
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-290__I02 — Positive leaf weight can improve the claimed separation/sample-size criterion
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 8, Section 2.4, the minimum-contrast inequality immediately after Proposition 4 and its conclusion that the sufficient training size is minimized at leaf weight0; reiterated in Remark 5 on PDF 9, Section 4 on PDF 15 and the abstract.

**Claim.** Adding a positive leaf weight changes the two class-specific contrasts in opposite directions. The paper concludes that their minimum cannot increase and, because the kernel bound increases, that the sufficient sample size based on Eq. 5 is always minimized by zero leaf weight. This is the theoretical rationale given for forcing the learned discriminance weight of leaves to0.

**Error and evidence.** Use the same legal prototypes, edit chains and `rho=3/2` above. Let `A_0=(tau_1,L,L)` and `A_1=(tau_1,L)` be the height1edits. Define nonleaf weights as follows:

| Subtree | Weight |
|---|---:|
| `T_0`, `T_1` | `1` |
| `A_1` | `1` |
| Every other nonleaf, including `A_0` and the chains | `1/100` |

Initially set the leaf weight to0. The possible non-root-edited queries are exactly `T_0,A_0` in class0 and `T_1,A_1` in class1. Their contrasts are

| Class/query | Leaf weight0 | Leaf weight `1/100` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `0/T_0` | `101/1600` | `141/1600` |
| `0/A_0` | `3/800` | `3/160` |
| `1/T_1` | `101/1600` | `77/1600` |
| `1/A_1` | `3/8` | `73/200` |

These values follow directly from Eq. 2 and the finite edit distribution. In particular, the expected leaf counts are

`E[L|class0]=(5+6*3+9*1)/16=2`,

`E[L|class1]=(3+6*2+9*1)/16=3/2`.

Thus adding leaf weightw raises each class0contrast by `w L(query)/2` and lowers each class1contrast by the same expression. The worst class originally has the smaller margin, so raising that margin while lowering the much larger other margin **increases the minimum**. The good set `height(x)<=1` has the same probability `7/16` in both comparisons. Its minimum contrast increases fivefold, from `3/800` to `3/160`.

The conclusion is still reversed after accounting for the kernel bound in Eq. 5. Over every possible edited query in either class, the exact maximal self-kernel is `101/100` before and `63/50` after adding the leaf weight. Nonnegative feature vectors and Cauchy–Schwarz make these valid global bounds on all pairwise similarities. The squared kernel-bound/minimum-margin ratio therefore decreases from

`[(101/100)/(3/800)]² = 652864/9`

to

`[(63/50)/(3/160)]² = 112896/25`.

Hence the actual Hoeffding criterion used by the paper gives a strictly smaller sufficient sample-size bound at the positive leaf weight, for the same good-set probability and confidence parameter. This directly contradicts its asserted universal optimum at0. It is a statement about the paper's separation/bound criterion; it does not claim a historical SVM test-error reversal.

The underlying inference is invalid independently of Issue I01: lowering one of two numbers and raising the other does not imply that their minimum decreases. Proposition 4's displayed use of the leaf count of `T_i[x]` also differs from the proof's correct edited-query leaf count, but correcting that notation leaves this counterexample intact.

**Reason for rejection.** The abstract and main development present zero leaf weight as a theoretically established improvement and use it to motivate the proposed discriminance construction. The model instead permits a strict improvement in precisely their stated criterion by giving leaves positive weight. Preserving the universal conclusion requires additional model or weight symmetry restrictions that are absent and exclude this legal example. Replacing the claimed theorem with a restricted result or an empirical heuristic would change a central theoretical contribution and the asserted justification for the method; the paper as written does not support acceptance on that contribution.

**Discovery method.** Noticed that the proof passed from opposite class-specific shifts to an inequality about their minimum without identifying which class had the smaller original margin.

**Verification method.** Computed every model outcome, contrast and global kernel bound in exact rational arithmetic; checked the entire good set rather than a single favorable pair; independently recomputed all values in a second implementation. Rechecked full rendered PDF 8 and the scope on PDF 4/9/15/27. The same finite model satisfies the original assumptions independently of the failed contrast-bound proof.

**Evidence files.** The exact primary and independent audit helpers and JSON/log files cited for I01; in particular `invalid_minimum_step_witness` in `targeted-controls.json` and `genton-bounded-qa.json`.

**Confidence: High.** All table entries and both squared ratios are exact, the model satisfies the original assumptions, and the inequality is reversed even after including the full similarity-range penalty used in the sample-size argument.

findings.title: Updating variance after every jump changes the posterior target
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-307__I01 — Updating variance after every jump changes the posterior target
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Algorithm 2, PDF 11, final Gibbs update and full-posterior output claim; ordinary conjugate updates specified in Section 2.2, PDF 6, steps3–4; Section 3, PDF 7, claimed Gibbs composition; waiting weight Eq. 4, PDF 8, and posterior estimator Eq. 12, PDF 12. Theorem 1, PDF 9, and its Appendix A proof, PDF 17–18, supply only the birth/death balance argument on which the full algorithm relies.

**Claim.** The conjugately collapsed continuous-time topology sampler can update the noise variance by ordinary Gibbs sampling after every topology jump and, with inverse-exit-rate waiting weights, sample the full posterior in Eq. 2. The proof treats the additional Gibbs step as a standard valid composition with the continuous-time birth/death process.

**Error and evidence.** A continuous-time sampler stopped at its next jump has a different invariant distribution from its occupation distribution. A usual Gibbs update preserves the posterior conditional, rather than the conditional distribution tilted by the exit rate that is required at jump times. The prescribed composition fails in the following Gaussian regression-tree model.

Use one predictor with observations `x=(-1,1)`, responses `y=(0,0)`, and the single available cut at zero. There are two valid nonempty trees: a stump `T0` and one split `T1`. Neither child admits a further nonempty split at that cut. Give each terminal mean an independent `N(0,1)` prior and let `s=σ²~IG(2,1)`, corresponding to the paper's `ν=4, λ=1/2`. Set the split/stump prior odds to `c=1/4`. For example, restricting the stated `α=1/2, β=0` splitting prior to valid trees gives unnormalized masses `1/2` and `1/8`. If unsplittable leaves are instead forced terminal, `α=1/5, β=0` gives the same odds. The argument works for every `0<c≤1`, so this convention does not determine the failure. All priors are proper and all variances are positive; no minimum-leaf sample count is assumed in the theoretical model.

Integrating the terminal means, as Algorithm 2 requires, gives the likelihoods, apart from the common `2π` factor,

\[
 m_0(s)=[s(s+2)]^{-1/2},\qquad m_1(s)=(s+1)^{-1}.
\]

The printed rates are therefore

\[
 r_0(s)=c\frac{\sqrt{s(s+2)}}{s+1}<1,\qquad r_1(s)=1.
\]

Every topology jump alternates between the two trees. Let `π(Ti,s)` denote the desired joint posterior. If `μ` is an invariant distribution of the embedded jump chain, the inverse-rate weighted occupation law is proportional to `μ(Ti,s)/ri(s)`. Consequently, the claimed target requires

\[
 \mu(T_i,s)\propto\pi(T_i,s)r_i(s).
\]

But `π(T0,s)r0(s)=π(T1,s)r1(s)`. Thus the necessary embedded law gives each tree probability `1/2` and gives `s` the **split-tree conditional posterior** `π1(s)∝IG(2,1)/(s+1)` at both trees.

Now consider the forced move from `T1` to `T0`, followed by the ordinary conjugate sweep specified on PDF 6. Drawing the terminal mean needed for the standard variance update gives

\[
 \mu_0\mid s,T_0,y\sim N\!\left(0,\frac{s}{s+2}\right),
 \qquad s'\mid\mu_0,T_0,y\sim IG(3,1+\mu_0^2),
\]

and hence

\[
 E[s'\mid s,T_0]=\frac{1+s/(s+2)}2.
\]

This sweep does not preserve the required jump-time law `π1`. There is an explicit moment contradiction. Define

\[
 C=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-u}}{u+1}\,du,
 \qquad D=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-u}}{u+1/2}\,du.
\]

Under `π1`, the substitution `u=1/s` gives density `u²e^{-u}/[(u+1)C]`. Exact integration and partial fractions yield

\[
 E_{\pi_1}[s]=\frac{1-C}{C},\qquad
 E_{\pi_1G_0}[s]=\frac{2+D}{8C},\qquad
 E_{\pi_1}[s]-E_{\pi_1G_0}[s]
 =\frac{6-8C-D}{8C}>\frac1{24}.
\]

The strict inequality has an exact rational certificate. Take

\[
 r=(7433/10000,\;6429/2500,\;3582/625,\;109539/10000),
\]

and, for `a=1` or `1/2`, set

\[
 \lambda_a=[a\prod_j(a+r_j)^2]^{-1},\qquad
 p_a(u)=\frac{1+\lambda_a u\prod_j(u-r_j)^2}{u+a}.
\]

The numerator vanishes at `u=-a`, so `p_a` is a polynomial. For `u≥0`, `p_a(u)≥1/(u+a)`. Its integral against `e^{-u}` is obtained exactly by replacing each monomial `u^k` with `k!`. Rational arithmetic gives

\[

 {226960564509393752525323177046523}<\frac35,
\]

\[

 {7254899228298096485451393829252609}<1.
\]

Algorithm 2 omits a terminal-mean draw after integrating the means from the rate calculation, despite requiring those means for a conjugate variance update. Adding the ordinary draw specified in Section 2.2 gives exactly the counterexample above. An ideal direct refresh from the variance conditional would also preserve the stump conditional, rather than the required split conditional. The PDF supplies neither a jump-tilted conditional update nor an independent calendar-time refresh rule that would resolve the problem.

As a separate numerical check, 256 independent chains, each with 40000 retained jumps after 8000 burn-in jumps, used the displayed rates and ordinary conjugate formulas. Eq. 12 estimated stump probability `0.8507723493`, with chain-level standard error `0.0000100102`; direct posterior integration gives `0.8473919752`. This illustrates the bias. The analytic invariant-law contradiction and rational moment certificate establish the error independently of simulation. Nine known-variance controls recover the correct conditional posterior with the same inverse-rate weighting.

**Reason for rejection.** Correct posterior sampling is the paper's central contribution. The displayed practical algorithm has the wrong occupation target even in a two-tree model satisfying its conjugate assumptions. Its conditional birth/death balance proof does not establish the full algorithm's claimed posterior validity or the associated Bayesian model averages. Repair requires changing the refresh timing or sampling from the distribution tilted by jump rates, proving joint invariance, and validating the changed procedure. That changes the sampler underlying the efficiency claims. This finding concerns the full-posterior algorithm; the fixed-variance conditional birth/death identity is not refuted.

Verified a strict moment gap with rational polynomial bounds, independent quadrature, formula-based simulation and positive known-variance controls. A separate reviewer independently reread the original pages and rederived the invariant-law and moment arguments.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 4.3, PDF 11–12; its proof in Appendix A.3, PDF 27, specifically the gradient branch of the stopping-time partition and the claimed one-step decrease attributed to Eq. (3.4). Compare Lemma 4.2 on PDF 11 and its proof on PDF 24–26.

**Claim.** Theorem 4.3 gives a polynomial hitting-time bound for approximate second-order stationary points under Assumptions 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1. Its proof partitions states outside the target set. Whenever

\[
\|\nabla F(X_{\tau_k})\|\ge2\epsilon_0,
\]

it takes a single SGLD step and asserts

\[
\mathbb E_{\tau_k}F(X_{\tau_k+1})
\le F(X_{\tau_k})-\epsilon_0^2\eta_{\tau_k+1}.
\tag{*}
\]

The proof attributes this inequality to Eq. (3.4) and the strong Markov property. Together with the small-gradient saddle-escape branch, it is the uniform negative drift used in the final telescoping and hitting-time bound.

**Error and evidence.** Inequality(*) can have the opposite sign under every stated second-order assumption and the theorem's parameter choices. Consider two-dimensional deterministic stochastic loss \(f=F\), so the stochastic-gradient noise is zero, with

\[
F(x,y)=1-\cos x+\frac1{10}(1+\cos y).
\]

It is globally nonnegative and bounded by \(11/5\). Its Hessian has norm at most 1 and is 1-Lipschitz. The sum of its positive Hessian eigenvalues is at most \(11/10\). Thus the stated assumptions hold globally with

\[
C_2=C_3=1,\quad C_0=11/5,\quad D_4=11/10,
\quad B_1=B_2=1.
\]

Choose target \(\epsilon=1\), \(\lambda_\epsilon=1/20\), and \(q=1/10\). Theorem 4.3 then defines

\[
Q=40\log1152>200.
\]

Its displayed volatility is

\[
\delta=\delta_0=2^{-3/2}C_6^{-7/2}1152^{-54/5}.
\]

For its sufficiently large \(C_6\), this gives \(0<\delta\le1/10\). Choose the permitted constant step \(\eta_0=\delta^2\), \(\alpha=0\). It satisfies both theorem restrictions: \(\eta_0\le B_2^{-1}\delta^2\) with equality, and \(\eta_0\le\log57.6\). The small-step restrictions in the preceding arguments also hold. Since \(Q^{-1}<\lambda_\epsilon\), the theorem's threshold is

\[
\epsilon_0=\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt Q}.
\]

Start at

\[
X_0=(x,0),\qquad x=\arcsin(\delta/2).
\]

Here \(\|\nabla F(X_0)\|=\delta/2\ge2\epsilon_0\), while its smallest Hessian eigenvalue is \(-1/10<-1/20\). It is outside the target SOSP set and belongs to the proof's single-step gradient branch.

The two Gaussian coordinates in the SGLD update give an exact expectation. Writing \(\eta=\delta^2\), \(g=\sin x=\delta/2\), and \(r=\delta^2\eta/2\), it is

\[
\begin{aligned}
D&:=\mathbb EF(X_1)-F(X_0)\\
 &= (1-e^{-r})(\cos x-1/10)
    +e^{-r}\{\cos x-\cos(x-\eta\sin x)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(0<\delta\le1/10\), \(\eta\le1/100\), \(r\le1/20000\), \(\cos x\ge99/100\), and \(1-e^{-r}\ge99r/100\). Taylor's inequality \(\cos(x-h)\le\cos x+h\sin x+h^2/2\), with \(h=\eta g\), therefore yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
D&\ge\eta\delta^2
\left[\frac{99}{200}\left(\frac{99}{100}-\frac1{10}\right)
-\frac14\left(1+\frac1{200}\right)\right]\\
&=\frac{1893}{10000}\eta\delta^2
>0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The proof instead requires \(D\le-\delta^2\eta/(4Q)<0\). The injected noise heats the positive-curvature coordinate more than this small gradient dissipates; the claimed negative drift is demonstrably false.

The existing escape lemma does not supply the missing estimate. At this same point, \(\lambda_H=1/10\), and Lemma 4.2 requires

\[
D_5=20\log576>100,\qquad T:=\eta_{o+1:n}\ge2D_5>200.
\]

Its gradient premise is at most \(\delta\sqrt{2/T}<\delta/10\), whereas the actual gradient is \(\delta/2\). This legal saddle state is covered by neither valid estimate supplied by the paper.

Reducing the step cannot resolve the sign: the same lower bound holds for every \(0<\eta\le\delta^2\). Reducing the volatility also leaves the construction and sign valid. A fixed numerical adjustment to the branch threshold cannot generally align the existing estimates: replacing \(1/10\) above by \(a\to0\), and choosing \(\lambda_\epsilon=a/2\), leaves the one-step heating scale proportional to \(\delta\), while the escape lemma's admissible gradient scale is at most

\[
O\!\left(\delta\sqrt{\frac{a}{\log(1/a)}}\right).
\]

A new estimate for the intervening gradient range, or a different block/Lyapunov argument, is needed. Such a repair may exist; the paper does not provide it.

**Reason for rejection.** A central advertised contribution is the new direct proof and explicit polynomial SOSP hitting guarantee. Its sole proof relies on the false drift(*) to cover states outside the target and then telescope expected decreases. The counterexample invalidates that coverage under the theorem's own global assumptions, and its other lemma does not cover the missing states. The stated main guarantee consequently lacks a valid derivation. I would change accept to reject for the paper as written until a sound argument covering these states and establishing the claimed bound is supplied. This finding does **not** assert that Theorem 4.3's hitting-time conclusion is false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the proof's stopping-time branches back to Eq. (3.4), I noticed that the positive Gaussian-noise term is of order \(\eta\delta_0^2\), while the claimed gradient threshold has square at most \(\delta_0^2/(4Q)\).

**Verification method.** Rechecked the definitions, constants and complete relevant proofs against the original PDF, including full rendered pages 11/26/27. Constructed the globally bounded cosine example, derived its Gaussian expectation exactly, and proved the positive increment by rational inequalities. Verified all assumptions, the theorem's step/volatility choices, off-target membership and failure of the existing escape-lemma premise. A separate exact-arithmetic helper and 15 stable numerical evaluations checked the derivation; independent root review rederived the expectation and rational lower bound.

 These are mathematical checks, not a rerun of author code.

**Confidence.** High. The failed proof inequality is contradicted by an exact expectation under globally verified assumptions, with a rational positive lower bound and independent rederivation. The claim is deliberately limited to the unsupported central proof, rather than an unestablished assertion that the theorem itself is false.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-339-I01
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Equation (6), PDF 6; Section 3.2, PDF 16–19, especially the equilibrium interpretation following Figure 6 on PDF 18; Section 3.4.2, PDF 24–26, including the stationary-IAT interpretation of Figure 11. Relevant qualifications are on PDF 3, the bias-fixing paragraph on PDF 25, and Appendix A.1 on PDF 27.

**Claim.** The paper uses a canonical parameter target proportional to \(\exp[-\beta L(\theta)]\). Its MNIST model in Section 3.2 is a direct affine map from 784 inputs to ten linear output logits, with softmax cross-entropy loss. It interprets million-step BAOAB trajectories as representative thermodynamic samples from the target ensemble and uses their parameter covariance for the loss-landscape analysis. The two-class version in Section 3.4.2 fixes output biases, computes IATs along leading parameter-covariance directions, and reports up to a factor of four improvement in real-data sampling/exploration using EQN. The stated experimental objective includes no weight prior, weight constraint or implemented localization.

**Error and evidence.** This target is not normalizable, even after the stated bias fixing. Write the logits as

\[
z_c(x)=w_c^Tx+b_c.
\]

For any \(v\in\mathbb R^{784}\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), transform every class weight by

\[
w_c\longmapsto w_c+t v.
\]

Every logit gains the same scalar \(t v^Tx\), so each softmax probability remains exactly unchanged:

\[
\frac{e^{z_c(x)+t v^Tx}}{\sum_j e^{z_j(x)+t v^Tx}}
=\frac{e^{z_c(x)}}{\sum_j e^{z_j(x)}}.
\]

Consequently every example loss, full-data loss and minibatch loss is constant in this direction. This holds for every dataset, independently of separability or inactive pixels. The 784 independent common-weight directions remain when all output biases are fixed. Free biases add another common-logit direction.

To show divergence of the full integral, choose any unit common-weight direction \(e\), and decompose the remaining parameter space orthogonally as \(\theta=s+q e\), with \(s\perp e\). Then \(L(s+qe)=L(s)\). On a compact set \(K\) of positive measure in the \(s\) coordinates, the finite continuous loss makes \(\exp[-\beta L(s)]\) bounded below by a strictly positive constant. Therefore, for every finite \(\beta>0\),

\[
\int_{s\in K}\int_{q\in\mathbb R}
 e^{-\beta L(s+qe)}\,dq\,ds=\infty.
\]

This uses a positive-measure cross-section, rather than incorrectly relying on a single measure-zero line. The stated full-parameter target is not a probability distribution and has no posterior parameter covariance. Lowering the temperature cannot confine an exactly flat direction.

The baseline dynamics displays the same obstruction. Project the unit-mass BAOAB update onto a common-weight direction. Its gradient force is zero for every minibatch, leaving

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{k+1}&=\alpha p_k+
\sqrt{(1-\alpha^2)/\beta}\,R_k,\\
q_{k+1}&=q_k+\tfrac h2(p_k+p_{k+1}),
\qquad \alpha=e^{-\gamma h}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The position is an integrated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck coordinate. Direct summation gives

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(q_n)}n
=\frac{h^2}{\beta}\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}>0.
\]

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 25, Theorem 36; PDF page 27, Theorem 40. The underlying failure is the CP canonical structure in Definition 22(ii), PDF page 16, and Lemma 24, PDF pages 18–19, propagated into the parameter count D, PDF page 23, and the function f in Eq. 25, PDF page 24. PDF page 28 expressly says the large-size/small-relative-rank restrictions are not required in the deterministic analysis.

**Claim.** Under the nested rank-one bases S1⊆⋯⊆SK of Section 3.1.2, generic factors/coefficients, and Assumption 1 (at least rk observations per column in source k), Theorem 36 claims a necessary and sufficient finite-completion criterion: a constraint subtensor of D slices must have f(S)≥|S| for every nonempty subset of its slices. Theorem 40 claims unique completion if an additional disjoint constraint subtensor from source K covers every row in each of the first d−1 modes. These concern literal CP rank defined in Eqs. 1/2, not Tucker rank or arbitrary matrix factors.

**Error and evidence: exact nested-union counterexample.** Set d=3, K=2, n1=n2=2, c1=1, c2=2, r1=1, and r2=2. Let

```
P = [[1,2], [3,6]],       Q = [[6,8], [15,20]].
U(:,:,1) = P,
U(:,:,2) = 2P+5Q = [[32,44], [81,112]],
U(:,:,3) = 3P+7Q = [[45,62], [114,158]].
```

P and Q are independent rank-one matrices: P=(1,3)^T(1,2), Q=(2,5)^T(3,4). Thus S1={vec(P)} is a strict subset of S2={vec(P),vec(Q)}. Source 1 has CP rank 1. Source 2 has CP rank 2: it has a two-term CP representation and its frontal matrix U(:,:,2) has nonzero determinant. Its coefficient matrix [[2,3],[5,7]] has determinant −1. All displayed original factor/allowed coefficient entries are nonzero; the zero coefficient of Q in source 1 is precisely the required nested model structure.

Observe entries (1,1),(1,2),(2,1) in each of the three frontal slices. Assumption 1 holds (three observations, versus source ranks 1/2). The constraint construction on PDF page 21 is explicit. In source 1 choose (1,1) as the single coefficient-solving base; the other two entries give constraint slices

```
C1: {(1,1),(1,2)}        [source 1]
C2: {(1,1),(2,1)}        [source 1].
```

In each source 2 slice choose base entries (1,1),(1,2); the extra observation gives

```
C3: {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)}  [source 2, first column]
C4: {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)}  [source 2, second column].
```

Here D=(2+2)·2−[1·1+2·1]−2=3. Choose the three-slice subtensor C1,C2,C3 for Theorem 36. Direct substitution into Eq. 25 gives:

| Subset | f | Size |
|---|---:|---:|
| C1 | 1 | 1 |
| C2 | 1 | 1 |
| C3 | 3 | 1 |
| C1,C2 | 2 | 2 |
| C1,C3 | 3 | 2 |
| C2,C3 | 3 | 2 |
| C1,C2,C3 | 3 | 3 |

The remaining C4 is disjoint, belongs to source K=2, and covers both rows in both modes: m1=m2=2=n1=n2. Therefore every stated deterministic condition of both Theorems 36 and 40 holds. If only the finite criterion is desired, observation (2,1,3) can even be omitted: C1–C3 still exist and meet the same seven inequalities with eight observed entries.

Nevertheless there is an exact continuum of different completions with these ranks and this same nested structure. For t near 8 define

```
Q(t) = [[6,t], [9+3t/4, (9+3t/4)t/6]],
b(t) = 20/(12-t),       a(t) = 32-6b(t),
d(t) = 28/(12-t),       c(t) = 45-6d(t).
```

Q(t) has determinant 0 and rank 1. The three slices are

```
P,
a(t)P+b(t)Q(t) = [[32,44], [81,132-5t/2]],
c(t)P+d(t)Q(t) = [[45,62], [114,186-7t/2]].
```

All nine observed entries are fixed for every t, while the two unobserved bottom-right entries vary linearly with t. For example, t=8 gives 112,158; t=9 gives 219/2,309/2. In a sufficiently small interval about 8 all factors remain nonzero, P/Q(t) remain independent, the coefficient determinant is −4/(12−t)≠0, and the first source 2 frontal matrix remains rank 2. Every member therefore has exactly the required CP ranks 1 and 2 and S1⊂S2. This contradicts finite as well as unique completability.

**Why genericity does not resolve the example.** The continuum is a generic property of this pattern, rather than an exceptional rational data coincidence. Write the uniquely completed first source as P=[[p,q],[r,rq/p]] (p≠0); normalize the other rank-one direction to Q11=1. Denote the observed source 2 columns by (x,y,z) and (X,Y,Z), listing entries 11,12,21. For a free t=Q12 define

```
beta(t)  = (p*y-q*x)/(p*t-q),
alpha(t) = (x-beta(t))/p,
v(t)     = (z-r*alpha(t))/beta(t),
Q(t)     = [[1,t],[v(t),v(t)*t]],
delta(t) = (p*Y-q*X)/(p*t-q),
gamma(t) = (X-delta(t))/p.
```

The first source 2 observed triple is preserved by construction. The second source 2 entry 21 is

```
r*X/p + [(p*Y-q*X)/(p*y-q*x)]*(z-r*x/p),
```

independent of t and equal to Z for every original nested rank-two model: the three observed vectors P,A,B lie in a common two-dimensional span. The first missing entry 22 is

```
(z-r*x/p)*t + r*y/p.
```

Its slope and all required denominators are nonzero for generic independent rank-one directions and generic coefficients. Thus it varies over an interval, while exact ranks and coefficient independence persist by continuity. The exclusions are zeros of nonzero polynomials in the original generically drawn factors/coefficients, so the failure persists with probability one under the paper's generic model. Forty-three independent rational-factor controls additionally verify this same formula without using the chosen fixed example.

**Underlying false step.** Definition 22 does not merely fix CP scaling/permutation ambiguities: for this K=2 example it requires the second CP component's first entry to be 0 in mode i0, for either possible i0=1 or 2. Consequently the first coordinate slice in that mode would be a single rank-one matrix. The actual tensor's corresponding slices have nonzero 2×2 minors −20 and −15. This shows that no such canonical representation exists, for either choice of i0. No auxiliary CP core is defined: the canonical vectors are used directly in the original tensor's sum of outer products, Eqs. 14/17/23. A matrix GL(r) basis transformation generally mixes rank-one components into higher-rank matrices and is not a legal CP gauge. The [primary 2017 paper, Lemma 3](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-189/17-189.pdf) cited to justify the base case was checked in its original PDF pages 7–9 and supplies the same unsupported matrix-to-CP extension, not a missing compensating core or change of coordinates.

**Reason for rejection.** Exact deterministic finite/unique sampling conditions are an explicitly advertised central contribution (abstract, executive summary PDF pages 6–7, Sections 5/6, conclusion PDF page 33). Both flagship deterministic criteria classify this genuine nested-union pattern as finite/unique even though generic data have infinitely many valid completions. Correcting the CP gauge requires replacing the unknown-dimension/algebraic-independence analysis and the claimed exact combinatorial criteria, rather than a local notation or constant correction. The probabilistic proofs of Theorems 42/43 additionally rely on those invalid criteria, so the printed derivation does not establish them; this small-size certificate is not claimed to falsify their distinct large-size probabilistic statements. Clustering and applications are not asserted experimentally false.

**Discovery method.** Noticed that Definition 22 fixes an entire identity block in one CP factor, then traced its use in D and f while reading the full completion proofs.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original rendered Definition 22, Lemma 24, Eqs. 24–28, Theorems 36/40 and the PDF page 28 statement separating deterministic from probabilistic restrictions. Constructed the nested rank-one family above, verified every subset inequality with exact rational arithmetic, and checked both rank and observation equalities at six distinct parameters. Independently re-derived the generic one-parameter family and executed 43 additional rational-factor controls. Read the primary cited canonical lemma directly. Full 36-page review, including references, and all six contact sheets completed; there are no appendices or empirical experiments beyond theoretical bound illustrations.

**Confidence.** High. Every deterministic hypothesis is explicitly checked, the continuum and rank certificates are algebraic, and the generic extension excludes an exceptional-data escape. Count the canonical-gauge failure and its repeated consequences for Theorems 36/40 as one underlying issue.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** The observed-count graph definition on PDF 1; model (3), random-effects distributions and Theorem 2 on PDF 7; Theorem 2 proof on PDF 18. PDF 2 explicitly distinguishes the graph of latent means from the graph of observed counts.

**Claim.** CONGA is a nonparametric graphical model for the conditional independence structure of the observed count vector. After introducing independent node-specific random effects \(\lambda_{tj}\sim D_j\), the paper identifies \(\beta_{jl}=0\) with \(X_{tj}\perp X_{tl}\mid X_{t,-(j,l)}\). The intended population parameter is \((\beta,G_1,\ldots,G_P)\), not an individually identifiable vector of fixed random effects.

It does not establish the claimed observed-count graph after those effects are integrated out. Here is a counterexample using exactly the paper's transformation and independently distributed node effects.

Take \(P=3\), \(F(x)=\arctan x\), \(\beta_{12}=\beta_{23}=1\), \(\beta_{13}=0\). Let \(\lambda_2=1\), and independently let each of \(\lambda_1,\lambda_3\) equal \(a=1/2\) or \(b=2\), with probabilities \(1/2,1/2\). These are valid finite-support mixing distributions with bounded log rates, finite moments and positive rates; they belong to the weak support of the Gamma-base Dirichlet-process specification. No dependence is inserted into the random-effects prior.

Define

\[
S_r(k)=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}\frac{r^x}{x!}
 \exp[-F(x)F(k)],\qquad
A_{rs}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{S_r(k)S_s(k)}{k!}.
\]

\[
\frac{S_b(k)}{S_a(k)}<e^{b-a}.
\]

To see strictness, write \(S_r(k)=e^r E_{N\sim\mathrm{Pois}(r)}[e^{-F(N)F(k)}]\). The integrand is strictly decreasing in \(N\), and a Poisson variable of rate \(b\) is a rate-\(a\) variable plus an independent nondegenerate Poisson increment. Thus the two Gram vectors are not proportional and

\[
A_{aa}A_{bb}>A_{ab}^2.
\]

Since \(F(0)=0\), the marginal joint probabilities at \(X_2=0\) are

\[
q_{uv}=P(X_1=u,X_2=0,X_3=v)
=\frac14\sum_{r,s\in\{a,b\}}
 \frac{r^u s^v}{u!v!A_{rs}}.
\]

For \(u,v\in\{0,1\}\), their independence minor is

\[
q_{00}q_{11}-q_{01}q_{10}
=\frac{(b-a)^2}{16}
 \left(\frac1{A_{aa}A_{bb}}-\frac1{A_{ab}^2}\right)<0.
\]

Therefore \(X_1\) and \(X_3\) are dependent conditional on \(X_2=0\), despite \(\beta_{13}=0\). Dividing by \(P(X_2=0)^2>0\) does not change the nonzero minor. The analytic strict inequality is independent of numerical precision. Continuity preserves the failure in nearby mixing distributions; it is not a requirement that a continuously based DP put positive probability on one exact finite-support distribution.

**Reason for rejection.** The central nonparametric construction does not have the observed conditional independence graph that its coefficients are claimed to encode. Its inferred zero/nonzero edges and neuron graph therefore lack that stated interpretation. Restricting every mixing distribution to a point mass removes the proposed nonparametric random-effects flexibility; relabeling the target as a latent-conditional graph changes the central contribution that the introduction explicitly distinguishes from an observed-count graph. Changing the joint normalization or mixing mechanism would require a different model and corresponding inference analysis. This warrants rejection of the paper as written, independently of any sampling implementation issue.

**Discovery method.** Traced the fixed-rate factorization in Theorem 2 through the subsequent random-effects specification and noticed that the rate-dependent joint normalizer remains inside the mixing integral.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered PDF 7 and 18 and the observed-versus-latent distinction on PDF 1–3. Derived the strict Gram determinant and conditional-probability minor above, verified the bounded-rate assumptions, and executed interval-arithmetic controls with explicit infinite-tail bounds. An independent reviewer separately derived the same Gram obstruction and numerical minor.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample uses the stated count support, exact arctangent transformation, independent node mixing and a zero claimed edge. The conditional-on-fixed-effects theorem is expressly preserved; the demonstrated failure is the advertised marginal observed-count interpretation.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-362-I02
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 4, PDF 8–10, particularly the new-rate proposal and MH adjustment on PDF 9; posterior credible-interval edge decisions on PDF 10–12. Authored `CONGA function.R` at prepublication commit `ff85fdbcb73ad3eb5f322d80ad1ab388133a2faf` (4 August 2020), new-rate acceptance calculation inside `CONGAfit`.

**Claim.** The adjusted proposals provide MCMC sampling of the stated pseudo-posterior, whose draws support posterior credible intervals and edge evidence. The method uses Gamma proposals for a new node rate, shrinks the proposed displacement by \(K_1<1\), and applies an MH acceptance step.

**Error and evidence.** The actual acceptance calculation does not account for the proposal or its shrinkage, and even evaluates the prior at the raw Gamma draw rather than the adjusted candidate. Its failure can be demonstrated in the elementary conjugate case without a long simulation.

Hold the other coordinates fixed, set \(\beta=0\), take one observation \(x=0\), and use the paper's \(a=b=1\). With one observation the DP rate marginal is its Gamma base and the new-rate branch is selected with probability one. The exact rate posterior is \(\mathrm{Exp}(2)\). Write the current rate as \(X\), the raw proposal as \(Z\sim\mathrm{Exp}(2)\), and choose the permitted \(K_1=1/2\). The adjusted proposal is \(Y=(X+Z)/2\).

The original source calculates

\[
R=\log L(Y)-\log L(X)
  +\log p_0(Z)-\log p_0(X)
=\tfrac32(X-Z),
\]

and accepts with \(\min(1,e^R)\). This is not the MH ratio for the adjusted proposal. For example, a proposal \(Y>2X\) has positive forward density but zero reverse density, since a reverse adjusted proposal cannot be smaller than \(Y/2\); the source can nevertheless accept it.

More decisively, start at the claimed stationary law, so \(X,Z\) are independent \(\mathrm{Exp}(2)\). Their difference \(D=Z-X\) has density \(e^{-2|d|}\). The exact one-step mean change is

\[
\begin{aligned}
E[X_{\rm next}-X]
&=\frac12\int_0^\infty d
 [e^{-7d/2}-e^{-2d}]\,\mathrm d d\\
&=\frac12\left(\frac1{(7/2)^2}-\frac1{2^2}\right)
=-\frac{33}{392}<0.
\end{aligned}
\]

A stationary integrable law cannot have this nonzero drift. Seven evaluations of the unchanged original likelihood functions and acceptance expressions reproduce \(R=1.5(X-Z)\) directly.

The source's finite sum \(B=100\) does not resolve the failure. Its actual one-observation target is proportional to \(e^{-x}/S_{100}(x)\), where \(S_{100}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{100}x^k/k!\). For \(x\le20\), the relative omitted Poisson tail is bounded by

\[
\epsilon=e^{-20}\frac{20^{101}}{101!}
 (1-20/102)^{-1}<10^{-35}.
\]

The tail bound is uniform on \([0,20]\) because Poisson upper-tail probabilities increase with their mean. The target normalizer differs from \(1/2\) by at most \(\epsilon/[2(1-\epsilon)]+e^{-20}\); outside this interval its normalized density is at most \(2e^{-x}\). Combining these bounds with \(|Y-X|\le(X+Z)/2\) bounds the difference between the truncated-target and ideal stationary-start drifts by less than \(10^{-6}\). The implemented truncated target's drift is therefore still below \(-0.08417\). The reproduction script checks this bound with outward-rounded arithmetic.

The defect also embeds in a data set with a nonsingular sample covariance, so it is not an artifact of the full function's undefined one-row initialization. Take three two-node observations \((0,0),(1,2),(2,1)\), \(\beta=0\), \(M_1=2\), and condition on the other two node-1 rates both being 100. The first rate's conditional DP posterior is the new-component density \(e^{-x}/S_{100}(x)\), together with an existing atom at 100 of mass below \(10^{-34}\). For current rate at most 20, the source's probability of copying that atom is at most \(e^{-60}/2\); outside, the bound \(p(x)\le2e^{-x}\) controls its mean contribution. The certificate bounds the total drift change from this embedding by another \(10^{-6}\), and the embedded conditional transition still has drift below \(-0.08417\). The arctangent-transformed sample covariance of these three rows is positive definite. The strict discrepancy also persists in a neighborhood of zero interaction coefficients by continuity.

The beta update has another manifestation of the same incorrect-target computation: its native `llhoodb` ratio uses only the conditional likelihood for the updated node, omitting the other affected node conditionals in the declared product pseudo-likelihood. In a two-node four-observation fixture its log ratio is approximately \(-0.1444497\), while the full product contributes \(-0.2888993\). These defects are counted as one issue with the posterior transition, not one issue per omitted term.

**Reason for rejection.** Correct pseudo-posterior computation is a central claimed contribution and the basis of the credible intervals used throughout the graph comparisons and neuron analysis. The supplied transition does not preserve even its elementary conjugate target, so those samples cannot be justified by the stated MH construction. A corrected transition and renewed posterior-based comparisons are required; extra burn-in cannot fix a wrong invariant law. This independently warrants rejecting the posterior-computation and empirical evidence as written. The check does not claim a reproduced numerical reversal of a historical graph ranking or an incorrect value for every reported edge.

**Discovery method.** Compared the adjusted proposals with the acceptance densities in Section 4, then traced them into the prepublication authored code.

**Verification method.** Rechecked rendered PDF 8–10. Recovered and Git-blob/size-verified the authored 2020 source; executed its six original inner function definitions and its original rate-acceptance expressions unchanged, in an isolated R environment. Derived the exact conjugate stationary-start drift and a finite-\(B\) error certificate, and checked the missing affected conditional with native functions. A second reviewer independently verified the drift algebra and centrality. This is an inner-kernel diagnostic; the complete `CONGAfit` covariance initialization is not defined for a one-row data matrix, and no historical complete-chain or 50-replication rerun is claimed.

The repository later added a `Modified sampling steps` directory. Its current README acknowledges issues with original implementations. Those postpublication versions are not evidence that the 2020 transition or printed results already used a corrected kernel; this report does not claim to have validated the newer algorithms.

**Confidence.** High for the published construction and verified historical source. The stationary-start drift is exact and the finite-sum implementation is covered by an explicit strict bound. Missing historical output arrays limit claims about particular edge decisions and comparison magnitudes, which are not asserted.

 Independently reviewed original source files are under unpublished audit files.

findings.title: Nonlinear sampling errors are treated as centered, invalidating the stochastic approximation and the main landscape proof
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-471__I01 — Nonlinear sampling errors are treated as centered, invalidating the stochastic approximation and the main landscape proof
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 1, PDF 12–13, and its sampled objective on PDF 11; Lemma 10, Appendix B, PDF 40; the comparison in Eq. A3 and its application of Lemma 10, Appendix A, PDF 33–34. The latter supports Lemma 6, then Lemmas 7–9 and Theorem 3's strict-saddle/no-spurious-minima claim, PDF 16 and 31–39, which is used in Corollaries 2–3, PDF 17.

**Claim.** Theorem 1 states that the objective and gradient obtained by sampling `n0` rows and `m0` columns per row approach the full objective and gradient at a rate proportional to `1/sqrt(n0)`. Its explanation explicitly says that increasing the row sample size makes their error vanish. Separately, the global landscape proof compares row-specific expressions containing inverse sampled Gram matrices with expressions using full Gram matrices. It applies Lemma 10 to make their average difference vanish as the number of independent rows increases. This comparison is needed to bound the Hessian terms and establish the central global-convergence guarantee.

These steps do not establish that the quantities being averaged have the asserted centers. Taking an inverse inside a sampled row produces bias that averaging more rows does not remove.

**Error and evidence.** Three exact checks establish the problem and its central proof dependency.

1. **Theorem 1 has a deterministic column-sampling counterexample.** Let `p=k=1`, `B=1_m`, `S=1`, `gamma=1`, and let every row of `A` consist of ones, with every entry observed. The required Frobenius norm of `S` is one, all inverses exist, and all data and feature entries are bounded. The full objective in Eq. 2, as a function of a scalar `s`, is

   \[
   c(s)=\frac1{1+ms^2}.
   \]

   For any selected subset of `m0` columns, the sampled objective on PDF 11 is instead

   \[
   c_t(s)=\frac1{1+m_0s^2}.
   \]

   Algorithm 2's stated side-information rule sets `m0=min(2p,m)=2` for `m>2`. At `S=1`, therefore,

   \[
   c(S)=\frac1{1+m},\qquad c_t(S)=\frac13,
   \quad \nabla c(S)=-\frac{2m}{(1+m)^2},\qquad
   \nabla c_t(S)=-\frac49.
   \]

   These values are deterministic: neither the selected rows nor the selected columns change them. Replicate the same bounded row any number of times and take `n0=n`. For example, with `m=4` the objective error is always `2/15`, and the gradient error is always `4/9−8/25=28/225`. They do not tend to zero as `n0` increases. Thus the claimed concentration around the full objective/gradient, with constants independent of the row sample size, is false. Allowing its constants to grow with `n0` would remove the advertised approximation conclusion.

   The actual no-side-information specialization uses all columns. This counterexample is not presented as a failure of that implementation's column selection. It refutes the stated general sampling theorem and the side-information justification.

2. **The averaging lemma used in the global proof is false as stated.** In Lemma 10, take independent `Xi~Bernoulli(1/2)`, `ai=0`, and `sigma_i=1/sqrt(log 2)`. Every individual tail premise holds for every `epsilon` in `(0,1)`: below `epsilon=1/2` its threshold exceeds one and the tail is zero; above it, the tail is `1/2≤epsilon`.

   But the average of these variables tends to `1/2`, not zero. At `n=1000` and `epsilon=0.01`, Lemma 10's threshold is

   \[
   2\sqrt{\frac{\log 25}{1000\log 2}}<\frac17.
   \]

   Hoeffding's inequality gives probability at least `1−exp(−12500/49)` that the average exceeds `1/7`. Consequently the event that the lemma claims has probability at most `0.01` has probability greater than `0.99`. A valid concentration result must center the average at its expectation, or separately control its bias.

3. **The problematic proof application also fails under the matrix-completion assumptions, at exact nonoptimal stationary points.** This rules out resolving the issue by adding a centering condition to the lemma without checking its use.

   Choose any integer `m≥3`, let `l=m−1`, `k=1`, `B=I_m`, and use the unregularized setting `1/gamma=0` of Theorem 3. Let

   \[
   S^*=\frac1{\sqrt m}(1,\ldots,1)^T,\qquad
   U^*=1_n,\qquad A=U^*S^{*T}.
   \]

   Define

   \[
   D=m^2-3m+3,\qquad
   S=\frac1{\sqrt D}(m-2,-1,\ldots,-1)^T.
   \]

   Both `S` and `S*` have unit Frobenius norm. Every `l`-row subvector of `S` has squared norm at least `(m−1)/D`. Thus both Assumptions 1–2 hold with, for example, `alpha²=(m−1)/(4D)>0`; the corresponding submatrices of `S*` and `U*` also exceed this lower bound. Taking `m>C+1` satisfies `l>Ck` for any proposed fixed sampling constant `C`.

   Under the stipulated row-sampling model, each row omits one uniform coordinate `J`. If `J=1`, the observed truth and candidate subvectors are proportional, so the residual is zero. If `J>1`, their inner product is exactly zero, because `(m−2)` is canceled by the `m−2` remaining negative coordinates. The fitted coefficient is then zero. In either case the row's profile gradient is exactly zero. Hence `grad c(S)=0` for **every possible sample**, satisfying any positive near-stationarity tolerance. The candidate has positive loss whenever at least one row omits a coordinate other than the first, an event of probability `1−m^(−n)`, while the truth has zero loss. The example is therefore not confined to points arbitrarily close to an optimum.

   Now use `M=e1` in Eq. A3. The sampled directional term is zero. If the full comparison is read using the unmasked true row `a=S*`, its per-row contribution, including the `1/m` factor, is

   \[
   h=\frac{(a^TS)(e_1^TP_Sa)}m
     =-\frac{(m-1)^2}{m^2D\sqrt D}\ne0.
   \]

   Thus the comparison error `−r h`, where `r=l/m`, is nonzero and deterministic for every `n`.

   Under the paper's explicit definition that `ai` has its missing entries zeroed, the comparison term is nonzero only when `J=1`, and its expectation is

   \[
   \mathbb E[h_J]
   =-\frac{(m-2)(m-1)^2}{m^3D\sqrt D}\ne0.
   \]

   Its average therefore converges to a nonzero value. Under either interpretation, the claimed bound on PDF 34, proportional to `r sqrt(D' k log n/(ln))` with a fixed finite constant `D'`, tends to zero while the actual error does not. The use of `l` instead of `r` in some subsequent displayed terms does not repair this failure. The witness meets the original row-sampling and rank assumptions; it is not based on singular sampled matrices.

Theorem 1 states that the objective and gradient obtained by sampling \(n0\) rows and \(m0\) columns per row approach the full objective and gradient at a rate proportional to \(1/\operatorname{sqrt}(n0)\).   2. The averaging lemma used in the global proof is false as stated. In Lemma 10, take independent \(\Xi \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), ai=0, and \(\sigma _{i}=1/\operatorname{sqrt}(\log 2)\). Every individual tail premise holds for every \(\epsilon\) in \((0,1)\): below \(\epsilon =1/2\) its threshold exceeds one and the tail is zero; above it, the tail is \(1/2\le \epsilon\).

    But the average of these variables tends to \(\frac{1}{2}\), not zero. At \(n=1000\) and \(\epsilon =0.01\), Lemma 10's threshold is

    \[ 2\sqrt{\frac{\log 25}{1000\log 2}}<\frac17. \]

findings.title: The recovery proof requires curvature in coordinates absent from every cascade likelihood
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-496__I01 — The recovery proof requires curvature in coordinates absent from every cascade likelihood
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Assumption 2, PDF 14, and its full `pK` dimensional Hessian construction, PDF 13; initialization in Section 4.3, PDF 11–12; Theorem 3 and Eq. 17–19, PDF 15; Theorem 4 and Eq. 20–21, PDF 16; the strong convexity step in Appendix A.1, PDF 33, and its use in Appendix A.2, PDF 34–39. The underlying model excludes self-infection on PDF 4, its likelihood uses strict predecessor sets in Eq. 1 and Eq. 5–6, PDF 5–6, and its low-rank parameterization appears in Eq. 8, PDF 9.

**Claim.** For known topic weights, the paper estimates the rank-one topic matrices `Θk=b1k b2kᵀ`, initializes by an unconstrained convex likelihood minimization followed by leading singular vectors, and proves that Algorithm 2 converges linearly to the true balanced factors up to statistical error. The abstract states consistency, and PDF 2 identifies the theory as a new contribution beyond the conference version. Its only initialization and recovery theorems require Assumption 2:

\[
 \mu I_{pK}\preceq H(\Theta^{[i]})\preceq L I_{pK},\qquad \mu>0.
\]

The preceding definitions explicitly put the full columns of the `p×p` matrices into `Θ[i]`, including their diagonal entries. The paragraph after the assumption explicitly concludes strong convexity in the full `p²K` dimensional collection. It is not a condition on a quotient space with known diagonals.

**Error and evidence.** Every diagonal rate is absent from the likelihood, so this assumption is impossible for the paper's cascade model, even locally at the true parameter and with arbitrarily many cascades.

For an infected target `i`, Eq. 1 and Eq. 5 involve rates `αji` only for nodes satisfying `tj<ti`. For an uninfected target, Eq. 6 involves sources with `tj<T<ti`. A node cannot satisfy either condition with `j=i`. The source is conditioned on at time zero; once a node is infected, the model records no further infection of that node. Thus the likelihood is independent of every `αii`. This argument applies to both the exponential and Rayleigh kernels used in the paper. Leaving a nonzero diagonal in the formal product in Eq. 8 does not create observations of self-infection; explicitly subtracting that diagonal, as PDF 9 permits, gives the same invariance.

Let `Eii=e_i e_iᵀ`. For any topic `k`, vary `Θk` to `Θk+tEii`, holding other topics fixed. This changes only the self-rate of node `i` in each cascade, so the complete likelihood remains exactly constant for every allowed `t`. Consequently its gradient in that coordinate is zero and its Hessian annihilates that coordinate. In the notation of PDF 13, let

\[
 v=e_k\otimes e_i\in\mathbb R^{pK}.
\]

Then `Pᶜv=mᶜ_k e_i`, and the single-cascade likelihood Hessian satisfies `Qe_i=0`. Therefore

\[
 H(\Theta^{[i]})v
 =\frac1n\sum_c(P^c)^\top Q(\alpha_i^c)P^c v=0,
 \qquad \|v\|_2=1.
\]

Assumption 2 would instead require `vᵀHv≥μ>0`. There are at least `K` such null directions in every target-column block and at least `pK` in the full parameterization. Better topic separation, nonzero observable rates, favorable source coverage, or larger sample sizes cannot remove these directions. This is also a population problem, since averaging zero directional curvature still gives zero.

This does **not** make the conditional implication “if Assumption 2, then …” logically false: its premise has no instance under the defined likelihood. The error is presenting it as a recovery/consistency guarantee applicable to this cascade model and using that impossible curvature to justify the proposed initializer and convergence radius. The proof's opening strong convexity inequality on PDF 33 cannot hold for this likelihood.

The issue extends beyond replacing a dimension symbol or deleting diagonal rows. The initializer needs a full rank-one matrix, including the unobserved entries. The following exact example demonstrates why merely interpreting Assumption 2 on off-diagonal rates does not preserve the printed initialization argument.

Set `p=3`, `K=1`, and every topic weight to one. Observe the six cascades obtained by all permutations of timestamps `(0,1,2)`, with observation window `T=3`. For each target, denote its two off-diagonal incoming rates by `a,b`. Its averaged negative log-likelihood is

\[
 f_i(a,b)=\frac{4a+4b-\log a-\log b-2\log(a+b)}6.
\]

At `a=b=1/2`, its gradient is zero and its off-diagonal Hessian block is

\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1/3\\1/3&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \lambda_{\min}=2/3,\quad\lambda_{\max}=4/3.
\]

Thus this observable problem is well conditioned. Take the true full rank-one matrix and balanced factors to be

\[
 \Theta^*=\tfrac12 J_3,\qquad
 b_1^*=b_2^*=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,1)^\top.
\]

Convexity and the zero gradient show that any matrix with these off-diagonal entries is a global minimizer of the unconstrained nonnegative-matrix likelihood. In particular, for every `M≥0`,

\[
 \widehat\Theta_M=\tfrac12J_3+(M-\tfrac12)I_3
\]

is a minimizer with the same objective. The gradient at the truth is exactly zero, while

\[
 \|\widehat\Theta_M-\Theta^*\|_F^2=3(M-\tfrac12)^2
\]

is unbounded. For `M≥1/2`, its leading singular value is `M+1`; its balanced leading SVD factors are `sqrt((M+1)/3)(1,1,1)ᵀ`, which also diverge from the true factors. The printed unconstrained minimization does not control these free coordinates before the SVD step.

Even the natural convention of zero-filling the unused diagonal gives leading singular value one, rather than `3/2`, and initial factors `(1,1,1)ᵀ/√3`. The resulting squared factor error is

\[
 2(1-\sqrt{3/2})^2\approx0.10102.
\]

Using the tight off-diagonal constants `μ=2/3,L=4/3`, the stated radius in Eq. 19 is only `1/48≈0.02083`. This fixed error persists with oracle recovery of the observable rates; increasing sample size alone does not provide the claimed initialization. A diagonal-completion rule or a different initializer and its analysis is needed. This example diagnoses failure of the suggested off-diagonal repair; it is not represented as satisfying the impossible printed Assumption 2.

Additional structural identification is needed for factor recovery as well. For any `q>0`,

\[
 \Theta(q)=\begin{pmatrix}q&1\\1&1/q\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b_1(q)=b_2(q)=(\sqrt q,1/\sqrt q)^\top
\]

has nonnegative balanced factors, rank one and `g2=0`. All these matrices give exactly the same two observable rates, both one, hence identical cascade distributions. They are distinct under the paper's factor distance, which removes only the negative sign after balancing. Embedding these two active nodes into any larger network with zero remaining entries gives two-sparse factor columns. The example shows why balancing and a positive Hessian on observable edge coordinates alone do not identify all factors. It does not refute a theorem augmented with suitable new structural assumptions.

**Reason for rejection.** The new journal-version consistency and linear-recovery guarantee is a central claimed contribution. Its curvature premise cannot hold for any data from the defined cascade process. The only initialization proof and subsequent contraction rely directly on that unavailable full-matrix curvature. Removing the unused coordinates changes the target space and leaves the stated SVD initialization unjustified; the exact well-conditioned example demonstrates the problem, while the balanced sparse family shows a further identification requirement. Restoring an applicable result requires structural identification/completion conditions and an initialization/recovery analysis that the paper does not supply. This is a loss of the advertised theoretical guarantee, not a local display correction preserving the proof. The model and empirical Algorithm 1 comparisons may remain useful; no historical comparison is alleged to be numerically false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the likelihood into the Hessian assumption, noticed that the theory includes each diagonal topic entry even though every infection likelihood uses a strict predecessor set. Following this invariance into the unconstrained minimization and SVD initialization exposed the full dependency of the recovery proof.

**Verification method.** Read all 47 pages and appendices, then rechecked the model, dimensions, assumption, initialization and proof in the original rendered pages. Derived the universal null direction algebraically, independently derived the six-permutation likelihood and its exact Hessian, and checked both the arbitrary-diagonal and balanced-factor families. Recovered all ten source blobs from the repository explicitly linked on PDF 19, pinned to commit `be65cb10d742c5c6f1933238eb44b5f1c8de279f` dated March 21, 2020, and verified their Git blob SHA-1, sizes and SHA-256. The journal gives only a publication month, so no more precise prepublication attribution is assumed. Source `Data_generation.m` explicitly zeros the rate diagonal, and `likeli.m` and its gradients use the same predecessor exclusion.

Eight independent exponential/Rayleigh controls across four `(p,K)` sizes with arbitrary topic weights and censoring produced exactly unchanged likelihoods, gradients and Hessians after changing every topic diagonal. All relevant coordinate Hessian products were exactly zero. Separate native Octave checks ran the unchanged authored likelihood and gradient functions: the stationary three-node fixture, five arbitrary-diagonal minimizers and five balanced equivalent-factor fixtures agreed, and twelve random gradient checks matched central finite differences. These are bounded verification controls; the general proof is the algebra above.

A second reviewer independently inspected the original model, full-coordinate assumption and proof, including full rendered pages 9, 13, 14 and 33, and rederived the three Hessian blocks using exact rational arithmetic. Five free-diagonal/SVD cases, three balanced rank-one equivalences and radius `1/48` agreed. Independent evidence is in unpublished audit files, its adjacent Markdown note, and an unpublished audit file.

Reproducible helpers:

- Source and pinned metadata: an unpublished audit file
- Both verification processes completed with exit code zero; logs are an unpublished audit file and an unpublished audit file.

**Confidence: High.** Exact invariance of every cascade likelihood proves the null directions for every sample and both reported kernels. Exact stationary, positive-observable-curvature and rank-one ambiguity examples establish why the printed initializer/factor conclusion does not follow from simply dropping those coordinates. Authenticated authored routines and independent numerical controls agree. The finding concerns applicability and the central proof; it neither calls a vacuous conditional implication false nor claims a rerun of unavailable historical experimental arrays.
