has nonnegative balanced factors, rank one and \(g2=0\). All these matrices give exactly the same two observable rates, both one, hence identical cascade distributions. They are distinct under the paper's factor distance, which removes only the negative sign after balancing. Embedding these two active nodes into any larger network with zero remaining entries gives two-sparse factor columns. The example shows why balancing and a positive Hessian on observable edge coordinates alone do not identify all factors. It does not refute a theorem augmented with suitable new structural assumptions.

Reason for rejection. The new journal-version consistency and linear-recovery guarantee is a central claimed contribution. Its curvature premise cannot hold for any data from the defined cascade process. The only initialization proof and subsequent contraction rely directly on that unavailable full-matrix curvature. Removing the unused coordinates changes the target space and leaves the stated SVD initialization unjustified; the exact well-conditioned example demonstrates the problem, while the balanced sparse family shows a further identification requirement. Restoring an applicable result requires structural identification/completion conditions and an initialization/recovery analysis that the paper does not supply. This is a loss of the advertised theoretical guarantee, not a local display correction preserving the proof. The model and empirical Algorithm 1 comparisons may remain useful; no historical comparison is alleged to be numerically false.

Discovery method. While tracing the likelihood into the Hessian assumption, noticed that the theory includes each diagonal topic entry even though every infection likelihood uses a strict predecessor set. Following this invariance into the unconstrained minimization and SVD initialization exposed the full dependency of the recovery proof.

Verification method. Read all 47 pages and appendices, then rechecked the model, dimensions, assumption, initialization and proof in the original rendered pages. Derived the universal null direction algebraically, independently derived the six-permutation likelihood and its exact Hessian, and checked both the arbitrary-diagonal and balanced-factor families. Recovered all ten source blobs from the repository explicitly linked on PDF 19, pinned to commit be65cb10d742c5c6f1933238eb44b5f1c8de279f dated March 21, 2020, and verified their Git blob SHA-1, sizes and SHA-256. The journal gives only a publication month, so no more precise prepublication attribution is assumed. Source Data_generation.m explicitly zeros the rate diagonal, and likeli.m and its gradients use the same predecessor exclusion.

Eight independent exponential/Rayleigh controls across four \((p,K)\) sizes with arbitrary topic weights and censoring produced exactly unchanged likelihoods, gradients and Hessians after changing every topic diagonal. All relevant coordinate Hessian products were exactly zero. Separate native Octave checks ran the unchanged authored likelihood and gradient functions: the stationary three-node fixture, five arbitrary-diagonal minimizers and five balanced equivalent-factor fixtures agreed, and twelve random gradient checks matched central finite differences. These are bounded verification controls; the general proof is the algebra above.

A second reviewer independently inspected the original model, full-coordinate assumption and proof, including full rendered pages 9, 13, 14 and 33, and rederived the three Hessian blocks using exact rational arithmetic. Five free-diagonal/SVD cases, three balanced rank-one equivalences and radius \(\frac{1}{48}\) agreed. Independent evidence is in unpublished audit files, its adjacent Markdown note, and an unpublished audit file.

Reproducible helpers:

  • Source and pinned metadata: an unpublished audit file
  • Both verification processes completed with exit code zero; logs are an unpublished audit file and an unpublished audit file.

Confidence: High. Exact invariance of every cascade likelihood proves the null directions for every sample and both reported kernels. Exact stationary, positive-observable-curvature and rank-one ambiguity examples establish why the printed initializer/factor conclusion does not follow from simply dropping those coordinates. Authenticated authored routines and independent numerical controls agree. The finding concerns applicability and the central proof; it neither calls a vacuous conditional implication false nor claims a rerun of unavailable historical experimental arrays.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-585-I01
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 18, Section 6.2, paragraph after Eq. (20) asserting that isotropy and coordinate moment condition (17) imply Assumption 10(a); Theorem 6 on PDF page 19 and Theorem 7 on PDF page 21, especially their squared Euclidean estimation bounds. Assumption 10(a) is on PDF page 14; the coordinate complexity comparison is Theorem 5 on PDF pages 16–17. Page numbers are the original PDF's page numbers.

**Claim.** Theorems 6 and 7 assert that the minmax MOM logistic LASSO and SLOPE estimators attain

\[
\|\widehat t-t^*\|_2^2\le C(c_0,M,C_0)
\max\left\{\frac K N,\frac{s\log(ep/s)}N\right\}
\]

with probability at least \(1-2e^{-cK}\), for an isotropic design whose individual coordinates satisfy \(\|X_j\|_{L_q}\le M\sqrt q\) for \(1\le q\le C_0\log p\), an \(s\)-sparse oracle satisfying the high-probability bounded-logit condition (21), iid inliers, sufficiently large \(N\ge c s\log(ep/s)\), and \(K\ge7|\mathcal O|/3\). The preceding argument says these coordinate moments imply a dimension-independent \(L_{2+\epsilon}/L_2\) equivalence for every linear form. They do not. The following two-model construction satisfies the application theorems' stated conditions and makes their estimation rate impossible for every estimator.

**Error and evidence.** Let \(m\to\infty\), and set

\[
k=2^m,\qquad s=k^2,\qquad N=p=2^k,\qquad K=s.
\]

Let \(H\) be the Sylvester Walsh matrix of order \(s\), explicitly \(H_{r,j}=(-1)^{r\cdot j}\) for binary vectors \(r,j\in\{0,1\}^{2m}\), where the dot product is modulo2. Choose its row index \(R\) uniformly and an independent symmetric sign \(S\). Set \(X_{1:s}=S H_{R,:}\), and fill the remaining coordinates with independent symmetric Rademacher variables independent of \((R,S)\). Since \(H^\top H=sI\) and the global sign centers the constant Walsh column, \(\mathbb EX=0\) and \(\mathbb EXX^\top=I_p\). Every coordinate has absolute value 1. Thus all coordinate moment inequalities hold for every \(q\ge1\) with the fixed \(M=1\); fix \(C_0=4\), \(\epsilon=2\), \(c_0=1\).

Define \(t_1\) to equal \((\log4)/k\) on the first \(s\) coordinates and zero elsewhere, and \(t_2=2t_1\). Both are exactly \(s\)-sparse and have bounded Euclidean norms, and

\[
\|t_2-t_1\|_2=\log4.
\]

For model \(a\in\{1,2\}\), generate labels according to

\[
P_a(Y=1\mid X)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-\langle t_a,X\rangle)}.
\]

These are well-specified logistic models, and \(t_a\) is the unique population risk minimizer in the paper's full class \(F=\{x\mapsto\langle t,x\rangle:t\in\mathbb R^p\}\). Indeed, the logistic risk Hessian at every finite parameter is \(\mathbb E[\sigma(f)(1-\sigma(f))XX^\top]\), which is positive definite: its weight is strictly positive on the finite support and isotropy excludes a zero nontrivial linear form. All losses and moments are finite for each family member. The loss is convex and 1-Lipschitz, \(F\) is convex, and \(F\subset L_2\).

Every Walsh row except the constant row sums to zero. Consequently, \(\langle t_1,X\rangle=0\) with probability \(1-1/s\), and equals \(\pm k\log4=\pm\log(N^2)\) on the remaining event; the second oracle has twice these logits. Both therefore satisfy

\[
P_a(|\langle t_a,X\rangle|\le1)=1-1/s.
\]

This satisfies (21) for all sufficiently large \(m\) for **every fixed finite** \(C'=c(M,C_0)\) asserted by the paper. There are no outliers and all observations are iid. Also \(K\mid N\), \(K\le N\), \(N/[s\log(ep/s)]\to\infty\), and \(s/p\to0\). Thus the sample/block-size requirements hold eventually for every fixed theorem constant. This construction uses bounded coordinates, sparse oracles and bounded coefficient norms. Each family member is a fixed finite distribution specified before drawing its iid sample. The dimension-dependent family is legitimate because the theorem constants depend only on the same fixed \(c_0,M,C_0\), and no uniform-in-direction design parameter appears in the stated hypotheses.

The joint observation laws differ only on the constant Walsh row, whose probability is \(1/s\). Conditional on its positive sign, the respective success probabilities are

\[
q_1=\frac{N^2}{1+N^2},\qquad q_2=\frac{N^4}{1+N^4}.
\]

For the negative sign the difference has the same magnitude. Hence, with total variation normalized as the supremum over events,

\[
\operatorname{TV}(P_1,P_2)=\frac{q_2-q_1}{s}
 <\frac1{sN^2},\qquad
\operatorname{TV}(P_1^{\otimes N},P_2^{\otimes N})
 <\frac1{sN}\longrightarrow0.
\]

By contrast, the theorems' squared estimation scale is

\[
\max\{K/N,s\log(ep/s)/N\}
=\frac{s\log(ep/s)}N\longrightarrow0,
\]

and their failure probability tends to zero. The specified tuning is the same under these two laws: \(c_0,M,C_0,N,p,s,K\) all coincide. If either stated theorem held, choosing the nearer of \(t_1,t_2\) to its estimator would distinguish the two models with both error probabilities tending to zero. But every test has the sum of its two error probabilities at least \(1-\operatorname{TV}(P_1^{\otimes N},P_2^{\otimes N})\to1\). This is a contradiction. It also covers randomized estimators using independent random seeds.

The exact failed premise explains this impossibility. For the unit vector \(v\) equal to \(1/k\) on the first \(s\) coordinates and zero elsewhere, \(\langle X,v\rangle\) is zero except for values \(\pm k\) with total probability \(1/s\). Thus

\[
\|\langle X,v\rangle\|_{L_2}=1,\qquad
\frac{\|\langle X,v\rangle\|_{L_4}}
{\|\langle X,v\rangle\|_{L_2}}=s^{1/4}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

No dimension-independent \(C'=c(1,4)\) satisfies Assumption 10(a). Theorem 5 compares Rademacher complexity using coordinate moments and an unconditional dual norm; it cannot supply this missing all-direction moment or logistic curvature assumption.

**Reason for rejection.** Logistic LASSO and SLOPE under weak coordinate moment assumptions are two explicit principal applications, identified in the abstract/introduction and presented as optimal robust estimation guarantees. Both coefficient-recovery theorems are false under their stated assumptions, even without outliers and with uniformly bounded coordinates. This is not a constant, tuning or implementation correction: the information bound applies to every estimator. A valid guarantee requires a genuinely stronger directional moment/curvature assumption and excludes designs explicitly allowed by the published statements, substantively narrowing the advertised robustness result. Those two principal claims must be withdrawn or replaced for the paper to be acceptable as written. The conditional meta-theorems retaining an explicit local Bernstein condition and the Huber applications imposing all-direction subgaussianity are not refuted; neither is the displayed excess-risk bound asserted false by this construction.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the claimed weak-moment logistic applications back to their local Bernstein premise, I noticed that a coordinate moment condition was being used to assert a moment equivalence for every linear combination. I tested a bounded-coordinate Walsh design whose dependent coordinates concentrate one linear form on a rare event.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original statements, definitions and assumptions on PDF pages 3–5,9–11,14,16–21, including full rendered pages 14,16–21, and completed the rest of the 47-page paper. Constructed the two exact well-specified logistic laws above; verified centering/isotropy, all coordinate moment conditions, unique sparse global oracles, oracle condition (21), block/sample conditions, bounded coefficient norms and vanishing total variation. Applied the exact testing inequality to contradict the advertised Euclidean guarantees. Independent integer Walsh and rational-probability computations supplement the derivation; they do not replace its arbitrary-constant asymptotic argument.

**Confidence.** Very high. The contradiction is an explicit information-theoretic impossibility under the stated application assumptions, with exact design/probability identities. The omitted directional condition is explicitly retained elsewhere in the paper and is not imposed in Theorems 6/7; the PDF's purported derivation of it is itself false. The two theorems share one underlying error and are counted as one issue.

 Computational checks: an unpublished audit file and the corresponding `targeted-checks.json`/`.log` in the same checks directory. Whole-paper coverage/source-search limits are recorded there. These are independent mathematical controls. No failure of historical simulation results or native author experiment rerun is claimed.

 This QA is a focused independent check, not a second complete paper review.

findings.title: The central training-time comparison charges DKRR for communication initialization it does not perform
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-592__I01 — The central training-time comparison charges DKRR for communication initialization it does not perform
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Simulation3, PDF28, the paragraph identifying communication Step1 with ordinary DKRR training; Table1 PDF29; Figure8 PDF30 and Figure10 PDF31, with the training-time conclusion immediately below Figure10. Compare the definition of ordinary DKRR in Eqs1–3 PDF4–5 with communication initialization in AppendixB PDF34. In the linked release: `DKRRC_tool/DKRR_train.m`22–27, `DKRRC_tool/DKRRC_train.m`23–34, and `plotfig8to10_Hsim.m`16–26; the same error appears in `plotfig8to10_sim.m`.

**Claim.** Simulation3 compares ordinary DKRR with the proposed communication method at machine counts that keep relative MSE within5% of global KRR. The paper assigns communication Step1's computational work to ordinary DKRR as well, then concludes that, in3D, communication substantially reduces training time even with32 iterations. The paragraph below Figure10 identifies this accuracy-preserving computational advantage as the paper's main focus. Data-transmission time is explicitly excluded; the issue below persists under that same convention.

**Error and evidence.** The baseline is charged a different training procedure from the ordinary DKRR estimator being compared.

For a worker with `n_j` training examples, ordinary DKRR needs its local matrix `K(D_j,D_j)`, solves its local ridge problem and retains its coefficients. Its local kernel construction involves `n_j^2` pairs. Predictions on a future test set are evaluated later. Ordinary DKRR does not need predictions on the other workers' training examples. This follows directly from Eqs1–3 and agrees with the authors' `DKRR_train.m`, which constructs only the local Gram at line22, inverts its regularized version at23 and forms coefficients at24.

The communication initializer instead constructs `K(D,D_j)` with `N*n_j` entries, extracts its local submatrix, solves, and evaluates the local predictor on all N training points. These operations initialize subsequent global-gradient communications. They are all inside the Step1 timer in `DKRRC_train.m`27–34. For equal blocks, the cross-Gram therefore has m times as many kernel pairs as DKRR's local Gram, plus the additional all-N prediction multiply.

Nevertheless, both released Figure8–10 plotting scripts assign the ordinary baseline time as:

```matlab
TimeTr_tmp = TimeTr_DKRRC{i}{k,j};
TrTime_DKRR(k,i,j) = mean(TimeTr_tmp.Step1);
```

They do not use the ordinary DKRR training timer. Thus the plotted baseline includes communication-specific cross-machine work which its own training routine never performs. This matches the original PDF28 assertion that the two Step1 costs are the same. The correct local kernel-work term is proportional to `N^2*tau/m^2`, while communication initialization uses `N^2*tau/m`. The printed `O(N^2*tau/m+N^3/m^3)` remains a valid loose upper bound for ordinary DKRR; the finding is the invalid identification and measured baseline charge, not that this Big-O upper bound is logically false. A cubic solve can dominate both asymptotically.

The source is the repository linked by the [official JMLR page](https://jmlr.org/papers/v21/19-592.html): [DKRRCJMLR](https://github.com/18357710774/DKRRCJMLR), commit `b6b00e018c6c004b5ec6c930475d2764805f4806`, May19,2020. All39 original file blobs were checked against Git blob SHA1 and SHA256. The release follows April2020 publication; exact historical timing arrays were not recovered. Source attribution alone is therefore limited, but the wrong timer rationale is also explicitly present in the original PDF.

**Reproducible checks of material consequence.** Unchanged authored training and testing functions were run under Octave with one disclosed adapter implementing Euclidean `pdist2`. An independent finite-feature RKHS reconstruction first checked18 fixtures in1D/3D: every native communication iterate agreed with Eq6 to below2e-15 in test prediction, and the initial communication estimate agreed with ordinary DKRR. The timing comparison therefore concerns the paper's estimator, rather than a substituted algorithm. A further24 paired timing fixtures measured baseline inflation from2.255× to14.083×.

A matched-accuracy check then used the paper's3D generator: iid uniform `[0,1]^3`, its stated compact Wendland regression target, independent Gaussian training noise of variance0.2, the stated Wendland kernel,1000 noiseless test targets, N3000 and lambda2/N. These are the first displayed varying-N sample size and its released selected lambda. Across all30 fresh native seeds, global KRR's mean MSE was0.00429896029665. Applying the released5% tolerance and50-step convergence filter to the full machine grid gives:

| Method | Machines | Communications | Mean MSE | Actual training time, seconds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ordinary DKRR |4|0|0.00449685757348|0.0302773|
| Communication method |8|2|0.00433719721516|0.0369280|
| Communication method |8|4|0.00430585804297|0.0382684|
| Communication method |8|8|0.00429897987062|0.0409345|
| Communication method |8|16|0.00429880618011|0.0462559|
| Communication method |8|32|0.00429892624227|0.0568883|

The erroneous baseline charge is0.0945388 seconds instead of0.0302773. It produces apparent speedups for every listed communication count, whereas timing the actual DKRR routine produces slowdowns from1.22× to1.88×. These are mean times under the same mean-local-worker plus serial-aggregation convention. The full30-seed low-grid check contains15300 unique predictions. Machine counts22:2:60 are excluded without assuming monotonicity: for each, seed1's50-step MSE exceeds1.78e27, so that single nonnegative contribution already makes the30-seed mean fail the original convergence filter. All smaller even machine counts were checked. Ordinary DKRR at22:2:60 was separately evaluated on all30 seeds; its smallest high-grid mean MSE was0.00612084, above the5% upper cutoff0.00451391, so no untested baseline re-entry is assumed.

The consequence also occurs at the original headline sample size N20000, rather than only the smallest N. With lambda6/N and one fresh seed, ordinary DKRR with10 machines has MSE0.00105895686552 and training time0.331897 seconds. Communication with48 machines has:

| Communications | MSE | Training time, seconds | Slowdown versus actual DKRR10 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|8|0.00107731398225|0.494364|1.49×|
|16|0.00105461235233|0.563750|1.70×|
|32|0.00105347191392|0.702240|2.12×|

All four estimates meet the same5% criterion against the directly checked global-KRR MSE0.00105372876702. To verify that reference without a dense inverse, conjugate gradients solved the full Gram system `(K+6I)alpha=y` in111 iterations. Its residual2-norm was3.3871e-11. Since K is positive semidefinite, `||alpha−alpha_exact||_2 <= ||residual||_2/6`; multiplying by the test-kernel Frobenius norm gives prediction2-error at most6.4284e-9, RMSE uncertainty2.0329e-10, and the numerical MSE enclosure `[0.00105372875382,0.00105372878022]`. This easily separates every displayed relative error from5%. A stable12-machine communication reference independently agrees to7e-16 in MSE. Ordinary DKRR12 is not used as the fair large-N baseline because its fresh MSE fails5%, despite being the original paper's selected large-N machine count. Separately, timing that12-machine configuration measures0.233842 seconds for actual DKRR versus1.976818 seconds for the charged communication Step1, an8.45× inflation.

These fresh tests demonstrate that the accounting defect can reverse the accuracy–time conclusion under the paper's own synthetic conditions, including its largest sample size. They do not establish that every communication configuration is slower, or reconstruct every original figure ordinate. Octave, the distance adapter, machine load, fresh random draws and unrecovered historical MATLAB arrays limit such a stronger claim.

**Reason for rejection.** The central computational evidence compares the proposed algorithm with a baseline charged substantial extra work specific to the proposed algorithm's initialization. Consequently Figures8/10 and the associated assertion of an accuracy-preserving speed advantage do not establish the advertised comparison. The fresh matched-accuracy reversals show that this is consequential, including at N20000. Correcting the timer requires a validated replacement comparison and reconsideration of a contribution explicitly identified as central; it cannot be treated as a local display correction with the central computational conclusion already preserved. The statistical rate bounds, machine-count enlargement and algebra of the communication iteration are not refuted by this finding. The rejection-level consequence is loss of the main empirical accuracy–speed evidence as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Table1's operation counts into the source timing plots, noticed that ordinary DKRR was assigned the communication initializer's cross-Gram cost. Followed this suspicion into the two distinct native training routines and the plotting assignment.

Its local kernel construction involves \(n_{j}^{2}\) pairs. Predictions on a future test set are evaluated later. Ordinary DKRR does not need predictions on the other workers' training examples. This follows directly from Eqs1–3 and agrees with the authors' DKRR_train.m, which constructs only the local Gram at line22, inverts its regularized version at23 and forms coefficients at24.

The communication initializer instead constructs \(K(D,D_{j})\) with \(N*n_{j}\) entries, extracts its local submatrix, solves, and evaluates the local predictor on all N training points. These operations initialize subsequent global-gradient communications. They are all inside the Step1 timer in DKRRC_train.m27–34. For equal blocks, the cross-Gram therefore has m times as many kernel pairs as DKRR's local Gram, plus the additional all-N prediction multiply.

Nevertheless, both released Figure8–10 plotting scripts assign the ordinary baseline time as:

findings.title: The finite-validation selection guarantee is false under the stated local moment assumptions
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-636__I01 — The finite-validation selection guarantee is false under the stated local moment assumptions
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 30, PDF page 35; its proof on PDF pages 36–38, especially the uniform constant in (106)–(107) on page 37. The introductory version is Theorem 5 on PDF page 4. Assumptions 1–2 are on PDF pages 2–3. The constructive global complexity argument in Corollary 31, PDF pages 38–39, invokes this estimate; introductory Corollary 6 gives the corresponding result.

**Claim.** Under Assumptions 1–2, run K independent SGD trajectories with step size r j^(-rho), training batch M, and independent uniform initializations in a bounded open set A. Select the candidate minimizing its empirical loss on a shared independent validation batch. Write B for the paper's validation batch size, to distinguish it from training M. Theorem 30 asserts constants R0, delta0, rbar, c independent of n, M, B, K and the allowed step amplitude r such that, for epsilon in (0,1),

```
P(f(selected candidate) - inf f >= epsilon)
 <= c K / (epsilon^2 B)
    + [q + c {epsilon^(-2) n^(-rho) + M^(-1) n^(1-rho)
               + r(1 + M^(-1/2) n^(1-rho))/D}]^K,

q = |A \ V_(R/2,delta)(x0)| / |A|,
D = R/2 - 2 delta > 0.
```

The positive-part convention in the paper's denominator is immaterial because the witness uses D>0. Assumption 2 bounds the second moments of the loss and its gradient on each compact parameter set; it imposes no global or n-uniform moment bound on the candidate distributions. The following counterexample uses the ordinary first-index empirical minimizer among actual candidates. It does not exploit the theorem statement's omission of explicit candidate membership.

**Error and evidence: an admissible fixed model.** Let theta=(x,y) in R^2. Define eta(t)=exp(-1/t) for t>0 and zero otherwise, and the smooth cutoff

```
chi(x) = 1                                  if x <= 1,
         eta(2-x)/(eta(2-x)+eta(x-1))         if 1 < x < 2,
         0                                  if x >= 2.

f(x,y) = chi(x) x^2 + (1-chi(x))(1+exp(-x)),
w(x)   = exp((1-chi(x)) x) >= 1.
```

Let phi(t)=630 t^4(1-t)^4 on (0,1), zero elsewhere, let X be uniform on [0,1], and set

```
F((x,y),z) = f(x,y) w(x) phi(w(x) z).
```

Phi is globally C3, positive on (0,1), has integral 1 and maximum 315/128. Every sample loss is nonnegative and C3 in theta. Changing variables t=wz gives E F(theta,X)=f(theta). Differentiation is valid on every compact parameter set; equivalently, the exact identities integral phi=1 and integral t phi'=-1 give E grad F=grad f. Loss and gradient are jointly continuous and bounded on each compact parameter set times [0,1]. Therefore every compact second-moment bound in Assumption 2 holds, even with a pointwise bound over the bounded data space.

The function f is globally smooth. Its global minimum is zero exactly on the straight line M={0} x R. On U=(-3/4,3/4) x R it equals x^2, so M intersect U is a nonempty one-dimensional smooth manifold and its Hessian is diag(2,0), of rank 1. All parts of Assumption 1 hold. Choose rho=3/4 and initialize uniformly on the bounded open set

```
A = A_good union A_bad,
A_good = (-1/2,1/2) x (0,1),
A_bad  = (2,3) x (0,1).
```

The two components have equal area. A run is initialized bad with probability 1/2. Choose x0=(0,1/2) on the minimum manifold.

**Good candidates always have positive validation loss.** Fix r with 0<r<32/315. For every finite M and every realization, a good trajectory obeys

```
x_j = x_(j-1) [1 - 2 r j^(-rho) M^(-1) sum_m phi(X_(j,m,k))].
```

The bracket lies in (1/2,1]. Thus a nonzero good coordinate remains nonzero inside (-1/2,1/2), and its true loss is below 1/4. Every independent validation sample belongs to (0,1) almost surely, where phi is strictly positive. Every good candidate consequently has strictly positive empirical validation loss. The initial value x=0 is a probability-zero exception.

**Bad candidates have true loss greater than 1 while their empirical loss vanishes.** First consider their population-gradient paths. They stay in x>=2 and satisfy

```
x_j = x_(j-1) + r j^(-rho) exp(-x_(j-1)),
exp(x_j) >= exp(x_(j-1)) + r j^(-rho),
w(x_n) >= exp(2) + r sum_(j=1)^n j^(-rho).
```

The last lower bound diverges uniformly over the bad initial component, while f(x_n,y)=1+exp(-x_n)>1. If all B validation samples exceed 1/w_min, where w_min is a lower bound on every bad candidate's final w, then every bad candidate has empirical loss exactly zero. Conditional on the training paths, this common event has probability at least 1-B/w_min. The selector must then pick a bad candidate whenever at least one exists, since all good empirical losses are strictly positive.

**The contradiction uses finite training batches.** Fix finite n and K before increasing M. There is a common compact set containing every finite-M trajectory and every population path through time n. To see this explicitly, start with a ball of radius R_0 containing the compact closure of A, put a_j=r j^(-rho), and recursively choose

```
G_j = sup {|grad F(theta,z)| : |theta| <= R_(j-1), 0 <= z <= 1},
R_j = R_(j-1) + a_j G_j.
```

Each G_j and R_j is finite by continuity. The radius recursion bounds every batch average, independently of M, and also bounds its expectation. On the final ball the conditional variance of a centered batch-gradient error is at most C_n/M. The gradient of f is Lipschitz there. Finite induction in j, Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound over the fixed K trajectories show convergence in probability to the population paths as M tends to infinity, uniformly over the initial closure. Thus some finite sufficiently large M makes all path errors arbitrarily small.

After the first population update every bad x is at least 2+r exp(-3). Choose a path tolerance t<r exp(-3)/4. On the simultaneous approximation event, bad final coordinates remain greater than 2, and

```
w_min >= exp(-t) [exp(2) + r sum_(j=1)^n j^(-rho)].
```

For fixed B choose finite n making this exceed 100 B. Next choose finite M making the approximation event have probability at least .99. Conditional on this event, the validation support-miss probability is at least .99. Hence with epsilon=1/2,

```
P(f(selected)-inf f >= epsilon) >= 1 - 2^(-K) - .02.
```

No infinite training batch is substituted into the theorem. The finite-M existence argument and the strict empirical ordering provide finite violating parameters.

**Quantifier order refuting every proposed theorem constant.** Suppose the theorem supplies positive R0, delta0, rbar and c. Choose fixed positive R<=min(R0/2,1/4) and delta<=min(delta0/2,R/16). The paper's tube is {|x|<delta, |y-1/2|<R/2}, inside A_good, so q=1-delta R<1 and D=R/2-2 delta>0. Choose a fixed r below rbar and 32/315, with cr/D<=(1-q)/8. Set qstar=(1+q)/2. Choose K with qstar^K<1/16 and 2^(-K)<1/16. Choose finite B with cK/(epsilon^2 B)<1/16. Then choose finite n making both c epsilon^(-2)n^(-rho)<(1-q)/8 and the support lower bound above greater than 100 B. Finally choose finite M large enough for the finite-path approximation and to make its two M-dependent terms contribute less than (1-q)/4 to the bracket.

The claimed bracket is then at most qstar, so the claimed upper bound is less than 1/8. The actual failure probability exceeds 1-1/16-.02>.9. This contradicts Theorem 30 with one fixed admissible model, for every possible choice of its constants. In particular, r is fixed before n; the argument does not rely on separate uniform-step-size defects in other propositions.

**Failed proof step.** Before (106), PDF page 37, the proof invokes bounded support and Lemma 19 to obtain a Chebyshev constant independent of n. In this bounded-data witness every fixed-n candidate support actually is bounded, as the radius recursion proves. Those compacts grow with n. Assumption 2 and Lemma 19 give only compact-dependent constants. Indeed, changing variables gives

```
integral_0^1 phi(t)^2 dt = 4410/2431,
Var(F(theta,X)) = f(theta)^2 [(4410/2431) w(x) - 1],
```

which diverges along the bad population paths. The proof has no n-uniform validation variance control. Fixed-n compactness cannot justify (106)–(107) with the constant quantified in Theorem 30.

**Reason for rejection.** Theorem 5/30 is the central step that turns the best true-risk value among random restarts into an implementable choice using finite validation data. That step is false under the paper's assumptions, and the computational global-convergence proof in Corollary 6/31 depends on it. A repair needs a global or uniform candidate-loss moment restriction, projection/stopping/truncation of candidates, or a validation procedure/budget adapted to their growing loss distributions. These changes restrict the permitted models or change the claimed algorithm and its rate. An arbitrary n-dependent Chebyshev constant loses the advertised validation estimate. This is a false central guarantee, not a request for extra experiments or a scalar correction. Local convergence and the oracle best-true-risk restart argument are not refuted. This report does not separately claim that this fixture disproves Corollary 31 at its particular prescribed parameter scaling; its stated proof is unsupported once the required selection theorem fails.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the passage from the oracle minimum over independent runs to the finite empirical selector, noticed that a local compact-moment assumption was used as a uniform validation bound for unrestricted SGD candidates. Constructed a bad valley whose loss concentrates on increasingly rare bounded-data events.

**Verification method.** Rechecked Assumptions 1–2, the tube definition, Theorem 5/30, Lemma 19 and (101)–(107) against the original PDF and inspected the rendered equation pages. Proved the expectation, manifold, gradient, support-miss, finite-M approximation and quantifier claims above. Exact rational controls verify two normalized polynomial bumps and eight parameter-order contradiction skeletons; 18 population-gradient diagnostics corroborate the path inequalities and empirical ordering. A second reviewer independently reread the original assumptions/proof and rendered pages 35–38, checked polynomial moments, 12 recurrence fixtures, 12 holdout probabilities and four arbitrary-constant parameter orders, and confirmed the missing n-uniform moment control. These numerical diagnostics support the analytic construction; they are not presented as finite-batch simulations at the potentially enormous violating parameters. No historical experimental/code failure is alleged in this theoretical paper.

**Confidence: High.** The fixed model satisfies every stated assumption with bounded data, nonnegative C3 losses and a globally smooth risk. The strict selector ordering and finite-M approximation refute the theorem's exact probability bound. Independent original-PDF and algebraic/probability checks agree. Confidence concerns this selection theorem and the dependency of the complexity proof, not a stronger claim that local SGD convergence is impossible.

Finally choose finite M large enough for the finite-path approximation and to make its two M-dependent terms contribute less than (1-q)/4 to the bracket.

The claimed bracket is then at most qstar, so the claimed upper bound is less than 1/8. The actual failure probability exceeds 1-1/16-.02>.9. This contradicts Theorem 30 with one fixed admissible model, for every possible choice of its constants. In particular, r is fixed before n; the argument does not rely on separate uniform-step-size defects in other propositions.

Failed proof step. Before (106), PDF page 37, the proof invokes bounded support and Lemma 19 to obtain a Chebyshev constant independent of n. In this bounded-data witness every fixed-n candidate support actually is bounded, as the radius recursion proves. Those compacts grow with n. Assumption 2 and Lemma 19 give only compact-dependent constants. Indeed, changing variables gives

integral_0^1 phi(t)^2 dt = 4410/2431,
Var(F(theta,X)) = f(theta)^2 [(4410/2431) w(x) - 1],

which diverges along the bad population paths. The proof has no n-uniform validation variance control. Fixed-n compactness cannot justify (106)–(107) with the constant quantified in Theorem 30.

Reason for rejection. Theorem 5/30 is the central step that turns the best true-risk value among random restarts into an implementable choice using finite validation data. That step is false under the paper's assumptions, and the computational global-convergence proof in Corollary 6/31 depends on it. A repair needs a global or uniform candidate-loss moment restriction, projection/stopping/truncation of candidates, or a validation procedure/budget adapted to their growing loss distributions. These changes restrict the permitted models or change the claimed algorithm and its rate. An arbitrary n-dependent Chebyshev constant loses the advertised validation estimate. This is a false central guarantee, not a request for extra experiments or a scalar correction. Local convergence and the oracle best-true-risk restart argument are not refuted. This report does not separately claim that this fixture disproves Corollary 31 at its particular prescribed parameter scaling; its stated proof is unsupported once the required selection theorem fails.

Discovery method. While tracing the passage from the oracle minimum over independent runs to the finite empirical selector, noticed that a local compact-moment assumption was used as a uniform validation bound for unrestricted SGD candidates. Constructed a bad valley whose loss concentrates on increasingly rare bounded-data events.

Verification method. Rechecked Assumptions 1–2, the tube definition, Theorem 5/30, Lemma 19 and (101)–(107) against the original PDF and inspected the rendered equation pages. Proved the expectation, manifold, gradient, support-miss, finite-M approximation and quantifier claims above. Exact rational controls verify two normalized polynomial bumps and eight parameter-order contradiction skeletons; 18 population-gradient diagnostics corroborate the path inequalities and empirical ordering. A second reviewer independently reread the original assumptions/proof and rendered pages 35–38, checked polynomial moments, 12 recurrence fixtures, 12 holdout probabilities and four arbitrary-constant parameter orders, and confirmed the missing n-uniform moment control. These numerical diagnostics support the analytic construction; they are not presented as finite-batch simulations at the potentially enormous violating parameters. No historical experimental/code failure is alleged in this theoretical paper.

The strict selector ordering and finite-M approximation refute the theorem's exact probability bound. Independent original-PDF and algebraic/probability checks agree. Confidence concerns this selection theorem and the dependency of the complexity proof, not a stronger claim that local SGD convergence is impossible.

findings.title: The stated one-order conditions do not identify a DAG
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-664-I01 — The stated one-order conditions do not identify a DAG
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 7, Theorem 2(A); page 8, Theorem 4(A); page 9, Algorithm 1; pages 12–13, Assumption 7(A), Theorem 8 and Corollary 10; Appendix A page 27 and Appendix C page 30.

**Claim.** An additive noise model with independent centered errors and causal minimality has a uniquely identifiable DAG if, for one true topological ordering \(\pi\), every node \(j=\pi_m\) and its descendant \(k\) satisfy

\[
\sigma_j^2<\sigma_k^2+
\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\mathbb E[X_k\mid X_{\mathrm{Pa}(k)}]\mid X_{\pi_1},\ldots,X_{\pi_{m-1}}\right).
\]

The forward algorithm greedily chooses the smallest conditional variance and is claimed consistent under the corresponding positive-margin condition. Faithfulness and a unique topological ordering are not premises of these statements.

**Error and exact evidence.** Let independent centered Gaussian variables have variances

\[
A\sim N(0,2),\quad B\sim N(0,1),\quad e\sim N(0,1/4),\qquad
C=\tfrac12 A+\tfrac32 B+e.
\]

The DAG \(G\) has exactly \(A\to C\leftarrow B\), with true order \((A,B,C)\). The common covariance in coordinates \((A,B,C)\) is

\[
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\0&1&3/2\\1&3/2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det\Sigma=1/2>0.
\]

All forward comparisons in Theorem 2(A) are strict:

| Node and descendant | Required left side | Required right side |
|---|---:|---:|
| \(A,C\), empty prefix | \(2\) | \(\operatorname{Var}(C)=3\) |
| \(B,C\), prefix \(A\) | \(1\) | \(\operatorname{Var}(C\mid A)=5/2\) |

Now the *same Gaussian joint distribution* has the second additive-noise representation

\[
B=z_B,\quad C=\tfrac32 B+z_C,\quad
A=-2B+\tfrac43 C+z_A,
\]

where the independent centered Gaussian errors have variances
\(\operatorname{Var}(z_B)=1\), \(\operatorname{Var}(z_C)=3/4\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(z_A)=2/3\). For example,
\(z_C=C-3B/2\) and \(z_A=A+2B-4C/3\); direct multiplication gives their joint error covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(1,3/4,2/3)\) in error order \((z_B,z_C,z_A)\). Gaussianity then gives independence, not just uncorrelatedness.

This second DAG \(G'\) has three edges \(B\to C\), \(B\to A\), \(C\to A\), and order \((B,C,A)\). It too satisfies every forward comparison:

| Node and descendant | Required left side | Required right side |
|---|---:|---:|
| \(B,C\), empty prefix | \(1\) | \(3\) |
| \(B,A\), empty prefix | \(1\) | \(2\) |
| \(C,A\), prefix \(B\) | \(3/4\) | \(\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B)=2\) |

Both models have Borel measurable linear functions, strictly positive finite noise variances, observed variables only and causal minimality. To check the latter under the paper's full definition, the required parent–child conditional covariances for \(G\) are \(\operatorname{Cov}(A,C\mid B)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(B,C\mid A)=3/2\). For \(G'\) they are \(\operatorname{Cov}(B,C)=3/2\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(B,A\mid C)=-1/2\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(C,A\mid B)=1\). All are nonzero. The extra marginal independence \(A\perp B\) makes \(G'\) unfaithful, which is explicitly allowed by the paper; it does not violate causal minimality.

Thus two distinct DAGs *inside the claimed class* generate exactly the same observational distribution. This directly contradicts identifiability, regardless of sample size, estimation accuracy or implementation.

The inconsistency consequence can also be seen without simulation. Algorithm 1 first selects \(B\), since marginal variances are \(1,2,3\). Given \(B\), it selects \(C\), since
\(\operatorname{Var}(C\mid B)=3/4<2=\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B)\). It returns \((B,C,A)\), whereas the only valid topological orders of \(G\) are \((A,B,C)\) and \((B,A,C)\). All these selection gaps are strict, so consistent covariance estimates make its probability of a valid order for \(G\) tend to zero, contrary to Theorem 8's bound tending to one.

This witness also meets the stated finite-sample premises: Assumption 7(A) holds with \(\tau_F=1/4\); the fixed positive definite covariance admits Assumption 5 (e.g. \(\rho_{\min}=1/72\), \(\rho_{\max}=6\)); and its finitely many eligible edge partial correlations are nonzero and bounded below one, so Assumption 6 holds with sufficiently small \(\kappa(n)=c/\sqrt{\log n}\). Consequently the original forward consistency claim in Corollary 10 is affected as well.

**The backward branch fails for the same reason, even with faithfulness.** A second certificate shows this is not repaired simply by imposing faithfulness or choosing the sparsest representation. Take independent Gaussian errors and

\[
A\sim N(0,2),\quad B=2A+e_B,\quad C=\tfrac12 A+e_C,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(e_B)=1,\quad\operatorname{Var}(e_C)=1/4.
\]

This fork \(A\to B,A\to C\), with order \((A,B,C)\), satisfies Theorem 2(B): \(\sigma_B^2=1>\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B)=2/9\) and \(\sigma_C^2=1/4>\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B,C)=2/11\). The same joint Gaussian distribution has the chain representation

\[
C\sim N(0,3/4),\quad A=\tfrac43 C+z_A,\quad B=2A+e_B,
\qquad\operatorname{Var}(z_A)=2/3,
\]

with independent Gaussian errors. This chain \(C\to A\to B\), with order \((C,A,B)\), also satisfies Theorem 2(B): \(2/3>\operatorname{Var}(C\mid A)=1/4\), \(1>\operatorname{Var}(A\mid B,C)=2/11\), and \(1>\operatorname{Var}(C\mid A,B)=1/4\). Both covariance matrices equal

\[
\begin{pmatrix}2&4&1\\4&9&2\\1&2&3/4\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Both DAGs have two edges and are faithful: their only nontrivial conditional independence is \(B\perp C\mid A\). Exact enumeration of all three pairs with empty or singleton conditioning sets verifies this. Algorithm 2 removes \(B\) first (conditional variance \(1\), versus \(1/4\) for \(C\) and \(2/11\) for \(A\)); it then removes \(A\), since \(\operatorname{Var}(A\mid C)=2/3>1/4\). Its returned order \((C,A,B)\) is invalid for the original fork. This second certificate concerns Theorem 2(B); the first certificate supplies the additional literal Theorem 4(A)/Assumption 7(A) consistency contradiction. They are one underlying error: conditions along one chosen order do not protect other greedy prefixes/suffixes.

**Where the proof fails.** Appendix A begins, “Without loss of generality, assume that the true ordering … is unique.” This is not a harmless relabeling: the original collider DAG above has two valid orders, and the fork has two valid sink-elimination choices. Its forward Step (1) then replaces “\(k\in\mathrm{De}(\pi_1)\)” by every \(k\ne\pi_1\), concluding \(\operatorname{Var}(A)<\operatorname{Var}(B)\), which is false in the first certificate and is not implied by Theorem 2(A). Choosing another source first is not automatically safe, because the condition was checked along the original ordering's prefixes: after choosing \(B\), it does not impose the needed \(2<3/4\) comparison between \(A\) and \(C\). The backward proof makes the analogous unsupported extension from ancestors to all other nodes. Appendices B–C repeat the uniqueness assumption. The original PDF pages were checked; no global theorem premise restricting to uniquely ordered DAGs or requiring the condition for every valid ancestral prefix resolves this.

**Reason for rejection.** The title, abstract and principal contribution are a new identifiable class with heterogeneous noise variances and a consistent uncertainty-scoring algorithm without faithfulness. The exact same-law pair disproves that class's central identification theorem and its forward recovery guarantee. Fixing an index, a constant or a proof estimate cannot distinguish identical distributions. A repair must substantively restrict the model class—for example, replace the stated one-order descendant condition by conditions covering all relevant ancestral prefixes, or actually require a unique topological ordering (excluding ordinary multi-root DAGs such as this collider). Those are additional structural assumptions, not straightforward corrections preserving the advertised class. The equal-noise special case or other restricted algorithms may remain valid; they do not establish the paper's central heterogeneous-noise claim as written. This would change an accept recommendation to reject.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the induction, checked why an arbitrary greedy root choice should preserve a condition expressed using one fixed ordering's prefixes. The Appendix's asserted uniqueness prompted a two-root collider construction.

**Verification method.** Read all 34 original PDF pages, including complete Appendices A–D. Rechecked rendered pages 7, 8, 12, 27–30. An independent exact-rational control constructs both same-law pairs, verifies equal covariance matrices and diagonal error covariance, enumerates every stated forward/margin and backward comparison, checks eligible causal-minimality conditioning sets and the second pair's faithfulness, and executes both population greedy rules. Twelve independent Gaussian sample controls at \(n=1000,10000,100000\) all returned the same incorrect forward order for \(G\). The exact algebra, rather than these samples, proves the claim false. These are targeted checks of the printed algorithms; no historical figure rerun is claimed.

**Confidence: High.** The two Gaussian covariance matrices agree exactly over rational arithmetic, every relevant assumption is explicitly checked, and the failure is already present with population conditional variances. The uniqueness assertion in the appendices is explicitly addressed rather than ignored.

**Independent verification:** A second reviewer rechecked the original assumptions and rendered Theorem2/proof pages, independently verified the exact same-law certificates, all relevant comparisons and greedy failures, and assessed their centrality.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-718-I01
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 6, PDF pages 12–13, Algorithm 2 and its dual-variable exchange rule; Appendix D, PDF pages 28–35, updates (82)–(86), the fixed saddle-point argument (108)–(116), and the convergence conclusion after (130), including (133). The dynamic convergence result is also advertised in the abstract, introduction and conclusion, PDF pages 1–2 and 19.

**Claim.** The dynamic extension D-GADMM converges to the optimal consensus solution under the same closed, proper, convex local objectives and saddle-point assumptions used for static GADMM. Interior workers and their head/tail assignments may change with the chain topology, while the first and last workers stay fixed. Topology may refresh every iteration. Section 6 expressly permits predefined logical-chain sequences on an unchanged physical graph. At a change, each physical worker retains its outgoing right dual and sends it to its new right neighbor, which replaces its incoming left-dual copy. Algorithm 2 initializes every primal and dual variable at zero.

**Error and evidence.** Under those rules, D-GADMM can converge to a non-consensus two-cycle even for four scalar strongly convex quadratic losses. Set

```
N = 4, dimension = 1, rho = 1, tau = 1,
f_i(x) = (x-b_i)^2/2,  b = (0,1,-1,0).
```

Alternate chains P=(1,2,3,4) and Q=(1,3,2,4), starting with P. Every chain is connected and includes each worker once; workers 1 and 4 remain the endpoints. The head sets are respectively {1,3} and {1,2}. The sequence can be agreed in advance on a complete fixed physical network, so it satisfies the explicit Section 6 option without requiring a particular chain-construction heuristic. The losses are finite, smooth, strongly convex, closed and proper. Each subproblem has a unique exact minimizer, rho is positive, and saddle points exist. The unique consensus optimum is x*=0, with total objective 1.

Write the state in physical-worker order as

```
z = (x1,x2,x3,x4; lambda1,lambda2,lambda3),
```

where lambda_i is worker i's retained outgoing dual. For a current path with left and right neighbors l,r, (82)–(86) give

```
x_i+ = (b_i + lambda_l - lambda_i + x_l_used + x_r_used)/(1+degree_i),
lambda_i+ = lambda_i + x_i+ - x_r+,  i != 4.
```

Missing boundary terms are zero. Heads use old tail values and tails use the new head values. The incoming copy is the outgoing dual of the new left neighbor. The four scalar minimizers for P are

```
x1+ = (-lambda1 + x2)/2,
x3+ = (-1 + lambda2 - lambda3 + x2 + x4)/3,
x2+ = (1 + lambda1 - lambda2 + x1+ + x3+)/3,
x4+ = (lambda3 + x3+)/2.
```

For Q they are

```
x1+ = (-lambda1 + x3)/2,
x2+ = (1 + lambda3 - lambda2 + x3 + x4)/3,
x3+ = (-1 + lambda1 - lambda3 + x1+ + x2+)/3,
x4+ = (lambda2 + x2+)/2.
```

The intended right-neighbor quadratic is used for worker 1, correcting the undefined left-neighbor subscript in printed (83); that local typo is not the cause of the failure.

Exact rational substitution gives

```
e = (9,-1,-25,23; 17,23,-47)/89,
o = (-9,25,1,-23; -17,47,-23)/89,
P(e) = o,  Q(o) = e.
```

This cycle attracts the prescribed zero initialization. Let T be the linear part of the two-step affine map Q composed with P. Computing its seven columns by applying the displayed updates to the seven coordinate basis vectors gives the exact induced infinity norm

```
||T||_infinity = 13/18 < 1.
```

Consequently,

```
||z_(2m)-e||_infinity <= (13/18)^m * 47/89,
z_(2m+1) -> o.
```

Every entry of the rational matrix T, the exact substitutions and the norm calculation are saved in the reproducible evidence below. This is a contraction proof for the all-zero start, rather than merely an example initialized on the cycle.

The current-path primal residuals tend to

```
P phase: (-34,24,24)/89,
Q phase: (34,-24,-24)/89,
```

and therefore do not tend to zero. At both phases the sum of the local objectives tends to 6403/7921, rather than the consensus optimum 1. Its absolute optimality gap tends to 1518/7921. Thus both the primal-residual conclusion following (130) and the objective conclusion (133) fail under the stated assumptions.

**Why the proof fails.** At the consensus optimum, the unique outgoing duals in physical-worker order are (0,1,0) for P and (0,0,-1) for Q. Retaining a worker's outgoing edge dual while changing its neighbor does not retain its nodal dual balance. A single fixed saddle-point dual cannot be used as in (108)–(116) for both topologies. The tail groups and weights in the proposed Lyapunov function (125) also change, so differences with a fixed current graph do not telescope into (126)–(130) across graph changes. Moreover, a vanishing combined term r±delta after (130) would not by itself show its two components vanish separately. These steps concern the same failed dynamic convergence argument and are counted as one issue.

**Reason for rejection.** D-GADMM and its convergence under changing networks are an explicitly named central contribution. The claimed guarantee is false for its stated algorithm even with exact subproblem solutions, smooth strongly convex losses, connected chains and the required zero start. A boundary-symbol or proof-sign correction cannot remove the attracting cycle. Restricting to a fixed chain drops the advertised extension. Preserving nodal dual balance through a different dual transport rule, or using node-based dual variables, changes the algorithm and requires a corresponding convergence argument. The paper as written therefore lacks a valid dynamic algorithm with its advertised guarantee, which warrants rejection. The static GADMM convergence result in Theorem 2 is not refuted.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Appendix D's Lyapunov telescoping argument, noticed that the same optimal dual was used while each physical worker's outgoing edge and head/tail group could change. Tested the smallest nontrivial alternating interior permutation.

**Verification method.** Read the entire paper and all four appendices; rechecked the original rendered algorithm, dual exchange description, expanded updates and final proof pages. findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page18, AppendixB, proof of Lemma6, the last inequality of Eq.(15). The sign flip is defined on PDF17. The affected dependency runs through Eqs.(16)–(18), Lemma6 (PDF17–19), Lemma3 (PDF12/14–15), and the main exact-recovery Theorem1 (PDF8, Eqs.(10)–(12)).

**Claim.** For contractive dynamics

\[
x_t=\nabla f(A_\star x_{t-1}+B_\star u_{t-1}),
\]

the paper establishes a nearly dimension-linear observation horizon for its convex estimator to recover the parameters exactly. The assumptions include strong convexity/smoothness of \(f\), the global approximation

\[
\left\|\frac{\nabla f(x+y)-\nabla f(x-y)}2-F(x)y\right\|
\le\varepsilon\|y\|,
\tag{7}
\]

independent centered isotropic symmetric input coordinates with a bounded directional Orlicz norm, column coherence, contraction, and a positive threshold \(\theta\) from Eq.(10). Lemma6 supplies the uniform small-ball probability at that threshold. Its proof replaces a difference caused by flipping one input coordinate with a linear feature involving all the other coordinates, while charging only a single-column approximation error.

**Error and evidence.** By definition, \(u^{-i}\) flips only coordinate \(i\). Thus

\[
\frac{u-u^{-i}}2=u_i e_i,
\qquad
\frac{u+u^{-i}}2=u_{\setminus i}.
\]

The correct center and direction for applying Eq.(7) to the gradient difference in Eq.(15) are \(a+B_\star u_{\setminus i}\) and \(B_\star e_i u_i\). The printed inequality instead uses \(F(a)B_\star u_{\setminus i}\) as the signal. The following exact nonlinear instance demonstrates that the probability inequality is false under the paper's assumptions.

Take \(n=1,p=9\), \(A_\star=1/10\), \(B_\star=(1,\ldots,1)\), \(\beta=10\), and independent Rademacher input coordinates. Define

\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2/2,&x\le0,\\51x^2/100,&x\ge0,\end{cases}
\quad
g(x):=f'(x)=\frac{101}{100}x+\frac1{100}|x|.
\]

This is the paper's admissible leaky activation: \(f\) is differentiable, \(1\)-strongly convex and \(51/50\)-smooth, and \(g(0)=0\). Choose

\[
F(a)=\frac{101}{100}+\frac1{100}\operatorname{sgn}(a),
\qquad\varepsilon=\frac1{100}.
\]

For every center \(x\) and direction \(y\), the error in Eq.(7) has magnitude at most \((|y|-|x|)_+/100\le |y|/100\). Contraction is \((51/50)(1/10)=51/500<1\). Column coherence is exactly1, and \(B_{\star\setminus i}B_{\star\setminus i}^{\mathsf T}=8\) for every \(i\).

The input meets every input condition with \(\alpha=2,K=2,\eta=3\). In particular, for every unit \(h\), the Rademacher moment generating bound and an independent standard Gaussian \(Z\) give

\[
\mathbb E e^{\langle h,u\rangle^2/4}
=\mathbb E_Z\mathbb E_u e^{Z\langle h,u\rangle/\sqrt2}
\le\mathbb E_Ze^{Z^2/4}=\sqrt2<2,
\]

and \(\mathbb E\langle h,u\rangle^4\le3\). The literal Eq.(10) threshold is

\[
\theta=\frac35\frac{99}{100}\sqrt8
-\frac1{50}\sqrt{\log30}
\approx1.643201.
\]

It satisfies \(51/50<\theta<199/100\). These strict inequalities also follow without numerical rounding from \(14/5<\sqrt8<3\) and \(\sqrt{\log30}<2\).

Let the unit vector \(w=(1,0,\ldots,0)\) select only the state coordinate. For any restarted state, write \(a=A_\star x^{(\ell)}_{t-1}\). The penultimate probability in Eq.(15) involves

\[
\frac12|g(a+B_\star u)-g(a+B_\star u^{-i})|
\le\frac{51}{50}|u_i|=\frac{51}{50}<\theta.
\]

Its event therefore has probability0, uniformly in \(a\). The last probability in that equation involves instead

\[
\left|F(a)\sum_{j\ne i}u_j\right|-\frac1{100}\ge\theta.
\]

Since \(F(a)\ge1\), this event holds exactly when the sum of the eight remaining signs is nonzero: every nonzero such sum has magnitude at least2. Its probability is

\[
1-\frac{\binom84}{2^8}=\frac{93}{128}.
\]

Including Eq.(15)'s factor \(1/2\), its last inequality asserts

\[
0\ge\frac{93}{256},
\]

which is false. This is a counterexample to an indispensable proof inequality. It does not demonstrate that Lemma6 or Theorem1 themselves are false.

**Reason for rejection.** The nonlinear small-ball argument is the paper's only justification for the excitation bound in Lemma3 and hence the high-probability covariance and exact-recovery guarantee in its sole main statistical theorem. The false step imports the spectral energy of the unflipped complement into an observation difference containing only one input column. The subsequent correct linear Paley–Zygmund calculation cannot justify that replacement.

A sign or flip-definition correction does not establish the printed guarantee. Flipping the complement gives center \(a+B_\star e_i u_i\) and direction \(B_\star u_{\setminus i}\), so Eq.(7) charges \(\varepsilon\|B_\star u_{\setminus i}\|\). Flipping all coordinates similarly charges \(\varepsilon\|B_\star u\|\). These have Frobenius scale, rather than the maximum-column scale used in Eq.(10). For \(B_\star\) comprising \(k\) copies of \(I_n\), coherence is1 and column norm is1, while \(\|B_\star\|_F=\sqrt{kn}\). Such a replacement imposes a new dimension-dependent restriction and does not cover the stated positive-\(\theta\) class.

Establishing the advertised nonlinear, non-Gaussian recovery result requires a new small-ball argument or a materially narrower theorem. The convex estimator, direct quadratic/special-case arguments, and reported numerical convergence do not supply the missing general guarantee. Because that guarantee is a central claimed advance beyond earlier Gaussian-input theory, the demonstrated failure of its only supplied proof justifies rejection of the paper as written. A future proof could establish the theorem; this report makes no contrary claim and no claim of historical empirical failure.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma6 back to the central-difference assumption, the direction selected by the coordinate flip disagreed with the complementary-column feature used in Eq.(15).

**Verification method.** Read all20pages and both appendices, then rechecked the original full rendered17–19 and assumption/theorem pages. Derived the exact nonlinear instance and verified every relevant assumption. Fraction enumeration covered all512 sign vectors and9 coordinate choices at seven rational centers; the global Lipschitz argument covers every center. Independent root QA used five fresh rational centers,23040 sign/coordinate pairs and1025 central-difference checks, with an independent analytic premise/threshold derivation. Both helpers exited0 with substantive assertions passing. The initially simpler quadratic diagnostic gives the same false inequality.

**Confidence.** High. The false inequality is exact, all relevant model/input assumptions are verified, and the dependency to the main theorem is explicit. Confidence is in the demonstrated proof failure and the resulting unsupported general guarantee, rather than in a claim that the theorem's conclusion is false.

 The authored IJulia notebook was inspected and its model/objective/gradient executed in eight small cases under documented Julia0.6 compatibility changes. No exact Julia1.1.1 full100trial historical regeneration, original seeds or final figure commit was recovered. These limits are separate from the exact proof finding.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2020__accepted__v21-19-802-I01
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem2, PDF4; Lemma3, PDF6; AppendixA.2, Eq16 and its Gaussian-factor exclusion, PDF17; AppendixA.3, Eq19→Eq20, PDF18. The real-valued Gaussian-tail extension is highlighted in the introduction, PDF3, and the proof outline, PDF6.

**Claim.** Theorem2 states identifiability up to common translation from the complete observed-process law, for two real stationary hidden Markov chains whose transition kernels have Lebesgue densities and unique stationary distributions, whose marginals belong to a common M_rho with rho<3, and whose two-point transforms satisfyH1. Its additional exclusion says that if a hidden chain is Gaussian it is not iid. The noise distributions are arbitrary independent iid additive laws. Lemma3 asserts that adding independent positive-variance iid Gaussian noise to a stationary real Markov chain with a transition density can leave a Markov process only when the original chain is iid.

**Error and evidence.** The following exact continuous-state construction disproves both assertions. It uses two centered nondegenerate Gaussian noise distributions, so the counterexample does not rely on deterministic noise. Every relevant assumption, includingH1 for all complex arguments and the full Markov property for all sequence lengths, is checked below.

Set S=[0,1] union [2,3], Z=integral_S exp(x²/2)dx, and mu(dx)=Z^(-1)exp(x²/2)1_S(x)dx. Every x in S has the unique representation x=U+V with U in{0,2},V in[0,1] (irrelevant endpoints may be assigned arbitrarily). Write p=mu([2,3]), m=E_mu V, f(x)=1{U=2}−p and g(x)=V−m. They are bounded, nonconstant, have mu mean0, and |f|,|g|<=1. Let alpha=1/2 and

    K(x,dx′)=mu(dx′)[1+alpha*f(x)*g(x′)]  (x in S).

For x outside S define K(x,.)=mu. This is a Borel transition density on R and mu is stationary: integrating over x kills f, and integrating over x′ kills g. The density ratio to mu is in[1/2,3/2]. Hence the stationary distribution is unique by a uniform Doeblin minorization. The stationary chain is not iid, since

    E[f(X_i)g(X_(i+1))]=alpha E_mu[f²] E_mu[g²]>0.

Let eta_i be independent N(0,1), independent of the entire chain, and Y_i=X_i+eta_i. Its one-point density is h=mu*phi. In the one-point posterior, for every real y,

    mu(dx)*phi(y−x) ∝ 1_S(x)*exp(y*x)dx
      = exp(y*U) * exp(y*V) * (counting measure on{0,2}) * dV.

Thus U and V are independent conditional on this single noisy observation. If F(y)=E[f(X)|X+eta=y] and G(y)=E[g(X)|X+eta=y], then E[fg|y]=F(y)G(y). More explicitly,

    F(y)=exp(2y)/(1+exp(2y))−p,
    G(y)= [integral_0^1 v exp(yv)dv]/[integral_0^1 exp(yv)dv]−m.

Both functions are bounded and strictly increasing, so nonconstant. Expanding the joint density of any finite sequence gives

    p_Y(y_1,...,y_n)
      = product_i h(y_i) * product_(i=1)^(n−1)[1+alpha F(y_i)G(y_(i+1))].

To see this for all n, expand the n−1 factors in the X-chain density. Each X_i appears with at most one f and one g. Conditional on the y_i under the product of one-point posteriors, the f and g factor at each site, including adjacent selected factors. Consequently every term equals the corresponding term in the displayed product. This proves the complete process is Markov, not just that its triples satisfy conditional independence. Its transition density is

    L(y,dy′)=h(y′)[1+alpha F(y)G(y′)]dy′.

This has ratio in[1/2,3/2] to h; h is its unique stationary distribution. Moreover E_h F=E_h G=0 and its lag-one F/G moment is alpha E_h F² E_h G²>0. Hence Y is not iid. This already disproves Lemma3, including its transition-density and positive Gaussian-variance premises.

#### Entire-transform condition H1, exactly

Define A(z)=integral_0^1 exp(v²/2+zv)dv and B(z)=exp(2+2z)A(z+2). Then

    M(z)=E_mu exp(zX)=[A(z)+B(z)]/Z,
    M_f(z)=E_mu[f(X)exp(zX)]=[−p A(z)+(1−p)B(z)]/Z.

A(z) has no zeros when Re(z)>=0 or Re(z)<=−1. Indeed, with z=s+it, the positive weight w(v)=exp(v²/2+s v) is strictly monotone on(0,1) in these two cases. For t=0 the integral is positive. For t!=0, integration by parts and strict triangle inequality give

    |integral_0^1 w′(v) exp(itv)dv| < integral_0^1 |w′(v)|dv
      = |w(1)−w(0)| <= |w(1)exp(it)−w(0)|.

The integration-by-parts identity it*A(s+it)=w(1)exp(it)−w(0)−integral w′exp(itv) prevents A from vanishing. Strictness follows because w′ has constant sign and is nonzero on an interval, while exp(itv) cannot have constant phase there for t!=0. Thus zeros of A are confined to −1<Re(z)<0; zeros of A(z+2) to −3<Re(z)<−2. They never coincide. It follows that M and M_f have no common zero, since their two linear combinations of A,B have determinant1.

The two-point transform is

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 25, Section 4.1, Theorem 22, including the backward recurrence for `A_t` and the asserted efficiency bounds for the value and for `β_t`; PDF page 62, its proof's final claimed algebraic simplification. The dependent optimality discussion is Section 4.2 on PDF pages 25–26. Restricted-q efficiency is an advertised contribution in Figure 3 on PDF page 2 and the introduction on PDF page 3.

**Claim.** For continuously differentiable parametric q-models with compact parameter spaces and interior true parameters, Theorem 22 asserts

```
A_t = C_t^(-1) + C_t^(-1) B_t A_(t+1) B_t' C_t^(-1),
A_T = C_T^(-1),
EffBd(M_1q) = Var(v_0) + B_(-1) A_0 B_(-1)'.
```

It also states that `A_t` is the efficiency bound for estimating `β_t`, and gives the analogous result for `M_2q`. Here `C_t` is the variance-weighted second moment of the derivative of `q_t`, and `B_t` is the variance-weighted cross moment of the derivatives of `q_t` and `v_(t+1)`, exactly as defined on page 25. Section 4.2 uses this analysis to discuss efficient GMM and efficient direct-method estimation.

**Error and evidence.** A regular estimator has asymptotic variance strictly below this claimed lower bound in the following admissible model.

Take two reward periods, indexed `t=0,1` as in the paper's definition (`T=1`), with one action at each time. Both policies select that action, so every importance ratio is one. Let

```
x = s_0 ~ Bernoulli(p),
z = s_1 | x ~ Bernoulli(u_x),
r_0 | x ~ Bernoulli(a_x),      a_x = b_0 - b_1(1+u_x),
r_1 | z ~ Bernoulli(b_1(1+z)).
```

Use the paper's factorization: the first reward and transition are conditionally independent given `x`; the second reward depends only on `z`. The initial law, both transition probabilities, and both q-parameters are unknown. Choose

```
(b_0,b_1,u_0,u_1,p) = (3/4,1/4,1/4,3/4,1/2).
```

Then `a_0=7/16`, `a_1=5/16`, and the terminal reward means are `1/4` and `1/2`. All 16 possible `(x,z,r_0,r_1)` trajectories have positive probability. Rewards are bounded in `[0,1]`, and overlap holds with constants one. The q-functions are exactly

```
q_0(x;b_0) = b_0,
q_1(z;b_1) = b_1(1+z),
```

because `E[r_0+q_1(z)|x]=b_0`. They are differentiable, with compact parameter boxes, for example `b_0∈[.7,.8]`, `b_1∈[.2,.3]`, containing the truth in their interiors. There is a regular open neighborhood of the stated transition and initial probabilities. This is an MDP satisfying the restricted q-model; the corresponding history-based q-model is also satisfied. Its value is `ρ=b_0`, `v_0=b_0`, and `B_(-1)=1`.

Write `g_z=1+z`, `m_x=1+u_x`, `e_0=r_0+b_1g_z-b_0`, and `e_1=r_1-b_1g_z`. Their conditional variances are

```
V_x = Var(e_0|x) = a_x(1-a_x)+b_1^2 u_x(1-u_x),
sigma_1(z)^2 = Var(e_1|z).
```

At the chosen law, `V_0=33/128`, `V_1=29/128`. Define

```
C = E[1/V_x]                  = 3968/957,
B = E[m_x/V_x]                = 6016/957,
D = E[m_x^2/V_x]              = 9368/957,
C_1 = E[g_z^2/sigma_1(z)^2]   = 32/3.
```

Theorem 22 gives

```
A_0_printed = 1/C + B^2/(C^2 C_1)
            = 56175/123008 ≈ 0.4566776144641.
```

Now consider the jointly estimated conditional-moment instruments

```
psi_0 = e_0/V_x,
psi_1 = -m_x e_0/V_x + g_z e_1/sigma_1(z)^2.
```

Both have expectation zero. Conditional mean-zero residuals and the stipulated factorization give, by direct calculation,

```
Cov(psi) = J = [[ C, -B ],
                [-B, D+C_1 ]],
E[d psi / d(b_0,b_1)] = -J.
```

These estimating functions yield a regular estimator with covariance `J^(-1)`. Attainability does not require knowledge of the nuisance law: start from the root-n pilot

```
b_1_pilot = sum(g_z r_1)/sum(g_z^2),
b_0_pilot = mean(r_0+b_1_pilot g_z).
```

Estimate the transition and conditional-variance weights by finite-cell empirical frequencies and variances, then take the one-step update `b_pilot + J_hat^(-1) mean(psi(b_pilot))`. All cells have positive probability and all variances are positive, so these are smooth regular estimators in a neighborhood of the law. Estimating the weights contributes no first-order drift: derivatives of the weights multiply residuals whose conditional means are zero. Consequently the value estimator has asymptotic variance

```
(J^(-1))_00 = (D+C_1)/(C(D+C_1)-B^2)
             = 7341/16256 ≈ 0.4515871062992
             < 56175/123008.
```

Thus an explicit regular estimator beats the paper's claimed efficiency lower bound under its own assumptions.

A separate exact likelihood calculation checks all nuisance directions. Put `U=(r_0-a_x)/(a_x(1-a_x))`, `W=(r_1-b_1g_z)/(b_1g_z(1-b_1g_z))`, and `Z=(z-u_x)/(u_x(1-u_x))`. The score for the five unknown parameters is

```
S = (U, -m_x U+g_z W,
     1{x=0}(Z-b_1 U), 1{x=1}(Z-b_1 U),
     (x-p)/(p(1-p))).
```

Exact summation over the 16 atoms gives a nonsingular full Fisher matrix whose inverse's `(0,0)` entry is `7341/16256`. The influence function from the estimating functions has mean zero, variance `7341/16256`, and exact score cross-moments `(1,0,0,0,0)`. Both transition parameters and the initial-state nuisance are therefore accounted for. This is not an argument based only on a smaller model with known nuisances, or on nonregular superefficiency.

The failed algebra is visible in the proof on page 62. The joint information contains the `D` term. Eliminating the first parameter gives the Schur complement `C_1+D-B^2/C`, rather than `C_1`. Since `m_x` varies, `D-B^2/C>0`: earlier conditional moments provide information about the later q-parameter that a change in the earlier intercept cannot absorb. Orthogonality of the residual innovations does not remove that information. The same error makes the printed terminal-parameter bound `A_1=1/C_1` too large.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper explicitly presents restricted-q efficiency limits as a formal contribution, illustrates these models in Figure 3, and dedicates Sections 4.1–4.2 to deriving the bounds and identifying efficient estimators. The bound is false: a regular estimator has strictly smaller variance at a positive, bounded, correctly specified interior model. The associated optimality analysis cannot stand as written. Repair requires a coupled joint-information calculation and revised instrument/efficiency analysis, rather than changing a sign, constant, or index. In particular, the claim that optimal weighting of only the original linear-feature moments generally suffices needs revision. This invalidates an advertised information-bound and optimality contribution and warrants rejection of the paper as written, even though its unrestricted DRL contribution may survive. No additional subsidiary defects are combined to reach this severity judgment.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Theorem 22 to its appendix proof, the asserted simplification of joint conditional-moment information into a backward variance recurrence appeared to discard information about later parameters present in earlier moment restrictions.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original model definitions and Theorem 22 on PDF pages 1–3 and 25–26 and its proof on page 62; inspected full rendered pages 25, 26, and 62. Constructed the positive two-period model above and evaluated its full five-parameter Fisher information with exact rational arithmetic. Independently rederived the estimating functions, covariance, Jacobian, attainable one-step variance, and all five score cross-moments. Two further interior models also have printed bounds strictly larger than attainable variances: `.2772794794` versus `.2462244533`, and `.2745780139` versus `.2406337196`.

Reproduction code:

Exact outputs and independent assessment:

Both standalone exact checks completed with actual exit code zero and substantive success outputs. The full paper and appendices were reviewed after identifying the issue. All five blobs of the linked prepublication repository were authenticated and inspected, and bounded authored-source runs were performed. Missing final experimental arrays, Mountain Car code, environment modules, and learned CliffWalking Q-table prevent replication of the published empirical tables; those limits are separate from this exact theoretical counterexample.

**Confidence.** High. The witness satisfies the printed assumptions, has 16 strictly positive atoms, and produces a strict inequality between exact rational variances. Independent conditional-moment and full-likelihood calculations agree, including every unknown nuisance score. The demonstrated false claim is the restricted-q efficiency bound and its dependent optimality analysis; the report makes no claim that all of the paper's other theory or empirical conclusions are false.

Estimating the weights contributes no first-order drift: derivatives of the weights multiply residuals whose conditional means are zero. Consequently the value estimator has asymptotic variance

(J^(-1))_00 = (D+C_1)/(C(D+C_1)-B^2)
             = 7341/16256 ≈ 0.4515871062992
             < 56175/123008.

Thus an explicit regular estimator beats the paper's claimed efficiency lower bound under its own assumptions.

A separate exact likelihood calculation checks all nuisance directions. Put \(U=(r_{0}-a_{x})/(a_{x}(1-a_{x}))\), \(W=(r_{1}-b_{1}g_{z})/(b_{1}g_{z}(1-b_{1}g_{z}))\), and \(Z=(z-u_{x})/(u_{x}(1-u_{x}))\). The score for the five unknown parameters is

S = (U, -m_x U+g_z W,
     1{x=0}(Z-b_1 U), 1{x=1}(Z-b_1 U),
     (x-p)/(p(1-p))).

Exact summation over the 16 atoms gives a nonsingular full Fisher matrix whose inverse's \((0,0)\) entry is \(\frac{7341}{16256}\). The influence function from the estimating functions has mean zero, variance \(\frac{7341}{16256}\), and exact score cross-moments \((1,0,0,0,0)\). Both transition parameters and the initial-state nuisance are therefore accounted for. This is not an argument based only on a smaller model with known nuisances, or on nonregular superefficiency.

The failed algebra is visible in the proof on page 62. The joint information contains the \(D\) term. Eliminating the first parameter gives the Schur complement \(C_{1}+D-B^{2}/C\), rather than \(C_{1}\). Since \(m_{x}\) varies, \(D-B^{2}/C>0\): earlier conditional moments provide information about the later q-parameter that a change in the earlier intercept cannot absorb. Orthogonality of the residual innovations does not remove that information. The same error makes the printed terminal-parameter bound \(A_{1}=1/C_{1}\) too large.

Reason for rejection. The paper explicitly presents restricted-q efficiency limits as a formal contribution, illustrates these models in Figure 3, and dedicates Sections 4.1–4.2 to deriving the bounds and identifying efficient estimators. The bound is false: a regular estimator has strictly smaller variance at a positive, bounded, correctly specified interior model. The associated optimality analysis cannot stand as written. Repair requires a coupled joint-information calculation and revised instrument/efficiency analysis, rather than changing a sign, constant, or index. In particular, the claim that optimal weighting of only the original linear-feature moments generally suffices needs revision. This invalidates an advertised information-bound and optimality contribution and warrants rejection of the paper as written, even though its unrestricted DRL contribution may survive. No additional subsidiary defects are combined to reach this severity judgment.

Discovery method. While tracing Theorem 22 to its appendix proof, the asserted simplification of joint conditional-moment information into a backward variance recurrence appeared to discard information about later parameters present in earlier moment restrictions.

Verification method. Rechecked the original model definitions and Theorem 22 on PDF pages 1–3 and 25–26 and its proof on page 62; inspected full rendered pages 25, 26, and 62. Constructed the positive two-period model above and evaluated its full five-parameter Fisher information with exact rational arithmetic. Independently rederived the estimating functions, covariance, Jacobian, attainable one-step variance, and all five score cross-moments. Two further interior models also have printed bounds strictly larger than attainable variances: \(.2772794794\) versus \(.2462244533\), and \(.2745780139\) versus \(.2406337196\).
